## 12.2 FIRST MOMENTS

Let us define a useful utility function, which for a given numerical array returns a table with overview statistics. First, we define statistics used in the function itself and then implement it as one compact suite. Data are denoted as ![images](images/c12-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>, where subset of ![images](images/c12-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> observations are non-missing, ![images](images/c12-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

   

#### *Sample mean*

The sample mean is defined as:

(12.5)![equation](images/c12-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>N</mi> </mfrac> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math>  

#### *Sample standard deviation*

The sample standard deviation is defined as:

(12.6)![equation](images/c12-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <msqrt> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#956;</mi> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </msqrt> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math>  

#### *Sample skewness*

The sample skewness is defined as:

(12.7)![equation](images/c12-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>S</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <msqrt> <mi>N</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mfenced> </msqrt> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <mfrac> <mrow> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>N</mi> </mfrac> <msubsup> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </msubsup> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#956;</mi> </mfenced> <mn>3</mn> </msup> </mrow> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <msubsup> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </msubsup> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#956;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mfenced> <mrow> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>2</mn> </mrow> </msup> </mfrac> </mrow> </math> 

where for distributions that are unimodal and not heavy tailed suggests that distribution with negative skew is skewed to the left while positive skew is skewed to the right. For heavy-tailed distribution, the rule cannot be used.

 

#### *Sample kurtosis*

The sample kurtosis is defined as:

(12.8)![equation](images/c12-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>K</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>N</mi> </mfrac> <msubsup> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </msubsup> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#956;</mi> </mfenced> <mn>4</mn> </msup> </mrow> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <msubsup> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </msubsup> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#956;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mfrac> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>3</mn> </mrow> </math> 

and can be used to assess the heavy tails of the data. If the value is positive, the data are said to be leptokurtic, i.e. heavy-tailed relative to Gaussian distributions, while if value is negative, the data are said to be platykurtic, i.e. thin-tailed relative to Gaussian distribution.

 

#### *Min*

The minimum of the sample is derived from non-empty values.

 

#### *Max*

The maximum of the sample is derived from non-empty values.

 

#### *Number of observations*

The number of observations corresponds to ![images](images/c12-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>.

 

#### *Missing observations*

The number of missing observations is ![images](images/c12-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>.

The suite of tools is implemented in function `overviewStats`:

![](images/c12-gra-0012.png)

We run the example query using the `data` we have defined for histograms:

![](images/c12-gra-0013.png)

which gives the following table:

![](images/c12-gra-0014.png)

Data are slightly skewed to the left relative to its mean. Further, data are platykurtic, which naturally follows from the fact that the data come from the uniform distribution with no tails.

 

## 12.3 HYPOTHESIS TESTING

In this section, we focus on several useful routines, which are likely needed at the initial stage of data exploration. In such a stage, we need to review data quantitatively. Tests like comparing means of two samples, sign test or correlation between observations should be performed. We aim to provide tools which go beyond the usual comparison of two numbers. We aspire to encourage readers to formulate such comparison as tests and provide tools to evaluate such tests.

 

### 12.3.1 Normal ![images](images/c12-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values

For many statistics, we obtain a value which is asymptotically distributed as ![images](images/c12-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>. The question is how to form a statistical test to assess the statistical validity of the underlying test. Many tests result in statistics, which are in turn tested either against being different from zero or having a particular sign.

In this section, we focus on such test statistics. Generically, such statistics are under the null hypothesis distribution and standard normal variable. To assess whether we can reject the null hypothesis, we have to decide how likely it is for a given realised value to come from the standard normal distribution. To achieve this objective, we convert the normally distributed statistics into the ![images](images/c12-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value of a two-sided test numerically using the lookup table. This will allow us to statistically decide whether the statistics can likely come – with given confidence – from the standard normal distribution, i.e. implying that the null hypothesis cannot be rejected.

In order to calculate the ![images](images/c12-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value, we need to be able to calculate:

(12.9)![equation](images/c12-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

with![images](images/c12-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi></mrow></math> being the cumulative distribution function of ![images](images/c12-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> distribution. More importantly, we need to calculate the inverse cumulative distribution function, or,

(12.10)![equation](images/c12-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>x</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>p</mi> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

We use a table of values to map the function of ![images](images/c12-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> as expressed in the previous display. The approach is suitable for assessing the significance of a statistical test as we are often interested in several values only corresponding to normal confidence levels. Typical values of choice found in the literature are ![images](images/c12-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>0.1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>.

We define a table:

![](images/c12-gra-0015.png)

where we have not listed the full map in the code snippet. Value `(0.0005;3.29052673149190)` denotes that probability to observe ![images](images/c12-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>3.29052673149190</mn></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.0005</mn></mrow></math>, or, equivalently, ![images](images/c12-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>3.29052673149190</mn></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0.0005</mn></mrow></math>. For a two-sided test, we use ![images](images/c12-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>3.29052673149190</mn></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow></math>. Keep in mind that we have defined the table within the name space of the book as it is a key and static object for the analysis.

We can thus use the table `normTable` to approximate ![images](images/c12-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>. In particular, the algorithm to approximate the cumulative distribution function can proceed for a given non-negative ![images](images/c12-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> as follows. Go through the list of `normTable` element by element. Every element is a pair of numbers. Find the maximum second element such that it is smaller than ![images](images/c12-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>. Report corresponding first element. The cumulative distribution function is then ![images](images/c12-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math> the value returned by the provided algorithm. For negative values, we can proceed the same way by using ![images](images/c12-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></math> and not performing ![images](images/c12-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math> operation at the end.

When applied for finding the confidence level of the given statistics, this approach is conservative, as it gives lower bound on the significance level. This is a good practice when we approximate distributions for assessing the test. In addition, if `normTable` will contain values for ![images](images/c12-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>0.1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, only, this will perform the usual econometric evaluation of the test.

Let us implement three functions, which perform the appropriate ![images](images/c12-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value calculation for two-sided test, one-sided test for a null hypothesis ![images](images/c12-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> (“left”), and one-sided test for null hypothesis ![images](images/c12-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> (“right”):

![](images/c12-gra-0016.png)

We test the two-sided test on values:

![](images/c12-gra-0017.png)![](images/c12-gra-0018.png)![](images/c12-gra-0019.png)![](images/c12-gra-0020.png)![](images/c12-gra-0021.png)![](images/c12-gra-0022.png)

The pathological cases of smallest possible input 0 as well as large value are providing a valid outcome.

Further, the one-sided tests are given as:

![](images/c12-gra-0023.png)

giving results:

![](images/c12-gra-0024.png)![](images/c12-gra-0025.png)![](images/c12-gra-0026.png)![](images/c12-gra-0027.png)

and, finally, the third version of the test:

![](images/c12-gra-0028.png)

gives on the provided examples:

![](images/c12-gra-0029.png)![](images/c12-gra-0030.png)![](images/c12-gra-0031.png)![](images/c12-gra-0032.png)

We can thus obtain the ![images](images/c12-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value for a given value of statistics with ![images](images/c12-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> asymptotic distribution.

 

### 12.3.2 Correlation

The basic tool we have at our disposal to assess the dependence between two variables ![images](images/c12-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> is a correlation, or Pearson correlation, denoted as ![images](images/c12-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>&#961;</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Correlation is defined as the covariance of two random variables normalised by their respective variances:

(12.11)![equation](images/c12-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mrow> <mi>X</mi> <mi>Y</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>c</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>v</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Y</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mi>X</mi> </msub> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mi>Y</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></math> stands for covariance, and ![images](images/c12-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></math> stands for a square root of the variance of ![images](images/c12-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>, respectively. Correlation is a definite quantity if the variance for both random variables exists.

Correlation is bounded to range ![images](images/c12-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>, where values close to 1 suggest perfect correlation, values close to ![images](images/c12-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> imply that variables are anti-correlated, while uncorrelated variables have correlation close to zero. The obvious null hypothesis to test is:

*   ![images](images/c12-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: Two random variables are uncorrelated.
*   ![images](images/c12-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math>: Two random variables are correlated.

Let us stress that we have formulated the alternative hypothesis in rather plain English. The proper formulation should be that we reject the null hypothesis.

In order to assess this hypothesis in statistical terms, we assume that we have two samples ![images](images/c12-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>y</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math>, two draws of random variables ![images](images/c12-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>, respectively, and we have calculated the sample correlation ![images](images/c12-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math>. We assume that true correlation is ![images](images/c12-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>. We centre the correlation around the true value and normalise it by the estimate of its standard error:

(12.12)![equation](images/c12-math-0012.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mi>&#961;</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> <msub> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mi>&#961;</mi> </msub> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> <msqrt> <mfrac> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> </msqrt> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

This forms a statistic for which we need to know the asymptotic distribution. Its general form is rather complex. Luckily, the statistic ![images](images/c12-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></math> can be simplified for ![images](images/c12-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>:

(12.13)![equation](images/c12-math-0013.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mi>&#961;</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#961;</mi> <msqrt> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> </msqrt> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The centred and normalised correlation coefficient ![images](images/c12-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></math> follows distribution ![images](images/c12-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. We can thus use the statistics to form the following hypotheses:

*   ![images](images/c12-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: Two random variables have zero/non-negative/non-positive correlation.
*   ![images](images/c12-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math>: Two random variables have non-zero/positive/negative correlation.

The test is assessed by calculating ![images](images/c12-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></math> and comparing ![images](images/c12-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c12-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, respectively. When the corresponding inequality is satisfied, we can reject the null hypothesis, where ![images](images/c12-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is a corresponding critical value.

 

#### *12.3.2.1 Implementation*

The correlation is already implemented within `q` under the verb `cor`. Let us illustrate its use:

![](images/c12-gra-0033.png)![](images/c12-gra-0034.png)

The result shows a value different from 0, suggesting positive correlation. In order to test it, we have to calculate the statistic ![images](images/c12-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></math>. We do that in function `tStatsCorr`, which has two arguments: calculated correlation and size of the sample (the true correlation under the null hypothesis is by definition ![images](images/c12-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>):

![](images/c12-gra-0035.png)

Let us test the hypothesis (two-sided) that the correlation observed above is different from 0. First, we calculate the statistic ![images](images/c12-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></math>:

![](images/c12-gra-0036.png)![](images/c12-gra-0037.png)

The value is large. We assess its significance level against the normal asymptotic behaviour using a two-sided test:

![](images/c12-gra-0038.png)![](images/c12-gra-0039.png)

The result clearly shows that we can reject the null hypothesis of correlation being zero. The derived ![images](images/c12-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value is 0.001, which is in fact the lowest number in our lookup table and thus stands for any ![images](images/c12-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value smaller than or equal to 0.001.

 

### 12.3.3 ![images](images/c12-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </math>\-test: One Sample

Let us consider an independently drawn sample ![images](images/c12-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math> representing ![images](images/c12-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> draws of a random variable ![images](images/c12-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>, which has a population mean ![images](images/c12-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> and a standard deviation ![images](images/c12-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>. Our motivation is to form a hypothesis about the population mean inferred from the observed sample. The statistical procedure to achieve this objective is to use ![images](images/c12-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-test.

In general, ![images](images/c12-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-test is a statistical hypothesis test where the test statistics under the null hypothesis follow ![images](images/c12-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-distribution. ![images](images/c12-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-distribution is parameterised by one parameter ![images](images/c12-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, denoted as degrees of freedom. For ![images](images/c12-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8599;</mo></mrow></math>, the distribution converges to a normal distribution, while for ![images](images/c12-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> small, the distribution is fat-tailed.

Example of such a test statistic is the following variable:

(12.14)![equation](images/c12-math-0014.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#956;</mi> </mrow> <mfrac> <mi>&#963;</mi> <msqrt> <mi>N</mi> </msqrt> </mfrac> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math> is the sample average. The statistic under the null hypothesis is distributed as ![images](images/c12-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>; these can be used in the following statistical test about the population average:

*   ![images](images/c12-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The population mean is ![images](images/c12-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> (given the sample size ![images](images/c12-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> and population standard deviation ![images](images/c12-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>).
*   ![images](images/c12-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The population mean is different from ![images](images/c12-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>.

The test is inconvenient as it requires knowledge of a population standard deviation. This is, in practice, is hardly known and such an assumption in data analysis cannot be made. Fortunately, the ![images](images/c12-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-statistic can be modified such that we can replace knowledge of population standard deviation by its estimator:

(12.15)![equation](images/c12-math-0015.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>X</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#956;</mi> </mrow> <mi>s</mi> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> is the standard deviation of the mean defined as:

(12.16)![equation](images/c12-math-0016.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>s</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <msqrt> <mi>N</mi> </msqrt> </mfrac> <msqrt> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> </mfenced> </msqrt> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Note that there is a factor ![images](images/c12-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msqrt><mi>N</mi></msqrt></mrow></math> in front of the square root.

The adjusted statistic ![images](images/c12-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> follows ![images](images/c12-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. The estimator of the standard deviation of the mean cost us one degree of freedom. The word “cost” is used as it worsens the asymptotic behaviour and makes the statistics further from the normal distribution.

We can form the following hypotheses to test using the ![images](images/c12-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> statistic:

*   ![images](images/c12-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The population mean is equal/smaller or equal/larger or equal to ![images](images/c12-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>, given the sample size ![images](images/c12-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>.
*   ![images](images/c12-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The population mean is different/larger/smaller relative to ![images](images/c12-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>.

The three tests, i.e. a two-sided test and two one-sided tests, can be assessed as follows: we reject the null if ![images](images/c12-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c12-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, respectively. The critical value ![images](images/c12-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> depends on the significance level. In the subsequent part, we will assume the asymptotic limit holds and use the normal distribution to derive the critical values.

 

#### *12.3.3.1 Implementation*

The calculation of the ![images](images/c12-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> statistic is rather straightforward:

![](images/c12-gra-0040.png)

The input is the sample and the value of the mean we want to assess under the null hypothesis. The function returns the statistics. The assessment of the test is done using the function which maps the statistics to the corresponding ![images](images/c12-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value for a given test set- up. In this example, we use the two-sided test for ![images](images/c12-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> being equal to 0.45. The value of the statistic can be calculated as:

![](images/c12-gra-0041.png)![](images/c12-gra-0042.png)

while the map to the corresponding ![images](images/c12-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value is:

![](images/c12-gra-0043.png)![](images/c12-gra-0044.png)

The ![images](images/c12-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value of the test is ![images](images/c12-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, which suggests that we may reject the null hypothesis of mean being equal to 0.45 at ![images](images/c12-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> confidence level. Even though the true mean is 0.5, and the value tested 0.45 is smaller by ![images](images/c12-i0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, the size of the sample prevents us from rejecting the null and inclines towards the difference confidently.

 

### 12.3.4 ![images](images/c12-i0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </math>\-test: Two Samples

In the previous test, we tested one sample against a static mean value. In practice, we may want to test two samples that have the same mean. Let us consider an independently drawn sample ![images](images/c12-i0123.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math> representing ![images](images/c12-i0124.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> draws of a random variable ![images](images/c12-i0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>, which has a population mean ![images](images/c12-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and a standard deviation ![images](images/c12-i0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math>, and independently drawn sample ![images](images/c12-i0128.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>y</mi><mi>M</mi></msub></mrow></math> representing ![images](images/c12-i0129.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> draws of a random variable ![images](images/c12-i0130.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>, which has a population mean ![images](images/c12-i0131.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> and a standard deviation ![images](images/c12-i0132.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>.

The hypothesis to be tested is of the form:

*   ![images](images/c12-i0133.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The population means are equal, ![images](images/c12-i0134.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>.
*   ![images](images/c12-i0135.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The population means are different.

The test is done by constructing a suitable test statistic. The form of the statistic depends on the assumptions imposed on ![images](images/c12-i0136.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0137.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c12-i0138.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0139.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>, respectively. The stronger the assumptions, the closer to asymptotic behaviour but more prone to model error. In this text, we focus on the least restricted version of the two-sample ![images](images/c12-i0140.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-statistic, also known as Welch's test. In such a case, there is no assumption imposed on the relationship between ![images](images/c12-i0141.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0142.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c12-i0143.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0144.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>. The Welch ![images](images/c12-i0145.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>t</mi><mi>W</mi></msub></mrow></math> statistic is defined as:

(12.17)![equation](images/c12-math-0017.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>t</mi> <mi>W</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi>y</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>s</mi> <mi>W</mi> </msub> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0146.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>s</mi><mi>W</mi></msub></mrow></math> is defined as:

(12.18)![equation](images/c12-math-0018.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>s</mi> <mi>W</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msqrt> <mfrac> <mrow> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <msubsup> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mi>N</mi> </msubsup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </mfrac> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mi>M</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <msubsup> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mi>M</mi> </msubsup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi>y</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>M</mi> </mfrac> </msqrt> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The Welch's ![images](images/c12-i0147.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>t</mi><mi>W</mi></msub></mrow></math> statistic follows under the null hypothesis ![images](images/c12-i0148.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>t</mi><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub></msub></mrow></math>, where the number of degrees of freedom is:

(12.19)![equation](images/c12-math-0019.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>W</mi> <mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mi>f</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mfrac> <msubsup> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mi>N</mi> </mfrac> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <msubsup> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mn>2</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mi>M</mi> </mfrac> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mrow> <mfrac> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msubsup> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msubsup> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mn>2</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mrow> <mi>M</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfrac> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

We can again form following hypotheses to test using the ![images](images/c12-i0149.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>t</mi><mi>W</mi></msub></mrow></math> statistic:

*   ![images](images/c12-i0150.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The population mean ![images](images/c12-i0151.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> is equal/smaller or equal/larger or equal to population mean ![images](images/c12-i0152.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>.
*   ![images](images/c12-i0153.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The population mean ![images](images/c12-i0154.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> is different/larger/smaller to population mean ![images](images/c12-i0155.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>.

The three tests, i.e. the two-sided test and two one-sided tests, can be assessed as in the previous case. We reject the null if ![images](images/c12-i0156.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>t</mi><mi>W</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0157.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>t</mi><mi>W</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c12-i0158.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>t</mi><mi>W</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, respectively. The critical value ![images](images/c12-i0159.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></math> depends on the significance level. In the test, we will assume the asymptotic behaviour and consider the critical values based on a normal distribution.

 

#### *12.3.4.1 Implementation*

The calculation of the ![images](images/c12-i0160.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>t</mi><mi>W</mi></msub></mrow></math> statistic is given as:

![](images/c12-gra-0045.png)

We test the function using two samples with the same mean but different size and variance:

![](images/c12-gra-0046.png)![](images/c12-gra-0047.png)

The value is then transformed into the corresponding ![images](images/c12-i0161.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value using the normal distribution:

![](images/c12-gra-0048.png)![](images/c12-gra-0049.png)

The result suggests that we cannot reject the null hypothesis and we thus conclude that two samples have the same mean as implied by the alternative hypothesis.

 

### 12.3.5 Sign Test

The sign test is a non-parametric test to assess the statistical difference between pairs of observations drawn from two related populations. For example, consider a set of investors who invest every month and report their PnL. The investors can subscribe to the advisory service. If the general market conditions remain the same, the effect of the advisory service can be estimated by comparing the performance – the PnL – before and after the advisory service was obtained for a sample of investors. If the effect of the advisory service is not material, then PnL before the advisory service and PnL after it comes for every investor from the same distribution. Since every investor can have a different distribution of PnL – different mean, sigma, or kurtosis, for example – we cannot compare PnL across investors. Instead, we should assess the statistical properties of the difference of the PnL before/after across the sample. In particular, if the effect of the advisory effect is irrelevant, the distribution of differences should be symmetric around zero. On the other hand, if the difference is positive/negative, the advisory effect is correspondingly negative/positive.

Let us formulate the sign test explicitly: consider two related populations, ![images](images/c12-i0162.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0163.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>, and two related samples of pair draws, ![images](images/c12-i0164.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c12-i0165.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>. Each population is continuous, and the two populations are ordinal, i.e. we can order any pair ![images](images/c12-i0166.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>. We further denote the order as inequality between ![images](images/c12-i0167.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0168.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. For the sake of simplicity, we assume that ![images](images/c12-i0169.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is not possible (with probability 0), and discuss ties later in subsequent tests. Further, every two draws of pairs are independent of each other.

The ordinal variables may not be necessarily numeric. Consider for example a string of characters, which is not numeric, but we can easily sort a set of string alphabetically. We can always characterise the outcome of inequality numerically, in any case. We define the difference between ![images](images/c12-i0170.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0171.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> as ![images](images/c12-i0172.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> for numerical variables while for non-numerical variables the difference can be defined as:

(12.20)![equation](images/c12-math-0020.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#948;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#62;</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mtext>otherwise</mtext> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> 

Then, the basic formulation of the sign test states:

*   ![images](images/c12-i0173.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The difference between ![images](images/c12-i0174.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0175.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0176.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, has the same probability to be positive as negative.
*   ![images](images/c12-i0177.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The difference between ![images](images/c12-i0178.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0179.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is skewed towards positive or negative values.

Alternatively, we can formulate one-sided tests:

*   ![images](images/c12-i0180.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The difference between ![images](images/c12-i0181.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0182.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0183.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, is more likely to be positive/negative.
*   ![images](images/c12-i0184.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The difference between ![images](images/c12-i0185.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0186.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is either equally distributed for positive and negative values, or skewed towards negative/positive values.

Since the test is concerned with the sign, we can encode the difference as:

(12.21)![equation](images/c12-math-0021.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>z</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#952;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>&#948;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0187.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> is a Heaviside step function. For the purpose of the test, the draws with the same value, ![images](images/c12-i0188.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, are discarded.

Under the null hypothesis, the sample of sign variables ![images](images/c12-i0189.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is drawn from the binomial distribution with ![images](images/c12-i0190.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow></math>. The (relevant) properties of the binomial distribution ![images](images/c12-i0191.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mspace width="0.1em"/><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>N</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>p</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> can be summarised as follows:

*   Mean of the sum: ![images](images/c12-i0192.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>.
*   Variance of the sum: ![images](images/c12-i0193.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi>p</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>.

The binomial distribution can be approximated by the normal distribution ![images](images/c12-i0194.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfenced></mrow></math> for reasonably large ![images](images/c12-i0195.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>. In general, a population larger than 30 observations can be approximated by the normal distribution. This fact can be used to perform tests of the null hypothesis for symmetrically distributed differences ![images](images/c12-i0196.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

When the sample is small the normal distribution cannot be used and we have to calculate the properties of the probability distribution function explicitly. Namely, the probability density function of the binomial distribution is defined as:

(12.22)![equation](images/c12-math-0022.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>f</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>N</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mi>p</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mfrac linethickness="0"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>n</mi> </mfrac> </mfenced> <msup> <mi>p</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msup> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>p</mi> </mfenced> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>n</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

with the binomial number ![images](images/c12-i0197.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mfrac linethickness="0"><mi>N</mi><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mfenced></mrow></math> defined as

(12.23)![equation](images/c12-math-0023.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mfrac linethickness="0"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>n</mi> </mfrac> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>!</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>!</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> <mo>!</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

We can use the knowledge of the binomial probability distribution function to calculate the probability to observe ![images](images/c12-i0198.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> cases of ![images](images/c12-i0199.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> in the sample of ![images](images/c12-i0200.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> observations under the null hypothesis of ![images](images/c12-i0201.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow></math>. Besides, we can use the binomial probability to calculate the ![images](images/c12-i0202.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values for one-sided and two-sided tests, respectively. For example, for a one-sided test of observing ![images](images/c12-i0203.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> less frequently than ![images](images/c12-i0204.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> given we have observed ![images](images/c12-i0205.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> instances with ![images](images/c12-i0206.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> out of ![images](images/c12-i0207.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> cases, we calculate:

(12.24)![equation](images/c12-math-0024.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <mi>p</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>f</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>N</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0.5</mn> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The cumulative probability gives the likelihood to observe more extreme outcomes when the null of equal probabilities for both types ![images](images/c12-i0208.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0209.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> holds. We can proceed analogously for the inverted one-sided test and/or two-sided test.

  

#### *Example*

Let us continue with the example of advisory service and investors. Consider the case where there are 10 investors who subscribed to the advisory service and 9 of them have shown improved PnL after the subscription to advisory service. The result shows in plain terms improvement, but is this improvement statistically significant? Let us formulate the test as two-sided. In such a case, we need to calculate probability for events as extreme as the outcome we have recorded or even more extreme. Thus, we need to calculate ![images](images/c12-i0210.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> for ![images](images/c12-i0211.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>:

(12.25) ![equation](images/c12-math-0025.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left center right"> <mtr> <mtd class="eqnarray-1"> <mi>P</mi> </mtd> <mtd class="eqnarray-2"> <mo>=</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>f</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>10</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0.5</mn> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>f</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>10</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0.5</mn> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>f</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>9</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>10</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0.5</mn> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>f</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>10</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>10</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0.5</mn> </mfenced> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0.00098</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mn>0.0097</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mn>0.0097</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mn>0.00098</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="eqnarray-1"/> <mtd class="eqnarray-2"> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0.02136</mn> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

The value is below ![images](images/c12-i0212.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, which suggests a high probability that positive outcome of investors is not a statistical coincidence. We are in fact interested in a one-sided test where null is that investors' performance is not improved, tested against the null of being improved (in plain English, the alternative is that we reject the null). The probability for the extreme outcome is 0.01063.
