#### *12.3.5.2 Median Test*

The sign test can be used as the test for the median against a certain threshold value. Namely, for a sample of data ![images](images/c12-i0221.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0222.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>, we define a constant sample, ![images](images/c12-i0223.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0224.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>. Then, a sign test applied on pairs of sample points ![images](images/c12-i0225.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> tests the following hypothesis:

*   ![images](images/c12-i0226.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The median of the population from which ![images](images/c12-i0227.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is drawn is ![images](images/c12-i0228.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math>.
*   ![images](images/c12-i0229.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The median is different from ![images](images/c12-i0230.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math>.

First, the median is the value, which separates the higher half of the sample from the lower one. Thus, if we calculate the difference between the median and all the values in the sample, we get an equal number of positive and negative numbers. This is the nature of the sign test, and that is why we can quickly turn the sign test into the median test. The median test is considered by default to be a two-sided test. Further, it is clear that the median value as defined above is not unique for finite samples.

Further, we analyse the statistical power of the test given our sample size. We calculate the ![images](images/c12-i0231.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value of the median test for a range of tested median values `0.01 * til 101`. [Figure 12.4](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0004) depicts the ![images](images/c12-i0232.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values against the tested median values. Also, the plot contains a constant horizontal line at 0.05, which stands for statistical significance. All the cases when ![images](images/c12-i0233.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values are above the line say that we cannot reject the null that the median of the array is given a tested value. This is true for values within ![images](images/c12-i0234.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mn>0.41</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.55</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> range, which shows the accuracy of our test – given we know the true median being 0.5. The data for the figure has been prepared as:

![](images/c12-gra-0065.png)![FIGURE 12.4 Median test: images-value as a function of tested value](images/c12f004.png)

[**FIGURE 12.4**](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0004) Median test: ![images](images/c12-i0235.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value as a function of tested value

 

### 12.3.6 Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test

Wilcoxon signed-rank test is a paired difference test which is used to test the null hypothesis that for two related samples, their population mean ranks differ. It is an alternative for paired ![images](images/c12-i0236.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-tests which cannot be assumed to be normally distributed. The test is used for paired samples, i.e. samples which are related, or repeated draws. The observations in pairs come from the same distribution, we can order the pair, and each pair is randomly and independently drawn. The Wilcoxon test states the following null and alternative hypotheses:

*   ![images](images/c12-i0237.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The difference within the pair follows a symmetric distribution centred around zero.
*   ![images](images/c12-i0238.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The difference within the pair does not follow a symmetric distribution centred around zero.

Consider the sample with related pairs ![images](images/c12-i0239.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c12-i0240.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>. Define the difference within ![images](images/c12-i0241.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th pair as ![images](images/c12-i0242.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> and the sign of the difference ![images](images/c12-i0243.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>signum</mtext><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Further, before we construct Wilcoxon statistics, we filter out all cases with ![images](images/c12-i0244.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Let us denote the subsample without ties as ![images](images/c12-i0245.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c12-i0246.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0247.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math>.

Then, we calculate the Wilcoxon statistics as:

(12.26)![equation](images/c12-math-0026.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>W</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mi>i</mi> <msup> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </munderover> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#183;</mo> <msub> <mi>r</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0248.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the rank of the ![images](images/c12-i0249.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th pair, where differences have been sorted based on the absolute value of their difference, ![images](images/c12-i0250.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, with ties getting the average rank of the respective group.

The Wilcoxon statistic, ![images](images/c12-i0251.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math>, has under the null hypothesis the underlying distribution with mean 0 and variance:

(12.27)![equation](images/c12-math-0027.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mi>W</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <msqrt> <mfrac> <mrow> <msup> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mfenced> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>2</mn> <mo>&#183;</mo> <msup> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mfenced> </mrow> <mn>6</mn> </mfrac> </msqrt> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

For small samples, the reader has to consult with Wilcoxon (1950) to find critical values. We reject the null hypothesis (of a two-sided test) if ![images](images/c12-i0252.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c12-i0253.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> being critical value at a given confidence level.

For ![images](images/c12-i0254.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> large, the distribution of the ![images](images/c12-i0255.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> statistics follows a normal distribution. If we normalise ![images](images/c12-i0256.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> by its standard deviation ![images](images/c12-i0257.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>W</mi></msub></mrow></math>, we get ![images](images/c12-i0258.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>W</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi>N</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>. In such a case, we can use critical values from a standard normal distribution.

The Wilcoxon test is implemented in function `wilcoxonTest`. It accepts two arrays `x1` and `x2`, respectively, corresponding to ![images](images/c12-i0259.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0260.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>. The function calculates several outcomes arranged in the dictionary: Wilcoxon statistic ![images](images/c12-i0261.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math>, size of sample, standard deviation ![images](images/c12-i0262.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>W</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and normalized Wilcoxon statistic ![images](images/c12-i0263.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>W</mi></msub></mrow></math>:

![](images/c12-gra-0066.png)

Let us illustrate the functionality on two unrelated vectors:

![](images/c12-gra-0067.png)![](images/c12-gra-0068.png)

The test itself does not produce the ![images](images/c12-i0264.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value; it is our responsibility to assess the validity of the test. For that purpose, we can utilise `pValueTwoSided` function to obtain the ![images](images/c12-i0265.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value estimate:

![](images/c12-gra-0069.png)![](images/c12-gra-0070.png)

The test shows that we cannot reject the null at any significance level below 0.13, suggesting that we cannot reject the null hypothesis meaning, put plainly, that they have the same mean.

 

### 12.3.7 Rank Correlation and Somers' ![images](images/c12-i0266.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>

Previously mentioned measures aimed to work with numerical variables, i.e. cardinal numbers where we can sort and measure the difference between them. We have tacitly assumed to work with float types. In this section, we focus on ordinal variables and define some useful metrics to assess some hypothesis about them. Since for ordinal variables the notion of mean does not make much sense – though, we can still work with median – we focus our attention on the sorting of variables and ranking them.

Let us assume we have two ordinal variables ![images](images/c12-i0267.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0268.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>; for each of them we observe sample of size ![images](images/c12-i0269.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>, i.e. ![images](images/c12-i0270.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math>![images](images/c12-i0271.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>y</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Further, a pair ![images](images/c12-i0272.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> corresponds to the ![images](images/c12-i0273.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th draw of a pair ![images](images/c12-i0274.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>.

Somers' ![images](images/c12-i0275.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is a measure of ordinal association between two random variables, see Somers (1962). It takes values ![images](images/c12-i0276.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8712;</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c12-i0277.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> corresponds to the case when all observed pairs of the variables disagree while 1 states for perfect agreement. The definition of the Somers' *D* is based on the notion of concordance. We say that two pairs ![images](images/c12-i0278.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0279.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> are concordant if the ranks of both elements agree, i.e., ![images](images/c12-i0280.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0281.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math>, or, ![images](images/c12-i0282.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0283.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math>. If the ranks disagree, i.e. ![images](images/c12-i0284.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0285.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math>, or, ![images](images/c12-i0286.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0287.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math>, we say that two pairs are discordant. If there is equality, ![images](images/c12-i0288.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> and/or ![images](images/c12-i0289.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math>, we say that pairs are neither concordant nor discordant.

Let us arrange two samples into pairs ![images](images/c12-i0290.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>y</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>. Further, consider all possible pairs of pairs, i.e. if we denote pair ![images](images/c12-i0291.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> as ![images](images/c12-i0292.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>, then all pairs of pairs are ![images](images/c12-i0293.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0294.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0295.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8230;</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0296.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0297.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8230;</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0298.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>. There are ![images](images/c12-i0299.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> such combinations. Denote the number of concordant pairs out of all pairs as ![images](images/c12-i0300.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>N</mi><mi>C</mi></msub></mrow></math> and the number of discordant pairs as ![images](images/c12-i0301.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

First, let us define Kendall's ![images](images/c12-i0302.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> rank correlation:

(12.28)![equation](images/c12-math-0028.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#964;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Y</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>C</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>D</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mfenced> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Kendall's ![images](images/c12-i0303.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> is ![images](images/c12-i0304.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8712;</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>.

Meaning of ![images](images/c12-i0305.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> is a measure of pairs within ![images](images/c12-i0306.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> with unequal numbers. We can then define Somers' ![images](images/c12-i0307.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>Y</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>X</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> as:

(12.29)![equation](images/c12-math-0029.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>D</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>Y</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mi>X</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#964;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Y</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#964;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>X</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where the definition says that ![images](images/c12-i0308.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>Y</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>X</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> is the difference in the number of concordant and discordant pairs normalised by the number of unequal pairs in ![images](images/c12-i0309.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>. The role of normalisation is for the case of mass points in the distribution of ![images](images/c12-i0310.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>. For a continuously distributed variable which does not have “![images](images/c12-i0311.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi></mrow></math>” function in its distribution, Somers' ![images](images/c12-i0312.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> and Kendall's ![images](images/c12-i0313.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> rank coincide. The difference between the two is mainly for discrete observations.

Kendall's ![images](images/c12-i0314.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> rank correlation is symmetric while Somers' ![images](images/c12-i0315.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is asymmetric due to the normalisation factor. This is apparent for the case when one of the variables has mass points while the other one is continuously distributed. The distributions with mass points are a particular focus when Somers' ![images](images/c12-i0316.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is being used.

There is a further simplified formula for the case where ![images](images/c12-i0317.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> is discrete and ![images](images/c12-i0318.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> is binary. In such a case, Somers' ![images](images/c12-i0319.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> can be expressed as:

(12.30)![equation](images/c12-math-0030.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>D</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>Y</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mi>X</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>C</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>D</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>C</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>D</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0320.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>N</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the number of neither concordant nor discordant pairs with ![images](images/c12-i0321.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> while ![images](images/c12-i0322.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

Somers' ![images](images/c12-i0323.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is being used for regression where the dependent variable is binary or discrete while the independent variable can be of any type. Alternatively, Somers' ![images](images/c12-i0324.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> can be used to evaluate the performance of classification models, i.e. to assign the degree of association between model and true values.

Finally, let us complement the definitions of the rank correlations by Kruskal's ![images](images/c12-i0325.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math>. It is another coefficient measuring the similarity of ordering of the data for a pair of ordinal variables; see Goodman and Kruskal (1954). The ![images](images/c12-i0326.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> coefficient is defined as:

(12.31)![equation](images/c12-math-0031.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>C</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>D</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>C</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>D</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0327.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>N</mi><mi>C</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0328.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow></math> stand for a number of concordant and discordant pairs, respectively. Kruskal's ![images](images/c12-i0329.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> ranges ![images](images/c12-i0330.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8712;</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>. When there is no association between the two random variables, the ![images](images/c12-i0331.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> is close to 0.

Somers' ![images](images/c12-i0332.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>, Kendall's ![images](images/c12-i0333.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math>, and Kurskal's ![images](images/c12-i0334.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> are presented as descriptive statistics. In order to use them in the form of a test, we have two options. The first option is to calculate the small sample distribution of given statistics. Methods like bootstrap can be used. In such a case, we simulate a number of samples under the null hypothesis and evaluate the statistics for every simulation. Then, we collect the distribution of the statistics and create critical values based on the simulated distributions.

Alternatively, we may seek the analytic distributions of the test statistics. Its form may not be straightforward, and sometimes the analytic manipulations may be needed. Let us illustrate it for Kruskall's ![images](images/c12-i0335.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math>. We can define new statistics:

(12.32)![equation](images/c12-math-0032.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mi>&#947;</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#947;</mi> <msqrt> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>C</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>N</mi> <mi>D</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfrac> </msqrt> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where all variables have been defined so far, with ![images](images/c12-i0336.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> being a number of observations. The statistics follows ![images](images/c12-i0337.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. For large ![images](images/c12-i0338.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>, the normal distribution can be used. We can then form the hypothesis:

*   ![images](images/c12-i0339.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: There is no ordinal association between two random variables.
*   ![images](images/c12-i0340.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math>: There is an ordinal association between two random variables.

The one-sided/two-sided test can be run by comparing ![images](images/c12-i0341.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#947;</mi></msub></mrow></math> against critical values ![images](images/c12-i0342.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.

### 12.3.8 Multiple Hypothesis Testing

We finally mention an important problem which is crucial to be aware of when working with data. Let us imagine following setup: we have dependent variable ![images](images/c12-i0364.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> and 1000 features, ![images](images/c12-i0365.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>X</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>1</mn></mfenced></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>2</mn></mfenced></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>1000</mn></mfenced></msup></mrow></math>. Further, let us assume that there is no true correlation between the dependent variable and any of the features. We calculate correlation between the dependent variable and each feature, one by one, and assess the statistical hypothesis that the correlation is equal to 0.0 using ![images](images/c12-i0366.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></math>. What will be the result? Let us illustrate it right now numerically using 100 observations for every variable:

First, we generate the dependent variable:

![](images/c12-gra-0109.png)

and then generate 1000 features and assess it with the `tStatsCorr` function, where we calculate ![images](images/c12-i0367.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></math> based on correlation between `y` and new feature, and save it to an array:

![](images/c12-gra-0110.png)

[Figure 12.5](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0005) depicts the histogram of `draws` binned by `histBin` scheme with 40 bins. The values are distributed within a range spanning from ![images](images/c12-i0368.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2.87</mn></mrow></math> to 3.26. The histograms show a distribution similar in shape to the normal distribution. Importantly, it illustrates our assertion made previously that the statistic is a random variable drawn from a given distribution. This means that even under the null hypothesis, we find statistics with an extreme value given we made enough draws. Thus, if we perform hypothesis testing multiple times, we may end up with a false conclusion.

![FIGURE 12.5 Histogram of images for images realisations under the null hypothesis](images/c12f005.png)

[**FIGURE 12.5**](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0005) Histogram of ![images](images/c12-i0369.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></math> for ![images](images/c12-i0370.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1000</mn></mrow></math> realisations under the null hypothesis

The histogram has been produced as:

![](images/c12-gra-0111.png)

Let us further look on the outcome of the simulation exercise in more detail. The values of the ![images](images/c12-i0371.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></math> span interval ![images](images/c12-i0372.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>2.87</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3.26</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>, which suggests that we may reject the null hypothesis for some values. The ![images](images/c12-i0373.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values for the left tail of the distribution are:

![](images/c12-gra-0112.png)![](images/c12-gra-0113.png)

and for the right tail of the distribution, where we properly adjust the ![images](images/c12-i0374.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value to correspond to percentile:

![](images/c12-gra-0114.png)![](images/c12-gra-0115.png)

Given the value of 0.005 is the smallest value in the map between distribution value and ![images](images/c12-i0375.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values, we do realise very extreme values in the distribution. Every such observation on its own would correspond to an extreme value very unlikely to happen under the null hypothesis. How many such extreme values out of 1000 random realisations have exceeded the 0.05 confidence level to reject the null hypothesis? We can answer the question numerically as:

![](images/c12-gra-0116.png)![](images/c12-gra-0117.png)

Thus, 52 out of 1000 observations are rejected. This corresponds to statistical properties of the ![images](images/c12-i0376.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></math> under null being distributed according to the given distribution. This numerical exercise does not contradict the asymptotic behaviour, i.e. normal distribution, which may be seen as verification (not proof though) of the presented statements.

The previous example illustrates the fundamental issue with multiple testing. The problem occurs when we simultaneously test the number of hypotheses, or family of hypotheses. By the nature of statistical testing, we may infer an erroneous conclusion. The significance level used for testing individual hypotheses does not correspond to the significance level at the family level. If we want to impose the confidence level on the family level, we have to adjust the confidence level for every individual hypothesis.

The important concept to define is the family-wise error rate, or ![images](images/c12-i0377.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mi>W</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>, which stands for the probability to make at least one error, or Type-I error, in the family of tests. Let us assume that the family contains ![images](images/c12-i0378.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> individual tests. Further, each test is independent of the other tests. Let us assume that the probability of Type-I error for the individual test is ![images](images/c12-i0379.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Then, the probability of observing at least one test to show Type-I error, ![images](images/c12-i0380.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, is:

(12.33)![equation](images/c12-math-0033.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>m</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>l</mi> <mi>y</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>v</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>l</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mi>m</mi> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Let us illustrate it numerically for ![images](images/c12-i0381.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0382.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ranging from 1 to 100. [Figure 12.6](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0006) depicts the dependence of the family-wise error rate, ![images](images/c12-i0383.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, along the individual error rate, ![images](images/c12-i0384.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, which is constant. As the size of the family progresses, the family-wise error rate is increasing and reaching towards 1.0. For a family of size 100, the probability of at least one test to fail is 0.9940795, which is a value very close to 1.0. Data for the figure has been generated as:

![FIGURE 12.6 Individual error rate, images (constant dotted line), and family-wise error rate, images (increasing dotted line), as a function of the size of the family](images/c12f006.png)

[**FIGURE 12.6**](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0006) Individual error rate, ![images](images/c12-i0385.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (constant dotted line), and family-wise error rate, ![images](images/c12-i0386.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (increasing dotted line), as a function of the size of the family

![](images/c12-gra-0118.png)

In the case of individual tests to be perfectly correlated, we would observe:

(12.34)![equation](images/c12-math-0034.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>m</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>l</mi> <mi>y</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>v</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>l</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

irrespective of the size of the family ![images](images/c12-i0387.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>. If we cannot assume that tests are independent but not perfectly correlated, one often employs Boole's inequality (the union bound) – for any finite set of tests, the probability that at least one of the tests fails is no greater than the sum of the probabilities of the individual error rates:

(12.35)![equation](images/c12-math-0035.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>m</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>l</mi> <mi>y</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>m</mi> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>v</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>l</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

In order to resolve the discrepancy between individual error rates and family-wise error rate, we present three possible solutions on how to resolve it. In every case below, we assume a family of ![images](images/c12-i0388.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> tests, and null hypothesis being true for each of them. This is a weaker formulation of the problem. For every test, we measure statistics and obtain set of ![images](images/c12-i0389.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values, ![images](images/c12-i0390.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c12-i0391.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>.

 

#### *12.3.8.1 Bonferroni Correction*

The classical solution to family-wise error rate is a Bonferroni correction, introduced in Dunn (1958). The Bonferroni correction is defined as follows: given we want to set the significance level for the family of tests as ![images](images/c12-i0392.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, we reject the individual test when ![images](images/c12-i0393.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> satisfies:

(12.36)![equation](images/c12-math-0036.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mrow> <mi>B</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>f</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>m</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>l</mi> <mi>y</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mi>m</mi> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

for every ![images](images/c12-i0394.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>. We denote the corrected significance level at which we reject the null hypothesis as ![images](images/c12-i0395.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. The Bonferroni correction is implemented as:

#### *12.3.8.2 S&c.breve;idák's Correction*

Popular alternative to Bonferroni correction is S&c.breve;idák's correction, introduced in S&c.breve;idák (1967). The correction is exact when all tests are statistically independent. When individual tests are positively correlated, the outcome is conservative, while for negatively correlated tests, the outcome of the correction is less stringent and may not perform well. Given that we want to set the significance level for the family of tests as ![images](images/c12-i0396.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, we reject the individual test when ![images](images/c12-i0397.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> satisfies:

(12.37)![equation](images/c12-math-0037.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mrow> <mi>S&#38;c.breve;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>&#225;</mi> <mi>k</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>m</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>l</mi> <mi>y</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>m</mi> </mfrac> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

for every ![images](images/c12-i0398.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>. It is implemented as:

![](images/c12-gra-0122.png)

giving
