#### *12.3.8.3 Holm's Method*

The Holm's method was introduced in Holm (1979) and provides an algorithm which assures that the family-wise error rate is ![images](images/c12-i0399.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. The method works as follows:

*   Sort in ascending order the ![images](images/c12-i0400.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values of all individual hypotheses: ![images](images/c12-i0401.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></msub></mrow></math>. The set of indices ![images](images/c12-i0402.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math> orders the hypotheses accordingly, i.e. hypothesis ![images](images/c12-i0403.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub></mrow></math> is the one with lowest ![images](images/c12-i0404.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value.
*   For every index ![images](images/c12-i0405.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>, we define the critical value (12.38)![equation](images/c12-math-0038.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <msub> <mi>i</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>m</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>l</mi> <mi>y</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>k</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 
*   Find the smallest index, such that (12.39)![equation](images/c12-math-0039.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <msub> <mi>i</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> </msub> <mo>&#62;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <msub> <mi>i</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 
*   Reject the hypotheses ![images](images/c12-i0406.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><msub><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></msub></mrow></math>. In addition, ![images](images/c12-i0407.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></msub></mrow></math> stands for no hypothesis to be rejected.

In order to implement the Holm's method, we need to provide an array of ![images](images/c12-i0408.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>![images](images/c12-i0409.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values and the family-wise confidence level ![images](images/c12-i0410.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. The implementation reads:

![](images/c12-gra-0125.png)

Let us test the prescribed algorithm on two examples. The first example is composed of 100 random draws, where each draw is made from ![images](images/c12-i0411.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>U</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> corresponding to an individual ![images](images/c12-i0412.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value. The second example is the same case but draws are made from ![images](images/c12-i0413.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>U</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>. The family-wise confidence level is chosen to be ![images](images/c12-i0414.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow></math>. The first example gives:

![](images/c12-gra-0126.png)![](images/c12-gra-0127.png)

There is no hypothesis which would be rejected such that family-wise confidence level is 0.05.

The second example gives:

![](images/c12-gra-0128.png)![](images/c12-gra-0129.png)

There are seven hypotheses rejected altogether, such that the family-wise confidence level is at 0.05. If the underlying problem would be to find the factors, which are correlated with the dependent variable – see the problem at the beginning of this section – we would identify seven factors, which are correlated with the dependent variable at 0.05 confidence level.

 

#### *12.3.8.4 Example*

Finally, let us illustrate the multiple testing bias on the following example, which constitutes a moderately large number of features and still shows that multiple testing has to be performed properly. We have 10 features and 1 dependent variable. We want to make pairwise testing to find out whether there is a potentially dependent link between the feature(s) and the variable we want to model. We collect 1000 data points in our sample and choose confidence level ![images](images/c12-i0415.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow></math>. Further, the true data generating process does not have any link between features and the dependent variable. Thus, all detected dependencies are due to Type-I error.

For the set of 10 features, we calculate ![images](images/c12-i0416.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></math> and get the corresponding ![images](images/c12-i0417.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values for a two-sided test against the null hypothesis ![images](images/c12-i0418.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. The question to answer is whether there is a dependence between one or more features and the dependent variable. We perform 1000 realisations of the test.

In the first stage, we collect 1000 arrays of size 10 containing the ![images](images/c12-i0419.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values of the individual tests:

![](images/c12-gra-0130.png)

For every realisation of the test, we check whether there is at least one case with ![images](images/c12-i0420.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value below or equal to the confidence level chosen, 0.05. We record the number of realisations when at least one of the features shows statistical dependence:

![](images/c12-gra-0131.png)![](images/c12-gra-0132.png)

In ![images](images/c12-i0421.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>41.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of cases, we detect features which are significantly connected to the dependent variable. Thus, it is likely we may receive false results significantly many more times than the significance level would suggest. Ten features are far from what is usually perceived as a large number, and still, it may lead to a false conclusion quite frequently!

Let us repeat the test while making the Bonferroni correction:

![](images/c12-gra-0133.png)![](images/c12-gra-0134.png)

which leads to 15 cases, or, ![images](images/c12-i0422.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>0.15</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> cases in relative terms when a significant feature has been identified.

S&c.breve;idák's correction is performed analogously:

![](images/c12-gra-0135.png)![](images/c12-gra-0136.png)

and leads to the same number of cases when a significant feature has been observed.

Finally, Holm's method has a different functional form to apply, but is still very straightforward:

![](images/c12-gra-0137.png)![](images/c12-gra-0136.png)

The number of cases where a significant feature has been detected is the same.

The same results across the three methods is a consequence of our map between ![images](images/c12-i0423.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-stats and the corresponding ![images](images/c12-i0424.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-value. Our implementation through the lookup table is not granular enough to distinguish the nuances which are experienced in the current case. Nevertheless, all three methods significantly suppress the Type-I error and lead to the correct conclusion more often. We encourage readers to employ a more fine resolution of the map between ![images](images/c12-i0425.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-statistic and ![images](images/c12-i0426.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-values and thus confirm the difference between the methods. Finally, we encourage readers to explore other ways of applying the problem and observing different outcomes in the three methods.

# CHAPTER 13  
Linear Regression

 

In this chapter, we introduce the notion of linear regressions and implement it within `q`. The linear regression model should be a starting point for nearly any problem where we want to establish a relationship between factors on one side and a dependent variable on the other side. The linear regression is in nature close to understanding the correlation between variables. Why do we start with linear models which model the linear response of the system? The straightforward answer in the spirit of the famous physicist and Nobel prize winner Richard Feynman is “because we can solve them”.

Linear regression corresponds to the modelling of a function based on the first‐order Taylor expansion in the vicinity of a point ![images](images/c13-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>:

(13.1)![equation](images/c13-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <mfrac> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mi>f</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mfenced> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mi>r</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>l</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

which can be ultimately recast into a linear model

(13.2)![equation](images/c13-math-0002.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> </mfenced> <mo>&#8776;</mo> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where

![equation](images/c13-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtable columnalign="left"><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo form="prefix">=</mo><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mfenced><mo>+</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mfrac><mi>&#8706;</mi><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mfenced><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mfenced></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo form="prefix">=</mo><mfrac><mi>&#8706;</mi><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mfenced><mi>.</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math> 

In physics, making a linear approximation is a suitable tool to start to explore a new physical problem or to explain an observed phenomenon. Since we have mentioned Richard Feynman, see Veltman et al. (1994) for instance, famous Feynman diagrams for describing the interaction of the subatomic particles are a pictorial representation of an expansion of the interacting Hamiltonians in a small parameter (known as a perturbation expansion). The linear term in the expansion often provides enough insight to make reasonable physical assertions.

The linear models are easy to work with, easy to interpret and give us the first insight into our data. It is one of the most useful techniques in finance, economics and social sciences. Let us borrow a quote from Montgomery et al. (2012):

> Regression analysis is one of the most widely used techniques for analysing multi‐factor data. Its broad appeal and usefulness result from the conceptually logical process of using an equation to express the relationship between a variable of interest (the response) and a set of related predictor variables. Regression analysis is also interesting theoretically because of elegant underlying mathematics and a well‐developed statistical theory. Successful use of regression requires an appreciation of both the theory and the practical problems that typically arise when the technique is employed with real‐world data.

The term “regression” was introduced in an 1886 paper on genetics, evolution, and natural selection, *Regression towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature*, Galton (1886). Galton used the word in the sense of “regression towards the mean” or, put more bluntly, “regression towards mediocrity”. Galton was a pioneer in statistics. He computed correlations to make sense of empirical data and made extensive use of what would later become known as regression lines (Bulmer, 2003).

In this chapter, we provide the theory underlying the linear regression models and discuss its limitations. In the next chapter, we extend the material presented in this chapter and introduce the regularisation techniques. Regularisation can be considered as an extension, which helps us to generalise models such that they perform better on the unknown samples. This is an essential element to be introduced, and we encourage readers to not stop at this chapter but get straight ahead to the next one. Together, these chapters give the full and concise toolbox.

 

## 13.1 LINEAR REGRESSION

Let us start with the definition of the linear regression model. We use the matrix form to present the model. Let us denote ![images](images/c13-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>&#8469;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></math> the number of data points, ![images](images/c13-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>&#8469;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></math> the number of features, and ![images](images/c13-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> number of observations. The true underlying data generating process reads

(13.3)![equation](images/c13-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mi>p</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where the variables in the equation are:

*   ![images](images/c13-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math> are referred to as the inputs, or also regressors, independent variables, or explanatory variables.
*   ![images](images/c13-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math> are referred to as the outputs, or also regressands, or dependent variables.
*   ![images](images/c13-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math> are referred to as disturbance, or also noise, or error terms.

We can represent the model analogously in the matrix form:

[(13.4)](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-disp-0005)![equation](images/c13-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where

(13.5)![equation](images/c13-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="1em"/> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msubsup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msubsup> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msubsup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mn>2</mn> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msubsup> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msubsup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msubsup> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>11</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>12</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mi>p</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>21</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>22</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mi>p</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8945;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mn>2</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mi>p</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="1em"/> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="1em"/> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

The value of ![images](images/c13-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> determines the notation: for ![images](images/c13-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, the model is referred to as a simple linear regression model, while for ![images](images/c13-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, the model is referred to as a multivariate linear regression model. Variables ![images](images/c13-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> are given, i.e. provided in the data set. They are arranged in vector and matrix, respectively. On the other hand, vector ![images](images/c13-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></mrow></math> is composed of random variables.

Let us focus on the error terms and the different nature of disturbance and residuals. Let us notice that in [eq. 13.4](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0005), the term ![images](images/c13-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></mrow></math> is a random vector variable modelling the difference between the regressand ![images](images/c13-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> and the deterministic function ![images](images/c13-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> involving the regressors ![images](images/c13-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>. Since ![images](images/c13-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> depends on ![images](images/c13-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></mrow></math>, it is itself a random variable. However, when we are given ![images](images/c13-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> as well as ![images](images/c13-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> as data, we can then compute the deterministic quantity

[(13.6)](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-disp-0007)![equation](images/c13-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

which we call the residual. Confusingly enough, we use the same notation for ![images](images/c13-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> when it is a random variable as for its fixed sample when it is given. To recap, the disturbance is random while the residual is deterministic. [Eq, 13.6](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0007) is all very well, but we don't actually know ![images](images/c13-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> in it. Given the data, ![images](images/c13-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>, we need to fit the linear regression model and find a “good enough” estimate for ![images](images/c13-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>, say ![images](images/c13-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>.

[Eq, 13.6](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0007) is actually wrong; it should be

(13.7)![equation](images/c13-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

It remains to define the notion of “good enough”. We do that by minimising a suitable function of residuals, which has a meaning of information loss between features and dependent variables. This brings us to the ordinary least squares method.

 

## 13.2 ORDINARY LEAST SQUARES

In order to formulate the ordinary least squares, we have to make several assumptions:

*   for all ![images](images/c13-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> have a mean of zero, ![images](images/c13-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#54588;</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>;
*   for all ![images](images/c13-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> have the same finite variance, ![images](images/c13-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Var</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></math>, in other words, the random variables ![images](images/c13-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> are homoscedastic;
*   for all ![images](images/c13-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>, the ![images](images/c13-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> are uncorrelated, ![images](images/c13-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="normal">Cov</mtext><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>;
*   the regressors are non‐random and observable;
*   the regressors are not perfectly linearly correlated with each other.

The ordinary least squares, or OLS, is constructed as follows: we aim to find such a ![images](images/c13-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> in

(13.8)![equation](images/c13-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

which will minimise a certain loss function of the residual ![images](images/c13-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>. We use the squared error, which we'll now call the residual sum of squares (RSS)

(13.9)![equation](images/c13-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext>RSS</mtext> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mfenced> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mfenced> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

We will refer to the estimate as ![images](images/c13-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> that will give us the estimate of ![images](images/c13-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math>,

(13.10)![equation](images/c13-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>:</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

The OLS estimator is given as:

(13.11)![equation](images/c13-math-0012.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> </mfenced> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

We can prove this by first rewriting the RSS:

(13.12)![equation](images/c13-math-0013.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext>RSS</mtext> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

Using the denominator notation for vector‐by‐vector and scalar‐by‐vector derivatives,

(13.13)![equation](images/c13-math-0014.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mo>&#8711;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> </msub> <mtext>RSS</mtext> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mtext>RSS</mtext> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

When ![images](images/c13-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></msub><mtext>RSS</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, we get ![images](images/c13-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> (this is the so‐called normal equation), hence we obtain the solution ![images](images/c13-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math>. To check that this critical point is a minimum, we examine the Hessian matrix

(13.14)![equation](images/c13-math-0015.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfrac> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mtext>RSS</mtext> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

If ![images](images/c13-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> is full rank (i.e. has rank ![images](images/c13-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> if we allow the intercept and ![images](images/c13-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> if we don't; this implies that ![images](images/c13-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> is skinny or square), then ![images](images/c13-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> is positive definite and the critical point is indeed a minimum.

The important feature of the OLS estimator is that it is unbiased, i.e. conditional expectation of the estimator is the true value:

where we need assumptions imposed on the linear model to proceed with calculation, namely that ![images](images/c13-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#54588;</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mn mathvariant="bold-italic">0</mn><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Var</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>, for some constant ![images](images/c13-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></math>, which is the case when the following three assumptions from the classical linear regression model (CLRM) hold:

*   for all ![images](images/c13-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> have a mean of zero, ![images](images/c13-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#54588;</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>;
*   for all ![images](images/c13-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> have the same finite variance, ![images](images/c13-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Var</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></math>, in other words, the random variables ![images](images/c13-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> are homoscedastic;
*   for all ![images](images/c13-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>, the ![images](images/c13-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> are uncorrelated, ![images](images/c13-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="normal">Cov</mtext><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.

stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mfenced><mi>.</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math> 

If we were also to assume that the regressors, ![images](images/c13-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>, are non‐random and observable (another assumption from CLRM), we could get rid of the expectation operator and write ![images](images/c13-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Var</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

When we are writing ![images](images/c13-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> anywhere, we are also making another assumption from CLRM: that the regressors are not perfectly linearly correlated with each other; thus ![images](images/c13-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> is full rank, and therefore the inverse of the Gram matrix does exist.

 

## 13.3 THE GEOMETRIC REPRESENTATION OF LINEAR REGRESSION

In order to work with linear regressions and make the most of it, it is fundamental to understand the geometric representation of the OLS. For that purpose, we will work with a simple example: we are given the linear model:

(13.18)![equation](images/c13-math-0021.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where

(13.19)![equation](images/c13-math-0022.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>4</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>2</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>2</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mn>3</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

Our aim is to find an estimate ![images](images/c13-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>. Here ![images](images/c13-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> (we have a single feature) and ![images](images/c13-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> (we have three data points). Our data set consists of three data points, three ![images](images/c13-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> pairs: ![images](images/c13-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Because ![images](images/c13-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, all our ![images](images/c13-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> are univariate: 1, 3, and 4.

In the OLS procedure, we are fitting the regression line such that we are minimising the sum of squares of residuals. [Figure 13.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0001) depicts the objective function of the OLS procedure: we minimise the distance of every point from the regression line. The distance is depicted as a dashed line in the figure.

![FIGURE 13.1 The objective of the OLS procedure](images/c13f001.png)

[**FIGURE 13.1**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0001) The objective of the OLS procedure

It is worth stressing that we define the distance of a point to the fitted line using the projection on ![images](images/c13-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> axis. This is not the shortest distance we can come up with. [Figure 13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0002) depicts on the other hand the distance between the fitted line and the observed data defined as orthogonal projection, i.e. the shortest physical distance of a point to the fitted line. This objective function is used in other machine learning methods like Vector Support Machines or Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

![FIGURE 13.2 The orthogonal distance for linear fit](images/c13f002.png)

[**FIGURE 13.2**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0002) The orthogonal distance for linear fit

The OLS solution to the presented problem reads:

![equation](images/c13-math-0023.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtable columnalign="left"><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo form="prefix">=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"/><mtd columnalign="left"><mo form="prefix">=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>4</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math> 

giving the projected values of ![images](images/c13-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math>

(13.20)![equation](images/c13-math-0024.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>4</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>&#183;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>2</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>2</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>2</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math>  

### 13.3.1 Moore–Penrose Pseudoinverse

Let's have a look at our ![images](images/c13-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> in more detail:

![equation](images/c13-math-0025.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><munder><munder><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup></mrow><mo>&#65080;</mo></munder><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></munder><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></math> is called the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse matrix of ![images](images/c13-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>. In our example, we get

(13.21)![equation](images/c13-math-0026.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>+</mo> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mn>3</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mn>4</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>4</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>26</mn> </mfrac> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mfrac> <mn>3</mn> <mn>26</mn> </mfrac> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mfrac> <mn>4</mn> <mn>26</mn> </mfrac> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

One of its properties is ![images](images/c13-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>; in other words, ![images](images/c13-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></math> maps all column vectors of ![images](images/c13-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> to themselves while ![images](images/c13-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></math> need not be the identity matrix. Namely,

(13.22)![equation](images/c13-math-0027.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>+</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>4</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>26</mn> </mfrac> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mfrac> <mn>3</mn> <mn>26</mn> </mfrac> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mfrac> <mn>4</mn> <mn>26</mn> </mfrac> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> </mfenced> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>4</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>26</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>26</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>4</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>26</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>26</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>9</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>26</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>12</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>26</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>4</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>26</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>12</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>26</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>16</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>26</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>4</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>4</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

Then, we can explore the properties of the projected ![images](images/c13-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>:

(13.23)![equation](images/c13-math-0028.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <munder> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <munder> <munder> <mrow> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> </mrow> <mo>&#65080;</mo> </munder> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>+</mo> </msup> </munder> </mrow> <mo>&#65080;</mo> </munder> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi> </munder> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where the matrix ![images](images/c13-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup></mrow></math> is known as the hat matrix – because it takes ![images](images/c13-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> and puts a hat on it, ![images](images/c13-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>. In our example, the hat matrix reads:

It may seem to be confusing that ![images](images/c13-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi></mrow></math> is orthogonal projection, though we actually decided to minimise the lengths defined in [Figure 13.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0001), i.e. ![images](images/c13-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>, rather than the one in [Figure 13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0002).

The conflicting interpretation of the orthogonal projection is not real. The point of view hides orthogonal projection we took to visualise the data. In [Figure 13.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0001), we use the plot which represents the so‐called variable space view, ![images](images/c13-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#8477;</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow></math>, view of the linear regression: here each data point is indeed represented by a point, and the dimensions represent the features. Here we can see the regression line.

In order to see the orthogonal projection, we have to use the so‐called subject space view, which is ![images](images/c13-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#8477;</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math>. It is of different dimension relative to the objective space. [Figure 13.3](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0003) depicts the regression problem we face in the variable space. Here ![images](images/c13-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#375;</mi></mrow></math> appear as vectors represented by lines and the dimensions represent the data points. The orthogonal projection was hidden on the variable space view but became revealed on the subject space view. This in itself is a useful lesson in data science.

![FIGURE 13.3 Visualisation of the linear regression in the subject space](images/c13f003.png)

[**FIGURE 13.3**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0003) Visualisation of the linear regression in the subject space

In [Figure 13.3](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0003), we find our OLS solution by orthogonally projecting ![images](images/c13-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> (the light gray line) onto the column space of ![images](images/c13-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> (the dark gray line or hyperplane) – see the dashed gray line on the right plot.

In summary:

*   The hat matrix, ![images](images/c13-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi></mrow></math> is an orthogonal projection matrix that projects ![images](images/c13-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> onto the column space of ![images](images/c13-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> – the space spanned by the column vectors of ![images](images/c13-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>.
*   The result, ![images](images/c13-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>, is a linear combination of the columns of ![images](images/c13-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>.
*   The weights in this linear combination are given by the elements of ![images](images/c13-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>.
*   In our example, ![images](images/c13-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, so ![images](images/c13-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> has a single column. Thus the result, ![images](images/c13-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>, is a scalar multiple of that column, the scalar being our ![images](images/c13-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math>: ![equation](images/c13-math-0037.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mi ### 13.3.2 Adding Intercept

The solution we have defined so far is not the one we would likely use for practical considerations. If our goal is the line which fits the three data points the best, having ![images](images/c13-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is not the solution. The reason is that the chosen line goes through the origin. This is significant, and unless we want to impose it explicitly, we should release the intercept to take any value.

Including intercept within our framework is easy. We just prepend a column of ones to ![images](images/c13-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>, so it becomes the ![images](images/c13-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>‐dimensional matrix:

(13.32)![equation](images/c13-math-0038.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>4</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

and prepend ![images](images/c13-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> to the column vector ![images](images/c13-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>, so it becomes the ![images](images/c13-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>‐dimensional column vector

We can visualise the solution in the variable space. [Figure 13.4](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0004) depicts the regression line which is a solution to the OLS problem. The slope changed compared to the case when we enforced the fit going through the intercept. Visually, the distances of the observed points from the fitted line are significantly shorter compared to the restricted case. We thus obtain a better fit.

![FIGURE 13.4 The OLS solution with intercept included](images/c13f004.png)

[**FIGURE 13.4**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0004) The OLS solution with intercept included

When we add the intercept, the hat matrix now projects onto a plane, not onto a line. Namely, the hat matrix becomes:
