columnalign="center"> <mn>2</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>6</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>5</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>4</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> </mfenced> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> (13.44)![equation](images/c13-math-0052.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"/> <mtd columnalign="left"> <mo form="prefix">=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>14</mn> </mfrac> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>13</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>5</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>6</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>6</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>10</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mi>.</mi> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

As before, it projects ![images](images/c13-i0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> onto the column space of ![images](images/c13-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>, the resulting projection being ![images](images/c13-i0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>. However, now ![images](images/c13-i0128.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> has two (linearly independent) columns, not one, so the projection is onto a plane, not onto a line. If we increase ![images](images/c13-i0129.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and add more columns to ![images](images/c13-i0130.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>, if these columns are linearly independent, we will further increase the dimension of the column space of ![images](images/c13-i0131.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> onto which we project.

Recall that the equation of a plane orthogonal to a vector ![images](images/c13-i0132.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi></mrow></math> and containing a point ![images](images/c13-i0133.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> is given by ![images](images/c13-i0134.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. (We are simply stating a fact: ![images](images/c13-i0135.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0136.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> (the latter lies on the plane) are orthogonal.) In our case,

(13.45)![equation](images/c13-math-0053.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>14</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>9</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>14</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>7</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

is orthogonal to the plane that contains the column vectors of ![images](images/c13-i0137.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>: ![images](images/c13-i0138.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup></mrow></math>and ![images](images/c13-i0139.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>4</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup></mrow></math>. We can use either of them to work out the equation of the plane:

(13.46)![equation](images/c13-math-0054.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfrac> <mn>3</mn> <mn>14</mn> </mfrac> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>9</mn> <mn>14</mn> </mfrac> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mn>3</mn> <mn>7</mn> </mfrac> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>3</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>&#8658;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>3</mn> <mn>14</mn> </mfrac> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>9</mn> <mn>14</mn> </mfrac> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mn>3</mn> <mn>7</mn> </mfrac> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>3</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

The resulting OLS solution is a linear combination of the columns of ![images](images/c13-i0140.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>, the weights being given by the elements of ![images](images/c13-i0141.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>:

(13.47)![equation](images/c13-math-0055.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>25</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>14</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>23</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>14</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>11</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>7</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>3</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>4</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0142.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> is, by construction, the ![images](images/c13-i0143.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>‐intercept of the regression line and ![images](images/c13-i0144.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> is its gradient.

 

## 13.4 IMPLEMENTATION OF THE OLS

In this section, we implement the linear regression model in `q`. Following the underlying implementation, we discuss several advanced topics related to linear regression. Our final objective is to unite the code elements into an estimation suite which presents an alternative to linear regression toolboxes in other programming languages.

Before we start building the implementation in `q`, let us create a sample data set. Let us use the `multiNormal` function to generate the random sample and define independent variables:

![](images/c13-gra-0001.png)

We choose a simple well‐rounded linear model as the example used for the illustration of the OLS technique:

![](images/c13-gra-0002.png)![](images/c13-gra-0003.png)![](images/c13-gra-0004.png)![](images/c13-gra-0005.png)![](images/c13-gra-0006.png)![](images/c13-gra-0007.png)![](images/c13-gra-0008.png)![](images/c13-gra-0009.png)![](images/c13-gra-0010.png)![](images/c13-gra-0011.png)![](images/c13-gra-0012.png)![](images/c13-gra-0013.png)![](images/c13-gra-0014.png)

The correlation reflects the model as we set it up. Let us remind the reader that the correlation coefficient does not correspond to the parameters of the linear model as the variance of the features is not normalised. Further, for convenience, we arrange the data into the table – a more natural data structure.

![](images/c13-gra-0015.png)

Let us make an important note at this point about constants. In econometric literature, the constant plays a special role as it is frequently treated separately. For instance, a number of parameters in the linear model may be referred to a number of parameters corresponding to non‐constant features. We thus remind the reader to check the convention when comparing different books. In the following text, we will consider constant as a regular feature, which is constant and equal to 1 for every observation. Thus, we add a constant term into our data table:

![](images/c13-gra-0016.png)![](images/c13-gra-0017.png)

The OLS estimation is based on solving the system of linear equations with Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of matrix ![images](images/c13-i0145.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>. We take this opportunity to remind the reader that we can formulate the solution to the OLS as:

(13.48)![equation](images/c13-math-0056.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">+</mo> <mi>T</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> </mfenced> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

We choose this formulation for convenience; this affects the two building blocks we have to define to calculate the solutions to the problem: first, we need to define ![images](images/c13-i0146.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>:

![](images/c13-gra-0018.png)

and then also ![images](images/c13-i0147.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>

![](images/c13-gra-0019.png)

We then solve the equation for the ![images](images/c13-i0148.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math>'s using the `lsq` verb corresponding to:

(13.49)![equation](images/c13-math-0057.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

given as:

![](images/c13-gra-0020.png)![](images/c13-gra-0021.png)

The solution is an enlisted list of estimated parameters corresponding to features `‘const‘x1‘x2‘x3`, in a given order. The provided code allows us to find a solution for more than one set of dependent variables `y`, i.e. the column `‘y` in the `tabData` table can be itself composed of lists instead of float atoms. The usual problems where we need OLS do not give us more than one dependent variable, and thus we restrict ourselves to situations where we will have just one. In such a case, we need to get the solution from the list:

![](images/c13-gra-0022.png)![](images/c13-gra-0023.png)

We have thus obtained the solution in the form:

(13.50)![equation](images/c13-math-0058.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mi>.</mi> <mn>010413</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mi>.</mi> <mn>9998791</mn> <mo>&#42;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mi>.</mi> <mn>9974519</mn> <mo>&#42;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mi>.</mi> <mn>996775</mn> <mo>&#42;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>3</mn> </msub> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

The estimated coefficients truthfully reflect the true coefficients. The comparison is visual. In order to establish a statistical link, we need to estimate the properties of the estimator. In particular, we calculate the variance‐covariance matrix of the estimate. The diagonal terms of the matrix are the errors of the estimated values, or rather its squares. The variance‐covariance matrix reads:

![](images/c13-gra-0024.png)![](images/c13-gra-0025.png)

It is then straightforward to extract the sample errors of the estimated parameters:

![](images/c13-gra-0026.png)

Let us make clear that the size of the sample does not normalise the errors. This will be done when we calculate the statistical properties of the estimates, namely, the ![images](images/c13-i0149.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>‐statistic. Before we do that, let us summarise the results we have obtained so far in the form of a table:

![](images/c13-gra-0027.png)![](images/c13-gra-0028.png)

This concludes the estimation of the parameters of the OLS problem for a linear equation. In the following sections, we define several additional features, which complement the statistical information about the estimates and the estimated model.

 

## 13.5 SIGNIFICANCE OF PARAMETERS

In the previous section we calculated the OLS estimates of the parameters of a linear model. In this section, we assess the significance of the estimated parameters. First, we calculate the ![images](images/c13-i0150.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>‐statistic:

![](images/c13-gra-0029.png)

The ![images](images/c13-i0151.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>‐statistic is distributed according to the ![images](images/c13-i0152.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>‐distribution with degrees of freedom equal to a number of observations, ![images](images/c13-i0153.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>. We can evaluate the null hypothesis that a given coefficient comes from the distribution with zero mean. In order to evaluate the hypothesis, we need to be able to calculate the ![images](images/c13-i0154.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>‐distribution with general degrees of freedom. We overcome this task by sticking to approximation ![images](images/c13-i0155.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></math>, where the ![images](images/c13-i0156.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>‐distribution converges to a normal distribution.

Further, we may not need the probability at which we may reject the null hypothesis itself, but rather to check whether we can reject the null at several benchmark values. In particular, we stick to ![images](images/c13-i0157.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0158.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0159.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>99</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0160.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>99</mn><mi>.</mi><mn>9</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, respectively. We will use the “![images](images/c13-i0161.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></math>” notation, where ![images](images/c13-i0162.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></math> stands for a situation where we can reject the null at ![images](images/c13-i0163.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> confidence level, but not at a higher confidence level. Analogously, the case of ![images](images/c13-i0164.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></math> corresponds to ![images](images/c13-i0165.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> confidence level, ![images](images/c13-i0166.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo><mo>&#42;</mo><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></math> corresponds to ![images](images/c13-i0167.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>99</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c13-i0168.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo><mo>&#42;</mo><mo>&#42;</mo><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></math> corresponds to ![images](images/c13-i0169.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>99</mn><mi>.</mi><mn>9</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, respectively. Thus, having with every estimated parameter its corresponding number of “\*” gives the easy‐to‐read statistical assessment of the estimated model.

We create a function which assigns the corresponding number of “\*” for every given ![images](images/c13-i0170.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>‐statistic under the asymptotic approximation:

![](images/c13-gra-0030.png)

The confidence level of the estimated parameters thus reads:

![](images/c13-gra-0031.png)![](images/c13-gra-0032.png)

The result shows that all four parameters are statistically significant, or, we can reject the null hypothesis at a very high confidence level. Given that all the assumptions hold, all the estimated parameters contained within the model are true values. Since we know it is the case by knowing the true model, this result is not surprising. Still, we cannot assess the overall quality of the model used. This will be done in the following sections.

 

## 13.6 HOW GOOD IS THE FIT: *R*²

The question we have to answer is how good is the overall fit. The significance of individual parameters does not help. Imagine the model has four features, all significant. We include three of them into our model, where each of them will have coefficients significantly different from zero. This itself does not answer the question whether we have included all the features, or, in general, how much we do not know about the model. We can assert that we have acquired some knowledge about our model.

In order to answer the question about overall quality of the fit, we perform what is known as variance partitioning. Let ![images](images/c13-i0171.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> be the sample mean, and let us define:

*   Total Sum of Squares (TSS), sometimes also referred to as Sum of Squares, Total (SST, SSTO) and SYY: ![images](images/c13-i0172.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>;
*   Estimated Sum of Squares (ESS), sometimes also referred to as Sum of Squares, Model (SSM), Estimated Sum of Squares (ESS), and Sum of Squares, Regression (SSR, SSreg): ![images](images/c13-i0173.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>;
*   Residual Sum of Squares (RSS), sometimes also referred to as Sum of Squares, Error (SSE): ![images](images/c13-i0174.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>.

Notice that the abbreviations used in the literature can be quite confusing: Does “E” stand for “estimated” or for “error”; does “R” stand for “regression” or for “residual”? To avoid confusion, we shall stick with Total Sum of Squares (TSS), Estimated Sum of Squares (ESS), and Residual Sum of Squares (RSS).

If we define ![images](images/c13-i0175.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>&#8477;</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> as a vector all of whose elements are the sample mean ![images](images/c13-i0176.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math>, we can write these down in vector notation:
