If the model includes the intercept, the first column of ![images](images/c13-i0177.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> is a column of ones and, since ![images](images/c13-i0178.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></math>, the sum of the residuals is zero. This is equivalent to ![images](images/c13-i0179.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math>. By Pythagoras's theorem,

(13.57)![equation](images/c13-math-0065.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;" separators=""> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;" separators=""> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

hence

(13.58)![equation](images/c13-math-0066.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext>TSS</mtext> <mo>=</mo> <mtext>ESS</mtext> <mo>+</mo> <mtext>RSS</mtext> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

which is a fundamental result known as variance partitioning. Irrespective of whether our model includes the intercept, if we centre ![images](images/c13-i0180.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> by subtracting the sample mean ![images](images/c13-i0181.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> from each element, we notice that ![images](images/c13-i0182.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>TSS</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext>ESS</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext>RSS</mtext></mrow></math> simply amounts to the above application of Pythagoras's theorem.

Recall that, in a right triangle,

![equation](images/c13-math-0067.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mtext>adjacent</mtext><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mtext>hypotenuse</mtext><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> 

thus

![equation](images/c13-math-0068.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mi><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;" separators=""><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;" separators=""><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mtext>ESS</mtext><mtext>TSS</mtext></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext>TSS</mtext><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>RSS</mtext></mrow><mtext>TSS</mtext></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mtext>RSS</mtext><mtext>TSS</mtext></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>:</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> 

which is the quantity also known as the coefficient of determination. It indicates how much better the function predicts the dependent variable than the default predictor in the absence of any inputs – the mean value of the output. It is also sometimes described as the proportion of variance explained. This measure reflects how closely the model captures the data generating process.

Regression can be seen as an orthogonal projection of ![images](images/c13-i0183.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> onto the column space of ![images](images/c13-i0184.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>. An orthogonal projection minimises the length of the vector that represents the difference between ![images](images/c13-i0185.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> and the fitted values, ![images](images/c13-i0186.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>, i.e. minimises ![images](images/c13-i0187.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></mrow></math>. The fitted values are a vector in the column space of ![images](images/c13-i0188.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>. If we add a column to ![images](images/c13-i0189.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>, the column space of ![images](images/c13-i0190.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> either stays the same or gets more significant. Therefore, the orthogonal projection onto this new space cannot possibly be more extended since the original column space is a subspace of the new space.

The ![images](images/c13-i0191.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> coefficient takes values between 0 and 1, where 0 means that the linear model does not explain the data, while coefficient close to 1 suggests that explanatory power of the model is reliable. Interestingly, for the univariate models, the ![images](images/c13-i0192.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> coefficient is equal to the square of the Pearson correlation coefficient. The ![images](images/c13-i0193.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> is also referred to as a goodness‐of‐fit coefficient. The estimation procedure thus aims to provide such a model, which gives the highest possible ![images](images/c13-i0194.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>. Using the ![images](images/c13-i0195.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> as an objective of the researcher to maximise has its pitfalls. In particular, by adding one more variable into the model specification, the RSS term is decreasing – or, being precise, non‐increasing. Thus, by adding more and more terms, the RSS is minimised. Ultimately, by adding ![images](images/c13-i0196.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> independent variables, we may achieve a holy grail of regression ![images](images/c13-i0197.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, i.e. seemingly explain all the uncertainty in the data.

This is, however, spurious goodness because by adding more and more independent features, the number of degrees of freedom is decreasing. Further, the primary objective of the data analysis is to introduce a model as parsimonious as possible, which explains as much as possible. Thus, there is a trade‐off between a number of independent variables and the explanatory power of the model. The ![images](images/c13-i0198.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> measure, as introduced above, ignores the number of independent variables and solely focuses on explanatory power.

The implementation in `q` is straightforward:

![](images/c13-gra-0033.png)

and we can add this function into our OLS estimation suite.

![](images/c13-gra-0034.png)![](images/c13-gra-0035.png)

The value is very high, close to the maximum value of 1.0. This measure thus suggests that the model we have used for estimation of the data generating process is very close to the true model and the estimated model explains ![images](images/c13-i0199.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>99</mn><mi>.</mi><mn>8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of variance.

 

### 13.6.1 Adjusted R‐squared

There is a modification to the goodness‐of‐fit as introduced above which penalises the measure for the number of independent variables. The adjusted ![images](images/c13-i0200.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> is based on the same principles as ![images](images/c13-i0201.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>, i.e. the ratio of unexplained variance to the total variance, except that the measure of variance is adjusted for the total number of degrees of freedom. In particular, let us denote the adjusted ![images](images/c13-i0202.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> as ![images](images/c13-i0203.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> and define it as:

![equation](images/c13-math-0069.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtable columnalign="left"><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo form="prefix">=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mfrac></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"/><mtd columnalign="left"><mo form="prefix">=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"/><mtd columnalign="left"><mo form="prefix">=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0204.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math> denotes the adjusted residual sum of squares, ![images](images/c13-i0205.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math> is the adjusted total sum of squares, ![images](images/c13-i0206.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the total number of degrees of freedom for a model with ![images](images/c13-i0207.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> data points, ![images](images/c13-i0208.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> independent variables and constant, ![images](images/c13-i0209.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c13-i0210.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> is the total number of degrees of freedoms for a model equal to constant.

The adjusted ![images](images/c13-i0211.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> is no longer equivalent to the square of the correlation coefficient for the univariate model, neither it is a non‐increasing function with the number of independent variables added to the model. The adjusted measure contains the trade‐off between the explanatory power of the model and its parsimoniousness; thus the adjusted ![images](images/c13-i0212.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> is increasing with additional variables if the unexplained variance is decreasing faster than ![images](images/c13-i0213.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8764;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>.

It is worth noting that adjusted ![images](images/c13-i0214.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> is no longer bounded within ![images](images/c13-i0215.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>. The adjusted ![images](images/c13-i0216.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> can be an objective of the researcher when modelling the data as the trade‐off is fully reflected. However, we do not recommend to use the adjusted ![images](images/c13-i0217.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> as the criteria to be maximised without further considerations. The main problem is that incremental improvement to the adjusted ![images](images/c13-i0218.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> can still produce insignificant improvement of the model. The subsequent section considers a more appropriate tool to decide whether adding variables has a significant impact on the variance improvement.

We provide a function which implements the adjusted ![images](images/c13-i0219.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> defined in the previous display as:

![](images/c13-gra-0036.png)

The example under consideration shows very high adjusted ![images](images/c13-i0220.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>:

![](images/c13-gra-0037.png)![](images/c13-gra-0038.png)

The adjusted value is close to the unadjusted value and very high. The estimated model explains most of the variance; the unexplained variance is white noise without any pattern.

 

## 13.7 RELATIONSHIP WITH MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD ESTIMATION AND AIC WITH SMALL SAMPLE CORRECTION

Let us link the OLS procedure to the maximum likelihood estimation. This is interesting theoretically as well as useful from a practical perspective. It allows us to define additional criteria to assess the quality of the fit. Suppose that ![images](images/c13-i0221.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mover class="overset"><mo>&#8764;</mo><mtext>i.i.d.</mtext></mover><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Then, taking ![images](images/c13-i0222.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> as data, the observations have density functions ![images](images/c13-i0223.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#981;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfenced></mrow></math>, and the likelihood function of ![images](images/c13-i0224.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0225.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>, based on the sample, is

(13.59)![equation](images/c13-math-0070.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script">L</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8719;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <mi>&#981;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>;</mo> <msubsup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msubsup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>&#960;</mi> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>2</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mfenced> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

It is convenient to take the logarithms and thus we obtain the log‐likelihood

(13.60)![equation](images/c13-math-0071.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"> <mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="script">L</mi> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="left"> <mo form="prefix">=</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mi>n</mi> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>2</mn> <mi>&#960;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mi>n</mi> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> </mfenced> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> (13.61)![equation](images/c13-math-0072.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"/> <mtd columnalign="left"> <mo form="prefix">=</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mi>n</mi> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>2</mn> <mi>&#960;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mi>n</mi> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mtext>RSS</mtext> <mi>.</mi> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

We can use the log‐likelihood to find the estimated parameters. To find the critical points, we compute the first partial derivatives:

(13.62)![equation](images/c13-math-0073.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="script">L</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="left"> <mo form="prefix">=</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mtext>RSS</mtext> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mfrac> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> (13.63)![equation](images/c13-math-0074.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="script">L</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="left"> <mo form="prefix">=</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mi>n</mi> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>4</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mtext>RSS</mtext> <mi>.</mi> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

In order to confirm that the solution is the global maximum of the log‐likelihood and not just a saddle point, we have to add the Hessian matrix. This is not our objective at this point. We want to use knowledge of the log‐likelihood to strengthen our knowledge about the quality of the fit.

The ![images](images/c13-i0226.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> measure and its adjusted version serve to provide an absolute measure of how much variance was explained by the model. This measure, however, is not the only one we can use to evaluate models and decide which one to use. We introduce the Akaike Information Criteria, AIC, introduced by Akaike (1974).

Let us assume that we have a process at hand generated by a true model ![images](images/c13-i0227.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. We choose a model ![images](images/c13-i0228.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and want to find out how good the model ![images](images/c13-i0229.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> is to capture the dynamics of the data generated by model ![images](images/c13-i0230.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. If we know both the true model and the chosen model, we can use the information theory and calculate information loss using the Kullback‐Leibler divergence:

(13.64)![equation](images/c13-math-0075.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>D</mi> <mrow> <mi>K</mi> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>e</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msubsup> <mo>&#8747;</mo> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#8734;</mi> </mrow> <mi>&#8734;</mi> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>e</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> </mfenced> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>e</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfrac> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi>d</mi> <mi>x</mi> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

The knowledge of the true model is hardly known in reality. Thus calculating the information loss of a given model relative to the true model, i.e. having the absolute measure of quality for the chosen model, is not possible. Akaike showed that information loss as described above can be still utilised even when we do not know the true model. In particular, if we have two competing models ![images](images/c13-i0231.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0232.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> related to the same true and unknown model ![images](images/c13-i0233.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, we can derive criteria that will help us to decide which of the two models ![images](images/c13-i0234.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0235.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> is causing less information loss. The measure does not allow us to say how good the models are; they can be both very poor or very close to the true model and the criteria only allow us to compare their difference.

For a given model ![images](images/c13-i0236.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math>, Akaike defined the information criteria proportional to information loss implied by the model ![images](images/c13-i0237.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> as:

(13.65)![equation](images/c13-math-0076.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>A</mi> <mi>I</mi> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>&#183;</mo> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>&#183;</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi mathvariant="script">L</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0238.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> denotes the number of parameters in the model ![images](images/c13-i0239.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c13-i0240.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> is a log‐likelihood of the model ![images](images/c13-i0241.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math>.

For two competing models ![images](images/c13-i0242.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0243.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>, we calculate the corresponding AICs, ![images](images/c13-i0244.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0245.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>. The model with lower AIC is causing less information loss in the asymptotic limit of infinite sample size. This is the main result of Akaike.

The minimisation of the information criteria gives an intuitive explanation to two terms forming the AIC. The first term corresponds to a penalty which aims to discriminate in favour of complex models and prevent overfitting. The second term, on the other hand, corresponds to the quality of the fit. The AIC thus aims to balance the bias‐variance trade‐off and guide towards models which are truthful enough but not too complex.

The concept of comparing information criteria for two competing models does not constitute any form of hypothesis testing. The comparison brings a relative measure without any significance. The information criteria for two models can still be numerically interpreted. Let us assume we have two models ![images](images/c13-i0246.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0247.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> with similar information criteria ![images](images/c13-i0248.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0249.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>. Without loss of generality, let us assume that ![images](images/c13-i0250.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>. Then, the factor:

(13.66)![equation](images/c13-math-0077.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>A</mi> <mi>I</mi> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mi>I</mi> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> </mrow> </math> 

is proportional to probability that model ![images](images/c13-i0251.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> minimises the information loss relative to model ![images](images/c13-i0252.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math>.

For linear OLS‐based models, the comparison based on the AIC results in similar comparison. The advantage of the AIC is that it can be used for non‐nested models while measures derived from ![images](images/c13-i0253.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> (see ![images](images/c13-i0254.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>‐test below) can be used to compare nested models only.

Once we have obtained log‐likelihood, we can then calculate the AIC for a given model. We can stick to ![images](images/c13-i0255.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfenced></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup></mfenced></mrow></math> as this is the term which will vary across models for a given sample. In the implementation below, however, we keep the full formula for log‐likelihood:

![](images/c13-gra-0039.png)![](images/c13-gra-0040.png)

It is convenient to create a function which calculates the log‐likelihood, as it is one of the main concepts used in modern econometrics:

![](images/c13-gra-0041.png)

We can verify the function:

![](images/c13-gra-0042.png)![](images/c13-gra-0043.png)

Having in hand the log‐likelihood, we can formulate the AIC function:

![](images/c13-gra-0044.png)

The AIC for the example listed in this section gives:

![](images/c13-gra-0045.png)![](images/c13-gra-0046.png)

As we have mentioned in the paragraphs leading to this number, the AIC on its own does not give us any information. We cannot say whether ![images](images/c13-i0256.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1783</mn><mi>.</mi><mn>824</mn></mrow></math> is very small and thus information loss is small or if it is large and the model is unacceptable.

The calculation itself assumes the asymptotic holds, i.e. the size of the sample is infinite. This is not true as our sample contains ![images](images/c13-i0257.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></math> points. In such a case, the offset between the complexity of the model and its accuracy may adequately work. The small sample correction for AIC should thus be considered. In general, this task is very complicated and an analytic formula may not be possible to find for any model. Thus, methods like bootstrap are being used to have a numerical correction to AIC.

Fortunately, for the OLS model, or, for univariate model linear in parameters, where residuals are normally distributed, the analytic formula exists. In such a case, the AIC corrected for the small size of the sample, usually denoted as AICc, is defined as:

(13.67)![equation](images/c13-math-0078.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>A</mi> <mi>I</mi> <mi>C</mi> <mi>c</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mi>I</mi> <mi>C</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>p</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>p</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

Several observations are at the place: ![images](images/c13-i0258.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>I</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>I</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> as ![images](images/c13-i0259.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></math>, thus the small sample correction indeed works in the case of the finite sample. Further, the AICc is proportional to ![images](images/c13-i0260.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> and thus can be considered as a second‐order approximation to the relative information loss in the number of parameters.

The AICc implementation reads:

![](images/c13-gra-0047.png)![](images/c13-gra-0048.png)![](images/c13-gra-0049.png) 

## 13.8 ESTIMATION SUITE

Finally, we put all the components together to create the entire regression suite of the ordinary least square regression including all the additional statistics. The output of the function is a dictionary with various variables. The dictionary corresponds to a chosen model. The advantage of this approach, in this case, is that we can later create statistics, which allows us to assess the accuracy of a model, or to compare two or more models, as the AIC suggests. The estimation suite consists of the measures and statistics introduced above, where some of them have been directly incorporated into the suite rather than re‐use the functions introduced. We have also added treatment for missing values. In particular, whenever a missing value is observed among any feature, the row to which the missing value belongs is removed. This method is convenient when the data set has only a few missing entries. If the missing values are too frequent or present some pattern in the data, more sophisticated and tailored techniques will be needed.

![](images/c13-gra-0050.png)

Let us run the suite for the example:

![](images/c13-gra-0051.png)

with results in a comprised form that reads:

![](images/c13-gra-0052.png)

The output is useful in terms of containing all the information in a comprised and easy‐to‐retrieve way, but still beyond readability by a human user. For that purpose, we summarise the full results in a more convenient and standardised form:

![](images/c13-gra-0053.png)

The comprehensive outcome of the estimation of the OLS model with supplementary measures and statistics can be finally obtained as:

![](images/c13-gra-0054.png)![](images/c13-gra-0055.png)

We have achieved the estimation suite, which returns standard results for the estimation of the linear model using the OLS procedure. We can read from the output of all the relevant information. Further, the estimation suite can be easily extended for additional statistics and measures and readers can thus tailor the suite to their needs.

 

## 13.9 COMPARING TWO NESTED MODELS: TOWARDS A STOPPING RULE

The linear model and linear regression are very rarely run only once for a particular data set at hand. It is more common that the researcher has to estimate a series of various linear models and decide which model has the best explanatory power. A particular procedure may look as follows. We have a dependent variable and set of candidate features which may or may not explain the dependent variable. Among those features, we also count some higher power of the features themselves. The full model we can try is the full model with all the candidate features. Such a model will be likely too complex and overfit. We can thus try to remove some of the features or impose a constraint to set the parameters corresponding to those features to be zero, and run a restricted regression. Then, we can compare the outcomes and answer the question of whether the restricted model provides the same explanatory power as the full one. If it is so, we choose the restricted model as it is more parsimonious.

Using the ![images](images/c13-i0261.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>, or, better, the adjusted ![images](images/c13-i0262.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> is one possible way to do so. Instead of comparing two numbers without any statistical insight, we can formulate a proper statistical test based on the same features as ![images](images/c13-i0263.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>, which allows us to choose between two models. The way to do so is to use the ![images](images/c13-i0264.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>‐statistic.

The ![images](images/c13-i0265.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>‐statistic is a statistic used to decide whether the nested model – indexed with index 1 – brings a statistically significant improvement in terms of the explained variance relative to the basic model – indexed with index 2. The statistics are defined in terms of the difference between the two variances as follows:

(13.68)![equation](images/c13-math-0079.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>F</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>R</mi> <mi>S</mi> <msub> <mi>S</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>R</mi> <mi>S</mi> <msub> <mi>S</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>R</mi> <mi>S</mi> <msub> <mi>S</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0266.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> is the residual sum of squares of the nested model, ![images](images/c13-i0267.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> is the same quantity for the basis model from which the nested model was derived, and ![images](images/c13-i0268.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0269.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> stands for the number of degrees of freedom including the constant for the nested and the basic models, respectively. Further, it holds ![images](images/c13-i0270.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>.

The ![images](images/c13-i0271.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>‐statistic follows the ![images](images/c13-i0272.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></mrow></math>‐distribution with ![images](images/c13-i0273.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> degrees of freedom, or,

(13.69)![equation](images/c13-math-0080.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>F</mi> <mo>&#8764;</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="script">F</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mfenced> </msub> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

The test works as follows. We start with the basic model specification and estimate the properties of the model. Then, we propose an extension of the model by adding one or more independent variables into the regression specification and run the estimation procedure. Finally, we calculate the ![images](images/c13-i0274.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>‐statistic and test the following hypothesis:

*   ![images](images/c13-i0275.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The null hypothesis states that the nested model is not worse than the basic model in terms of the unexplained variance, or, ![images](images/c13-i0276.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>.
*   ![images](images/c13-i0277.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>H</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math>: The alternative hypothesis states that the basic model is an improvement relative to the nested model and decreases the unexplained variance, ![images](images/c13-i0278.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>.

The null hypothesis ![images](images/c13-i0279.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> is rejected at significance level ![images](images/c13-i0280.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> when ![images](images/c13-i0281.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>F</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>, where critical values are to be determined from statistical tables. When we reject the null hypothesis, the alternative hypothesis can be accepted as a result of the test.

The ![images](images/c13-i0282.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>‐statistic for comparing two nested models estimated by our procedures is implemented as:

![](images/c13-gra-0056.png)

Let us define the full model as the output of the `.quantQ.ols.fit` function as:

![](images/c13-gra-0057.png)

and the restricted model, which is a nested model derived from the `olsFull` by excluding the feature `‘x1` from estimation:

![](images/c13-gra-0058.png)

The ![images](images/c13-i0283.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>‐statistic – and in fact the ![images](images/c13-i0284.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>‐test itself – can be run:

![](images/c13-gra-0059.png)![](images/c13-gra-0060.png)

The value 97.61978 represents the value of the ![images](images/c13-i0285.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>‐test to be compared against corresponding critical values. The statistics are under a null hypothesis a value drawn from ![images](images/c13-i0286.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>996</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> distribution. If we set the confidence level at ![images](images/c13-i0287.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>99</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, the corresponding critical value is 6.66039692. Since the statistics exceed the critical value, we can confidently reject the null hypothesis in favour of using the full model. This is in agreement with our knowledge of the model itself.

For the sake of completeness, let us show the adjusted ![images](images/c13-i0288.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>:

![](images/c13-gra-0061.png)![](images/c13-gra-0062.png)

The adjusted ![images](images/c13-i0289.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> confirms the conclusion of the ![images](images/c13-i0290.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>‐test.

 

### 13.9.1 Comparing Two General Models

Another alternative tool to choose between the competing models has already been mentioned: the Akaike Information Criteria. The AIC is derived on the premises of information theory, and it does not require that two compared models are nested. On the other hand, it does not constitute a proper statistical tool. Thus, AIC may prefer one model against the other, but the difference between the models can be insignificant.

Let us stick to the example from the ![images](images/c13-i0291.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>‐statistic:

![](images/c13-gra-0063.png)![](images/c13-gra-0064.png)

The full model, `olsFull`, shows lower values of the AIC and thus suggests lower information loss. Quantitatively, the difference between AICs is very large. Let us calculate the probability corresponding to the case when `olsConstrained` has less information loss compared to the full model `olsFull`:

![](images/c13-gra-0065.png)![](images/c13-gra-0066.png)

The result suggests that the probability is equal to 0, which we have to interpret as very low rather than equal to zero.

 

## 13.10 IN‐/OUT‐OF‐SAMPLE OPERATIONS

In many practical applications, we have to predict the dependent variables. The usual problem presents as follows. We have a data set, where we are provided with both independent and dependent variables. Let us further call this data set an “in‐sample”. This data set looks like the example we have used so far, and we can use all the functions developed to estimate the model. Beyond that, we are provided with another piece of data, where we know only the independent variables, i.e. features, but we do not know the dependent variable; let us call this data “out‐of‐sample.” Our task is to predict the dependent variable for the out‐of‐sample data assuming that the data generating process is the same as for the in‐sample data.

Let us create an additional out‐of‐sample data set. The data are driven by the same data generating process as we have used so far, but come entirely out of the sample and the random component is not related to the one drawn previously.

![](images/c13-gra-0067.png)

We generate the dependent variable using the same parameters. We denote the out‐of‐sample data by appending `OUT` to the variable names:

![](images/c13-gra-0068.png)

Conveniently, we arrange the data into a table and add a constant into the data set:

![](images/c13-gra-0069.png)

Even though we want to predict the dependent variable out‐of‐sample, i.e. using features we have not used for estimation of the model, we still model the true dependent variable. We will use the true values to compare how good the estimated model is at predicting the unknown values.

Let us re‐run the OLS model and store the outcome:

![](images/c13-gra-0070.png)![](images/c13-gra-0071.png)

Let us apply the estimated model on the out‐of‐sample data stored in `tabDataOUT`. We explore the values:

![](images/c13-gra-0072.png)![](images/c13-gra-0073.png)

Further, we need to compare the predicted variable with the true one (given we know the true data generating process). Let us add the true values into the table:

![](images/c13-gra-0074.png)![](images/c13-gra-0075.png)

[Figure 13.5](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0005) depicts the scatter plot between the true values of the dependent variable `tabDataMODEL[‘y]` and the predicted values `tabDataMODEL[‘yPredicted]`. The points are scattered around the diagonal line suggesting accuracy in prediction. The Gaussian nature of the errors and the small size of the sample results in no outliers.
