[**FIGURE 13.5**](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0005) Comparison between true values and the predicted ones from table `tabDataMODEL`

We further utilise the structure of the table `tabDataMODEL`. In particular, let us create a function which calculates the root mean‐squared error, or ![images](images/c13-i0292.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math>, between the true and the predicted values. The ![images](images/c13-i0293.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> is defined as:

(13.70)![equation](images/c13-math-0081.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>R</mi> <mi>M</mi> <mi>S</mi> <mi>E</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msqrt> <mrow> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>N</mi> </mfrac> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mi>P</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>c</mi> <mi>t</mi> <mi>e</mi> <msub> <mi>d</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </msqrt> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0294.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> stands for ![images](images/c13-i0295.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th true value of the dependent variable, ![images](images/c13-i0296.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> stands for ![images](images/c13-i0297.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>‐th predicted value of the dependent variable, and there are altogether ![images](images/c13-i0298.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> observations.

The root‐mean‐squared error is a popular method to compare the predicted values to true ones. There is a number of alternatives in the literature, e.g. mean absolute error (MAE), which employs the sum of absolute values rather than the sum of squares and consequent square root. The reason for this stems from the sensitivity of the ![images](images/c13-i0299.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> to outliers, which are amplified due to the squares present in the equation.

The ![images](images/c13-i0300.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> is implemented as a function, which assumes that the first two columns in an input table are the relevant ones. In fact, due to the square and square root, the order of true and predicted variables does not matter. Further, the columns beyond the second one are not considered. The function reads:

![](images/c13-gra-0076.png)

The ![images](images/c13-i0301.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> of the results in `tabDataMODEL` can be then obtained as:

![](images/c13-gra-0077.png)![](images/c13-gra-0078.png)

The value we have obtained is not saying much when it stands isolated. We need some anchor to judge the ![images](images/c13-i0302.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> value and how the model performs out‐of‐sample. The possible application is to run the estimation for two or more setups, which will differ by the independent variables included in the model. In order to do that, we implement an estimation suite, which takes three arguments: the dependent variable, the matrix of independent variables, and the flag which determines how the in‐ and out‐of‐sample splitting is performed:

![](images/c13-gra-0079.png)

The in and out sample splitting can be done in two ways: if the `inOutFlag` variable is a scalar value, it should be between 0 and 1. Then, it represents the proportion of the data which are taken as in the sample or training sample. Data are taken from the beginning. This is motivated by the time series approach, where the out‐of‐sample data is conventionally taken as the most recent. Thus, the out‐of‐sample data is the remaining piece of the data.

On the other hand, we can specify explicitly which data to take as in‐sample and which to take as out‐of‐sample. In that case, the `inOutFlag` variable is an array of boolean indicators, where true stands for being included in the training sample, and false to be in the out‐of‐sample. The array is used in conditional evaluation, and thus 0 serves as false while non‐zero values are considered as true.

Let us show the example of the routine with ![images](images/c13-i0303.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>80</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of the data to be training sample, and with remaining ![images](images/c13-i0304.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> being the verification sample:

![](images/c13-gra-0080.png)![](images/c13-gra-0081.png)

Let us extract the ![images](images/c13-i0305.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> value:

![](images/c13-gra-0082.png)![](images/c13-gra-0083.png)

Now, we remove the variable `x1` and re‐run the regression:

![](images/c13-gra-0084.png)![](images/c13-gra-0085.png)

The value of ![images](images/c13-i0306.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> is much worse compared to the case with `x1` being included. We can thus say that variable `x1` is essential to estimate the model. It brings the value out‐of‐sample.

It is worth further exploring the behaviour of the function, when there is no out‐of‐sample part of the data:

![](images/c13-gra-0086.png)![](images/c13-gra-0087.png)

We encourage the reader to change our function, such that the function is resilient to such error and can work even in the case where the out‐of‐sample is empty. This will allow us to use the function for both the estimation as well as out‐of‐sample verification.

Let us also illustrate the estimation when the `inOutFlag` indicator is an array. We want to achieve the same result as when we use scalar value of `0.8`:

![](images/c13-gra-0088.png)![](images/c13-gra-0089.png)

The two implementations of the `inOutFlag` flag variable may not necessarily exhaust all options we want to employ. It is straightforward, however, to extend the implementation and build in additional functionalities.

 

## 13.11 CROSS‐VALIDATION

Finally, we extend the concept of in/out sample testing and introduce the cross‐validation. The cross‐validation is extended out‐of‐sample testing. The primary objective is to choose which model, among those provided, fits the model the best in terms of out‐of‐sample performance. The in/out sample splitting presented in the previous section relies on one particular type of splitting. The out‐of‐sample is fixed, and this may affect the outcome of the testing. If, for instance, the out‐of‐sample period is affected by some exogenous noise, the models tested can prove rather weak while they may be valid on the rest of the sample. It would thus make sense to try various in/out splitting schemes and derive the result from a sample of such outcomes.

Cross‐validation aims to achieve exactly this. We implement one particular cross‐validation scheme, which is the ![images](images/c13-i0307.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐fold cross‐validation. It is non‐exhaustive cross‐validation, as it involves ![images](images/c13-i0308.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> (chosen number) different schemes to split the sample into in‐ and out‐of‐sample parts. For every such split, the `olsInOut` function is being run and the ![images](images/c13-i0309.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> recorded. Finally, an average over ![images](images/c13-i0310.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> such values is calculated and used as the ![images](images/c13-i0311.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> for a tested model. Let us stress that for every splitting scheme, the estimated coefficients may be different. Our objective is to test the model, which plainly means the set of chosen features, and not the estimated values themselves.

The ![images](images/c13-i0312.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐fold cross‐validation works as follows:

*   Set the parameter ![images](images/c13-i0313.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>.
*   Split the sample into ![images](images/c13-i0314.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> equally sized parts. Parts are non‐overlapping and cover the entire sample. Let us index them as ![images](images/c13-i0315.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>Data</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c13-i0316.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, such that ![images](images/c13-i0317.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>Data</mtext><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mi>j</mi></msub><msub><mtext>Data</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math>.
*   For ![images](images/c13-i0318.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>:

1.  1.  – Define ![images](images/c13-i0319.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>Data</mtext><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mtext>Data</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0320.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>Data</mtext><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mtext>Data</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>.
    2.  – Estimate the model on the ![images](images/c13-i0321.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>Data</mtext><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and verify on the ![images](images/c13-i0322.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>Data</mtext><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
    3.  – Get the corresponding ![images](images/c13-i0323.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

*   Calculate the average ![images](images/c13-i0324.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>k</mi></mfrac><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

We judge the model based on the cross‐validated value ![images](images/c13-i0325.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>V</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.

We implement the ![images](images/c13-i0326.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐fold cross‐validation in the following function. It runs in the same manner as the `olsInOut` function. The third parameter is in this case an integer denoting the number of cross‐validations ![images](images/c13-i0327.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>:

![](images/c13-gra-0090.png)

The function returns an array of ![images](images/c13-i0328.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>![images](images/c13-i0329.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math>s:

![](images/c13-gra-0091.png)![](images/c13-gra-0092.png)

We can then calculate the average value and base our decision using the cross‐validated ![images](images/c13-i0330.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math>:

![](images/c13-gra-0093.png)![](images/c13-gra-0094.png)

The value we obtained corresponds to the one we have obtained with the `olsInOut` with ![images](images/c13-i0331.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>80</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of the sample being the in‐sample. Since our sample is simulated as being homogeneous, this is the result we are expecting. The cross‐validation reveals its power on more complex data with possible heteroscedastic nature.

 

## 13.12 CONCLUSION

We have implemented the ordinary least squares method in the form of an estimation suite. The suite contains a number of additional features, which helps us to assess the performance of a fit. This proves useful when we need to make an inference from the model. Besides, we have extended the routine for the in‐sample/out‐of‐sample estimation and provided the ![images](images/c13-i0332.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐fold cross‐validation. This altogether allows us to use the suite for a number of tasks ranging from model estimation and statistical inference to robust model selection. Last but not least, it outlined a way to extend the existing framework for additional functionalities. We will illustrate the extension in a subsequent chapter, where we add regularisation into our linear models.

# CHAPTER 14  
Time Series Econometrics

 

`kdb+/q` is a very powerful language to store, manage and analyse large data sets. Time series are data sets containing a set of values of observation at discrete points in time. Time series are present in nearly all fields of applications that rely on a form of data that measures how things evolve. One of the main objectives of time series analysis is the forecast of future realisations of a random phenomenon. One typical example of time series analysis in finance is the forecast of the evolution of a financial asset based on its historical returns, sometimes with the help of exogenous variables such as macroeconomic factors or intrinsic values of the underlying instrument.

This chapter presents the main forecasting techniques in time series analysis and shows how they can be implemented in `q`. The chapter is divided into two parts. The first part introduces the autoregressive and moving average processes, stationarity and Granger causality tests and vector autoregressive models. The second part presents a possible implementation of the processes in `q`.

 

## 14.1 AUTOREGRESSIVE AND MOVING AVERAGE PROCESSES

 

### 14.1.1 Introduction

A time series is a sequential set of data constructed chronologically over consecutive times t=0,1,2,... denoted ![images](images/c14-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Time series can be discrete, where data are usually sampled at equally spaced time intervals, or continuous. Time series containing records of a single variable are called univariate. Multivariate time series refers to records of more than one variable. Time series are non-deterministic by nature and are generally affected by four main components: a trend, and cyclical, seasonal and random components. A trend measures the long-term variations in a time series. The cyclical variation of a time series describes the medium-term changes in the data set over time, such as business cycles. A cyclic pattern exists when data exhibit rises and falls that are not of a fixed period. Seasonal variations are always of the fixed and known period. They reflect the fluctuations within a year during the season. The random variations in a time series are caused by unpredictable behaviours of the data that do not follow a particular pattern.

The following sections present the class of univariate ARMA and multivariate VARMA models capable of handling trend, cyclical and seasonal behaviour of time series.

 

### 14.1.2 ![images](images/c14-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>A</mi> <mi>R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </math> Process

To efficiently forecast the future of a finite series of random variables we need to admit that these variables are somehow dependent from each other. If it is not the case, the series is purely random and not predictable. This section introduces autoregressive processes.

Formally, the autoregressive process of order ![images](images/c14-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>, denoted as ![images](images/c14-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is defined as:

[(14.1)](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-disp-0001)![equation](images/c14-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo>+</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c14-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> are the parameters of the model, ![images](images/c14-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is a constant and ![images](images/c14-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> the white noise, i.e. ![images](images/c14-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>&#949;</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c14-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c14-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. Its expectation is ![images](images/c14-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>p</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>. If ![images](images/c14-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c14-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8704;</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> : ![images](images/c14-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, the process [14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0001) is wide-sense stationary and ![images](images/c14-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is identical for all values of ![images](images/c14-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. Denoting ![images](images/c14-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c14-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>p</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, i.e.

(14.2)![equation](images/c14-math-0002.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mi>c</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The variance of [14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0001) solves ![images](images/c14-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>p</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>V</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>. If the process ![images](images/c14-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> is homoskedastic, i.e. ![images](images/c14-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8704;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> : ![images](images/c14-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>,

(14.3)![equation](images/c14-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <msubsup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </msubsup> <msubsup> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The autocovariance ![images](images/c14-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> with ![images](images/c14-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> solves:

#### *14.1.2.1 Simulation*

The autoregressive model ![images](images/c14-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.82</mn><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> can be simulated as

![](images/c14-gra-0001.png)

where`eps` is a list of random normal numbers. Given the following 5 normally distributed random numbers generated with `genBoxMuller` from `simul` namespace:

![](images/c14-gra-0002.png)

returns

![](images/c14-gra-0003.png)

which corresponds to `-0.153913 (-0.153913*0.82)+2.22843 (2.102221*0.82)-0.320418 ...`

An implementation of the simulation of an ![images](images/c14-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> model is given by the function `simAR[phi;eps]` presented in the second part of the chapter.

To illustrate the behaviour of an autoregressive process, we simulate 100 paths of the ![images](images/c14-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> process ![images](images/c14-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.99</mn><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.1</mn><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>:

![](images/c14-gra-0004.png)

and depict this in [Figure 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0001).

![FIGURE 14.1 images simulated time series](images/c14f001.png)

[**FIGURE 14.1**](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-fig-0001) ![images](images/c14-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>A</mi> <mi>R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </math> simulated time series

We see from the figure that the values at time ![images](images/c14-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> are strongly positively correlated with the previous value at time ![images](images/c14-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and slightly negatively correlated with the value at time ![images](images/c14-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>. As such, the process bounces positively and negatively depending on the value of the error term ![images](images/c14-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> given by `100?.quantQ.simul.genBoxMuller[]`.

Processes containing independent random variables are not predictable. Indeed, the ![images](images/c14-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> model with ![images](images/c14-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> is the white noise ![images](images/c14-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>. To illustrate the phenomenon, let us simulate the ![images](images/c14-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> model ![images](images/c14-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.001</mn><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>:

![](images/c14-gra-0005.png)

[Figure 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0002) captures the abovementioned ![images](images/c14-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> process. We can clearly see that the process is nearly random. The low coefficient ![images](images/c14-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow></math> does not add much information over the white noise ![images](images/c14-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

![FIGURE 14.2 Simulated process images](images/c14f002.png)

[**FIGURE 14.2**](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-fig-0002) Simulated process ![images](images/c14-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.001</mn><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>

 

#### *14.1.2.2 Estimation of *AR*(*p*) Parameters*

The parameters ![images](images/c14-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c14-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> of the autoregressive process of order ![images](images/c14-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> presented in [14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0001) can be estimated using:

*   The least square method
*   The maximum likelihood method
*   The Yule-Walker equations

 

#### *14.1.2.3 Least Square Method*

Since the innovations ![images](images/c14-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> are uncorrelated with ![images](images/c14-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c14-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>, the ordinary least square – OLS – can be applied to estimate ![images](images/c14-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. The ![images](images/c14-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> process ![images](images/c14-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>p</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> is equivalent to ![images](images/c14-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. The OLS estimator minimises ![images](images/c14-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>. The ![images](images/c14-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> process can be represented in matrix form as:

(14.5)![equation](images/c14-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="bold">X</mtext> <mo>=</mo> <mtext mathvariant="bold">Y</mtext> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c14-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">Y</mtext></mrow></math> is a ![images](images/c14-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> matrix defined as:

![equation](images/c14-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">Y</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""><mtable><mtr><mtd class="array"><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi>&#8704;</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="array"><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi>&#8704;</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></mrow></math> 

and ![images](images/c14-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math>.

The OLS estimator of the parameters ![images](images/c14-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#265;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> solves:

[(14.6)](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-disp-0008)![equation](images/c14-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mtext mathvariant="bold">Y</mtext> <mo mathvariant="bold">&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mtext mathvariant="bold">Y</mtext> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <msup> <mtext mathvariant="bold">Y</mtext> <mo mathvariant="bold">&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mtext mathvariant="bold">X</mtext> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

and the variance as:

(14.7)![equation](images/c14-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mtext mathvariant="bold">X</mtext> <mtext mathvariant="bold">t</mtext> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#265;</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <msub> <mtext mathvariant="bold">X</mtext> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="bold">t</mtext> <mtext mathvariant="bold">&#8722;</mtext> <mtext mathvariant="bold">1</mtext> </mrow> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <msub> <mtext mathvariant="bold">X</mtext> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="bold">t</mtext> <mtext mathvariant="bold">&#8722;</mtext> <mtext mathvariant="bold">p</mtext> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

A `q` implementation of the OLS estimator of ![images](images/c14-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> models is given by the function `.quantQ.ts.estARP[data;p]` explained in the second part of the chapter.

 

#### *14.1.2.4 Example*

To empirically verify the convergence of the implementation of the OLS estimator, we estimate ![images](images/c14-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></math> simulated values of an ![images](images/c14-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> model:

![equation](images/c14-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.4</mn><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>0.3</mn><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> 

with ![images](images/c14-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

![](images/c14-gra-0006.png)

The estimated parameters ![images](images/c14-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#265;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

![](images/c14-gra-0007.png)

are close to ![images](images/c14-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c14-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.4</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c14-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow></math>.

 

#### *14.1.2.5 Maximum Likelihood Estimator*

Assuming that the innovation ![images](images/c14-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are independent, the likelihood function is:

![equation](images/c14-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>&#960;</mi><mfrac><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mtext mathvariant="bold">X</mtext><mtext mathvariant="bold">t</mtext></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mtext mathvariant="bold">X</mtext><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">t</mtext><mtext mathvariant="bold">&#8722;</mtext><mtext mathvariant="bold">1</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><msub><mtext mathvariant="bold">X</mtext><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">t</mtext><mtext mathvariant="bold">&#8722;</mtext><mtext mathvariant="bold">p</mtext></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> 

Maximising ![images](images/c14-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> means minimising ![images](images/c14-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mtext mathvariant="bold">X</mtext><mtext mathvariant="bold">t</mtext></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mtext mathvariant="bold">X</mtext><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">t</mtext><mtext mathvariant="bold">&#8722;</mtext><mtext mathvariant="bold">1</mtext></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><msub><mtext mathvariant="bold">X</mtext><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">t</mtext><mtext mathvariant="bold">&#8722;</mtext><mtext mathvariant="bold">p</mtext></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> and the method is equivalent to the least square estimator [14.6](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0008).

 

#### *14.1.2.6 Yule-Walker Technique*

Starting with the ![images](images/c14-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> process ![images](images/c14-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>, we multiply both sides of the equation by ![images](images/c14-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c14-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and take the expectation:

[(14.8)](#c14.xhtml#R_c14-disp-0012)![equation](images/c14-math-0012.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>h</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mi>E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>h</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mi>E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </mrow> </msub> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mi>E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>p</mi> </mrow> </msub> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>p</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <msub> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>h</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Let us denote the autocovariance of order h ![images](images/c14-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> as ![images](images/c14-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. The [equation 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0012) can be rewritten as:

![equation](images/c14-math-0013.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> 

Dividing both sides by the variance ![images](images/c14-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and denoting the autocorrelation of order ![images](images/c14-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> by ![images](images/c14-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> we get:

(14.9)![equation](images/c14-math-0014.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Since ![images](images/c14-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c14-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>:

(14.10)![equation](images/c14-math-0015.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mo>=</mo> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mo>=</mo> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mo>=</mo> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> 

are called the Yule-Walker equations. If ![images](images/c14-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c14-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> are known, ![images](images/c14-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> are obtained by solving the system of ![images](images/c14-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> equations. Since ![images](images/c14-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c14-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>, hence:

(14.11)![equation](images/c14-math-0016.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

In general, ![images](images/c14-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are unknown and need to be estimated from the sample. Denoting the sample autocorrelation ![images](images/c14-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> where ![images](images/c14-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>:

The estimator of ![images](images/c14-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> is ![images](images/c14-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math>. As ![images](images/c14-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> is a Toeplitz matrix with non-null diagonal ![images](images/c14-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, the Durbin-Levinson algorithm can be applied. Let us rewrite the ![images](images/c14-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> process with a double suffix:

![equation](images/c14-math-0018.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">p</mtext><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">p</mtext><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">p</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> 

Starting recursively with ![images](images/c14-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi></mrow></math> we have:

For ![images](images/c14-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c14-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> with ![images](images/c14-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
