Given a square real matrix ![images](images/c16-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>, the QR decomposition is a factorisation of the matrix into a product of ![images](images/c16-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c16-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi></mrow></math> is an orthogonal matrix and ![images](images/c16-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi></mrow></math> is an upper triangular matrix. Symbolically, it reads:

(16.10)![equation](images/c16-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

The decomposition is useful for many applications, and in particular, it is a basis for the QR algorithm to find eigenvalues of the square matrix.

There is a number of procedures to find the QR decomposition. The favoured method is, for instance, Householder reflection, which is a transformation that takes a vector and reflects it about some plane or hyperplane. The hyperplane is chosen such that the sub-diagonal part of ![images](images/c16-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> disappears. Another popular method is the numerically unstable Gram-Schmidt orthogonalisation process, which can be turned into an expression for the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi></mrow></math>. Last but not least, there is a method based on Givens rotations, which will be utilised in this chapter.

  

#### *Givens rotation*

The notion of Givens rotation is a general concept which stands for a rotation in a plane spanned by two coordinate axes. In the case of three dimensions with axes denoted as ![images](images/c16-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c16-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c16-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math>, Givens rotation is for example rotation in ![images](images/c16-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> plane, where all ![images](images/c16-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> coordinates of a rotated object are constant. In linear algebra, rotation can be represented by a square matrix. For Givens rotation, such a matrix has the form of:

[(16.11)](#c16.xhtml#R_c16-disp-0011)![equation](images/c16-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mi>&#952;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8230;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8945;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> <mtd/> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> <mtd/> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>&#952;</mi> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>&#952;</mi> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> <mtd/> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8945;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> <mtd/> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>&#952;</mi> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>&#952;</mi> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> <mtd/> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> <mtd/> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8945;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi></mrow></math> has a unit on the diagonal for every row but ![images](images/c16-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th and ![images](images/c16-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>\-th one, respectively. The two selected rows denote the plane in which the rotation takes place. The rotation in a two-dimensional space is given by

(16.12)![equation](images/c16-math-0012.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>&#952;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>&#952;</mi> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>&#952;</mi> </mfenced> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>&#952;</mi> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>&#952;</mi> </mfenced> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

The rotation matrix is thus present in ![images](images/c16-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th and ![images](images/c16-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>\-th rows/columns.

The QR decomposition can be found as follows:

*   Start with the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>.
*   Start with the first column.

1.  1.  – Start with the last row, indexed with ![images](images/c16-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>. Find Givens rotation ![images](images/c16-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>, which zeros the ![images](images/c16-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> element of the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>: ![images](images/c16-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
    2.  – Take the outcome of the previous step and find a Givens rotation ![images](images/c16-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></msub></mrow></math> (we use compact notation from now onwards), which zeros the ![images](images/c16-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> element of the matrix. Thus, ![images](images/c16-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. By nature of the Givens rotation matrix, it will hold ![images](images/c16-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> as well.
    3.  – Proceed upwards until the ![images](images/c16-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> element. At the end of this step, we have a matrix where the first column has all elements but the diagonal one is equal to zero.

*   Proceed with the second column and construct Givens rotations such that elements ![images](images/c16-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> are zero, starting with ![images](images/c16-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> element. Since this procedure does not involve any element with index 1, the property of the first column remains unchanged.
*   Proceed with the same procedure right to ![images](images/c16-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>\-st column.
*   Recollect the results.

At the end of the algorithm, we have

(16.13)![equation](images/c16-math-0013.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mfenced> </msub> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mfenced> </msub> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>p</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mfenced> </msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

The matrix ![images](images/c16-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi></mrow></math> is an upper diagonal matrix by construction. If we further denote

(16.14)![equation](images/c16-math-0014.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mfenced> </msub> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mfenced> </msub> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>p</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mfenced> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

we get

(16.15)![equation](images/c16-math-0015.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

which is the decomposition we were looking for once we will de-transpose the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup></mrow></math>, i.e. by transposing it one more time.

It remains to specify how to find the particular form of the Givens rotation matrix which will make the ![images](images/c16-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> element zero. Let us consider the input matrix ![images](images/c16-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>, and our objective to find ![images](images/c16-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></mfenced></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> such that ![images](images/c16-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mfenced></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. If we recall the form of the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">G</mi></mrow></math> in [equation 16.11](#c16.xhtml#c16-disp-0011), we write directly the equation for the ![images](images/c16-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> element to be zero:

(16.16)![equation](images/c16-math-0016.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>&#952;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> </mfenced> </msub> </mfenced> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mfenced> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>&#952;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> </mfenced> </msub> </mfenced> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> </mfenced> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

which can be used to find ![images](images/c16-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mfenced></msub></mrow></math>,

(16.17)![equation](images/c16-math-0017.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#952;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> </mfenced> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">arctan</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </msub> </mfrac> </mfenced> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

This concludes the algorithm which allows us to obtain the QR decomposition for any real square matrix.

 

### 16.2.2 QR Algorithm for Eigenvalues

We can proceed with the QR algorithm, which allows us to calculate all eigenvalues for a given real square matrix ![images](images/c16-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>. The QR algorithm works as follows:

*   We initialise the algorithm as ![images](images/c16-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>.
*   The algorithm proceeds in iterative steps, with ![images](images/c16-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> denoting the iteration step, starting at ![images](images/c16-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>:

1.  1.  – Calculate the QR decomposition: ![images](images/c16-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>.
    2.  – Update the matrix: ![images](images/c16-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>.
    3.  – Increase ![images](images/c16-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> and iterate.

*   The diagonal of the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> converges to the Schur form of ![images](images/c16-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> with eigenvalues being on the diagonal.

The algorithm is based on the similarity of the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> within the iteration steps. The similarity can be shown as:

(16.18)![equation](images/c16-math-0018a.png)(16.19)![equation](images/c16-math-0018b.png)(16.20)![equation](images/c16-math-0018c.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="left"> <mo form="prefix">=</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"/> <mtd columnalign="left"> <mo form="prefix">=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msubsup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"/> <mtd columnalign="left"> <mo form="prefix">=</mo> <msubsup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mi>.</mi> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

The matrices are similar; they represent the same operator expressed in two different bases. The algorithm thus transforms the matrix into a different basis. Further, the two matrices have the same eigenvalues.

If the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> has distinct real eigenvalues, the QR algorithm converges to the upper triangular matrix – the Schur form. The QR algorithm cannot produce complex values as it involves only addition and multiplication of real numbers. If the real matrix has complex eigenvalues, or conjugate pairs of eigenvalues, the QR algorithm does not converge to the upper triangular matrix. In such a case, the matrix will converge to a block-upper triangular form. Elements in the block will never converge – they correspond to the oscillation in the complex plane while those outside of the block carry the information about eigenvalues.

The convergence criteria of the algorithm cannot thus be formed merely by checking the upper diagonal form as the blocks may be present and are perfectly valid. Thus, it is more suitable to monitor the performance of the algorithm in a controlled way with regularly overseeing the outcome of the algorithm. Alternatively, we may use some upper bound on the errors and construct the indicator for the shape of the matrix. The algorithm as is formulated above is simple, but we have to pay the price by rather expensive calculations and oversight. There are specific techniques which speed up convergence in terms of numerical cost but they are beyond our scope.

The QR algorithm aims to find all the eigenvalues at the same time. It is possible to formulate a simplified version of the algorithm, when only the largest value is being sought. In such a case, instead of multiplying by the matrix, we multiply the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> by a vector. When the vector is normalised after every iteration step, the iteration converges towards the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue. This simplified method is thus suitable for searching the properties of the largest eigenvalue only.

The QR algorithm has an obvious weakness in the underlying assumption imposed on the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>. If the matrix does not have distinct real eigenvalues, the method fails. In such a case, a more advanced method is needed. The purpose of this section is to introduce the reader into the numerical calculations of eigensystems. In order to cover all the possibilities and provide efficient algorithms in such cases, we would have to devote the entire book to this goal.

 

### 16.2.3 Inverse Iteration

Let us assume that we are equipped with the knowledge of the complete set of distinct real eigenvalues. Our objective is to find corresponding eigenvectors. We will focus on the inverse (power) iteration algorithm. The algorithm is an iterative procedure which for a given approximation of the eigenvalue finds the corresponding eigenvector, or its approximation. Let us consider the square real ![images](images/c16-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> matrix ![images](images/c16-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> with true eigenvalues ![images](images/c16-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Further, we denote the approximation of the eigenvalue by indexing the variable with bar, i.e. ![images](images/c16-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mtext>&#8216;</mtext></msup></mrow></math> being a close approximation to ![images](images/c16-i0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math>.

The following procedure describes the inverse iteration algorithm:

*   Start with the approximated eigenvalue ![images](images/c16-i0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mtext>&#8216;</mtext></msup></mrow></math> to the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0123.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>.
*   Initialise the eigenvector ![images](images/c16-i0124.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>.
*   The algorithm proceeds in iterative steps, with ![images](images/c16-i0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> denoting the iteration step, starting at ![images](images/c16-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>:

1.  1.  – Calculate the updated vector: ![images](images/c16-i0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mtext>&#8216;</mtext></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>.
    2.  – Normalise vector ![images](images/c16-i0128.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> by its norm: ![images](images/c16-i0129.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.

*   Vector ![images](images/c16-i0130.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> converges to ![images](images/c16-i0131.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>&#955;</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

The numerical procedure requires us to calculate ![images](images/c16-i0132.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mtext>&#8216;</mtext></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>. This can be done either by solving

(16.21)![equation](images/c16-math-0019.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mtext>&#8216;</mtext> </msup> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

or by calculating the inverse of ![images](images/c16-i0133.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mtext>&#8216;</mtext></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Both approaches are valid; they differ by the numerical implementations.

Further, the closer ![images](images/c16-i0134.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mtext>&#8216;</mtext></msup></mrow></math> is to ![images](images/c16-i0135.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math>, the faster is the convergence. The algorithm can for very good approximations of eigenvalue converge in very few steps. If, on the other hand, the approximation is not good, the algorithm can converge to an eigenvector of another eigenvalue. The iteration also involves normalisation. We have chosen the ![images](images/c16-i0136.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> norm, where other normalisations are possible as well. The normalisation assures that convergence proceeds in terms of the orientation of the iterated vector and prevents an explosion of the vector in its norm.

In the next section, we implement both methods.

 

## 16.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF EIGENSYSTEM CALCULATION

We implement the numerical procedure to calculate the eigensystem for a real matrix ![images](images/c16-i0137.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> of dimension ![images](images/c16-i0138.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>. First, we need to generate a unit matrix:

![](images/c16-gra-0001.png)

which works as expected:

![](images/c16-gra-0002.png)![](images/c16-gra-0003.png)

We have stored the unit matrix into a temporary variable for further numerical checks. For the sake of curiosity, let us provide an alternative implementation of the unit matrix:

![](images/c16-gra-0004.png)

The definition is identical to the first one, as we can see from

![](images/c16-gra-0005.png)![](images/c16-gra-0006.png)

We encourage readers to compare and time the two approaches above and come up with further definitions using other verbs and/or adverbs.

The QR algorithm as introduced above is built upon the Givens rotation. We implement a function, which takes four arguments: the dimension of the matrix, the two coordinates ![images](images/c16-i0139.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0140.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>, and the angle of rotation ![images](images/c16-i0141.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math>, and returns the matrix with Givens rotation:

![](images/c16-gra-0007.png)

Let us produce the Givens matrix in a 4-dimensional space with a rotation in the space spanned by 2nd and 4th axis by angle of ![images](images/c16-i0142.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>:

![](images/c16-gra-0008.png)![](images/c16-gra-0009.png)

The form of the matrix is as expected. Let us rotate the unit matrix by such a matrix:

![](images/c16-gra-0010.png)![](images/c16-gra-0011.png)

The rotated unit matrix is equal to the rotation matrix itself. The example also reminds us of the `mmu` verb we use to multiply two matrices in `q`.

 

### 16.3.1 QR Decomposition

Let us proceed with the QR decomposition. Function `QRdecomp` implements the procedure. The input is the matrix we wish to decompose. The outcome of the function is three matrices: the original matrix, the rotated matrix, and the rotation matrix. The function itself contains iterative procedure, where we iterate over all coordinates which need to be set to zero. We have kept the iterated function within the main function and not separated it. The reason that it is important to run the function as `coord` is defined. We have stressed that in the description of the algorithm.

![](images/c16-gra-0012.png)

Let us apply the QR decomposition function on the product of two Givens rotation matrices. The first acts in 2nd and 4th coordinate space with angle ![images](images/c16-i0143.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> while the second one acts in 2nd and 3rd coordinate space with the same angle ![images](images/c16-i0144.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>.

![](images/c16-gra-0013.png)

We have saved the outcome into a temporary variable as it contains three matrices, which we will explore one by one. First, the input matrix reads:

![](images/c16-gra-0014.png)![](images/c16-gra-0015.png)

We encourage reader to verify that this matrix indeed corresponds to a stacked ration.

The second matrix contained in the outcome of the function is the rotated matrix. The matrix should be upper diagonal. Since we have created the matrix as two Givens rotations, the outcome matrix will be unit matrix (which is upper diagonal):

![](images/c16-gra-0016.png)![](images/c16-gra-0017.png)

Finally, the last matrix which is returned by the function is the rotation matrix:

![](images/c16-gra-0018.png)![](images/c16-gra-0019.png)

The rotation matrix corresponds to unwinding the two rotations: First, we rotate in the space spanned by the 2nd and 3rd coordinate by angle ![images](images/c16-i0145.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>. Then, we rotate in the 2nd and 4th coordinate space by angle ![images](images/c16-i0146.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>. We can verify it as:

![](images/c16-gra-0020.png)![](images/c16-gra-0021.png)

This verifies the functionality of the QR decomposition function.

We will use the QR decomposition to obtain the eigenvalues. The QR algorithm is an iterative procedure which iteratively employs the QR decomposition and updates the matrix. First, we implement the iteration. The input is the dictionary with a matrix, which is input in the function `QRdecomp`. In the beginning, the input matrix is being read. The QR decomposition is then found and the new iterated matrix is calculated as a product of the upper triangular matrix and the transposed orthogonal matrix. Besides, it contains counter to be able to control the iterations:

![](images/c16-gra-0022.png)

Let us define an example matrix we will use for the rest of this chapter for eigensystem calculation.

![](images/c16-gra-0023.png)![](images/c16-gra-0024.png)

Initialise the bucket in order to run the function:

![](images/c16-gra-0025.png)

and run the function explicitly in ten iterations:

![](images/c16-gra-0026.png)

which gives following output:

![](images/c16-gra-0027.png)

The matrix is getting shape close to the upper diagonal matrix. There are elements below the main diagonal which are very small. We need to wrap the iteration into a function which will control for precision. Function `algoQR` is such a function, which accepts as an argument dictionary with matrix to be decomposed, counter, and two control variables: the maximum number of iterations and the numerical precision:

![](images/c16-gra-0028.png)

Function iteratively transforms matrix by using the QR algorithm. There are two checks for the iterations to stop. The algorithm stops if the number of iterations exceeds the threshold or all the numbers below the diagonal are within a specialised numerical precision.

We initialise the input bucket:

![](images/c16-gra-0029.png)

and run the function, where we are interested in the upper diagonal matrix:

![](images/c16-gra-0030.png)

The matrix which is produced by the algorithm reads:

![](images/c16-gra-0031.png)

The elements below diagonal are smaller than the precision. The elements on the diagonal are the eigenvalues of the matrix `matExa`. We provide finally a routine which will extract the eigenvalues from the bucket and sort the eigenvalues in a descending order:

![](images/c16-gra-0032.png)

where eigenvalues are being produced as:

![](images/c16-gra-0033.png)![](images/c16-gra-0034.png) 

### 16.3.2 Inverse Iteration

At this step, we are equipped with the eigenvalues calculated by the QR algorithm. We will now implement the inverse iteration algorithm, which will for every eigenvalue numerically recover the eigenvector.

First, we define an ![images](images/c16-i0147.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> matrix norm, which we need within the algorithm:

![](images/c16-gra-0035.png)

and verify it on the matrix we use:

![](images/c16-gra-0036.png)![](images/c16-gra-0037.png)

We define the `inverseIteration` function, which takes four arguments: the matrix, the eigenvalues, the numerical tolerance, and the maximum number of iterations. Our implementation of the iterative algorithm uses the inverse matrix, `inv`. The problem using the matrix inversion occurs in the situation when we are provided with the exact eigenvalue. In such a case, the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0148.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mtext>&#8216;</mtext></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> is singular and cannot be inverted.

In order to overcome the singularity in the iterative algorithm, we have introduced perturbation into the eigenvalue. Thus, when we are provided with the exact eigenvalue, we distort it such that we have only an approximate solution. For such a solution, the iterative algorithm works and can proceed. We perform the check `0<sum{[x] (x=0nf) or (x=0wf) or (x=-0wf)} each raze inv[invMat]` at the beginning of each iteration. The perturbation is applied only during the initial call as it amends the eigenvalue directly. The function returns the eigenvector and we are thus not exposed to the perturbed value.

The normalisation within the iterations is using ![images](images/c16-i0149.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> matrix norm. Besides, in order to prevent flipping of the eigenvector by a multiplicative factor ![images](images/c16-i0150.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, we enforce the first element of the eigenvector to be non-negative. The function starts with a random vector with components being independently drawn from the uniform distribution defined over ![images](images/c16-i0151.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>;</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>. At the end of the iterations, the eigenvector is normalised by ![images](images/c16-i0152.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> norm to the unit modulus.

The function reads:

![](images/c16-gra-0038.png)

We calculate the eigenvectors to eigenvalues we have found in the previous section:

![](images/c16-gra-0039.png)

and revise the eigenvectors one by one:

![](images/c16-gra-0040.png)![](images/c16-gra-0041.png)![](images/c16-gra-0042.png)![](images/c16-gra-0043.png)![](images/c16-gra-0044.png)![](images/c16-gra-0045.png)![](images/c16-gra-0046.png)![](images/c16-gra-0047.png)

We can verify the eigenvectors by checking the property of eigenvectors, i.e. when the eigenvector is multiplied by the matrix itself and divided by the corresponding eigenvalue, the eigenvector is recovered.

![](images/c16-gra-0048.png)![](images/c16-gra-0049.png)![](images/c16-gra-0050.png)![](images/c16-gra-0051.png)![](images/c16-gra-0052.png)![](images/c16-gra-0053.png)![](images/c16-gra-0054.png)![](images/c16-gra-0055.png)

Indeed, the eigenvectors are recovered within the working numerical precision. That is why we have not used `∼` to compare the eigenvectors with their numerically recovered values.

Finally, we wrap the functions into a numerical suite which accepts as an input the matrix and returns sorted the list of eigenvectors in descending order, and a corresponding list of eigenvectors. The values are wrapped in the dictionary:

![](images/c16-gra-0056.png)

Finally, we obtain the full solution with the eigensystem of the matrix:

![](images/c16-gra-0057.png)![](images/c16-gra-0058.png)

We have flipped the dictionary to present the result in the form of a table. Every row corresponds to the different eigenvalue/eigenvector.

We encourage the readers to review the provided functions and suggest the generalisations. The obvious place to improve the provided algorithms is in the fact where we are perturbing the case when we have the correct eigenvalue. The more suitable solution would be to use the correct eigenvalues directly. Further, the algorithm does not work perfectly when there is a degenerate eigenvalue. This is a place for improvement as well.

 

## 16.4 THE DATA MATRIX AND THE PRINCIPAL COMPONENT ANALYSIS

The principal component analysis (PCA) is a popular statistical technique which transforms a set of data into a new orthogonal basis such that directions of the new basis are ordered in terms of variance contribution to the overall variance. This was introduced by Pearson (1901). In this section, we consider a ![images](images/c16-i0153.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional vector of features, where each feature is observed ![images](images/c16-i0154.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> times. Let us denote the ![images](images/c16-i0155.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> dimensional matrix of data as ![images](images/c16-i0156.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>. First, we discuss the data matrix and its properties and then use the findings to introduce the PCA.

 

### 16.4.1 The Data Matrix

In general, the data matrix![images](images/c16-i0157.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> is rectangular – not necessarily square. Eigenvalues, as we have seen in previous paragraphs, are not defined for rectangular matrices. There is thus another, closely related notion: singular values. The right and left singular values for a rectangular matrix ![images](images/c16-i0158.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> are the square roots of the eigenvalues of ![images](images/c16-i0159.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0160.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup></mrow></math>, respectively. The eigenvectors corresponding to those eigenvalues are referred to as the right and left singular vectors, respectively. What exactly do these matrices, ![images](images/c16-i0161.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0162.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup></mrow></math>, mean in terms of statistics if ![images](images/c16-i0163.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> is a data matrix?

Mathematically, we could model our observations as a ![images](images/c16-i0164.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional vector random variable ![images](images/c16-i0165.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math>. While it is customary to use uppercase letters for random variables, we shall use a lowercase letter for now, to distinguish the random variable ![images](images/c16-i0166.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> from the data matrix ![images](images/c16-i0167.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>. It is also customary to deal with column vectors, rather than with row vectors, so we shall assume that ![images](images/c16-i0168.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> is a column vector, i.e. ![images](images/c16-i0169.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>&#8477;</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Let us denote that this is inconsistent with the way the data is presented in the data matrix: the samples – which we model as realisations of the random variable ![images](images/c16-i0170.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> – occur as the rows of ![images](images/c16-i0171.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>, not as columns.

Let us define the covariance matrix. Namely, let ![images](images/c16-i0172.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> be a ![images](images/c16-i0173.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional random vector, ![images](images/c16-i0174.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>&#8477;</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Its covariance matrix is given by

(16.22)![equation](images/c16-math-0020.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mo mathvariant="bold-italic">&#931;</mo> <mo>:</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Cov</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> </mfenced> <mo>:</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Var</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#54588;</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#54588;</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> </mfenced> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#54588;</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> </mfenced> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> </mfenced> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msup> <mi>&#8477;</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#215;</mo> <mi>p</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

The covariance matrix is a generalisation of the variance for higher (than one) dimensional random variables: we may still write ![images](images/c16-i0175.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Var</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> instead of ![images](images/c16-i0176.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Cov</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>. It has nothing to do with a specific data sample (equivalently, with a specific data matrix); it has everything to do with the random variable ![images](images/c16-i0177.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> used to model the data. This random variable is a mathematical abstraction/idealisation, unlike a specific data sample.

The covariance matrix is not a random quantity, but we can only write down a specific covariance matrix if we assume that we “know” the distribution of the random variable ![images](images/c16-i0178.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math>; quite often we only pretend that we know it. Here we assumed that ![images](images/c16-i0179.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> is a column vector, i.e. ![images](images/c16-i0180.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>&#8477;</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

First, let us answer the question, what is the significance of the ![images](images/c16-i0181.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>\-th entry of the covariance matrix ![images](images/c16-i0182.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo mathvariant="bold-italic">&#931;</mo></mrow></math>? If we write the ![images](images/c16-i0183.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional random vector ![images](images/c16-i0184.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> as

(16.23)![equation](images/c16-math-0021.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

then the ![images](images/c16-i0185.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>\-th entry of ![images](images/c16-i0186.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo mathvariant="bold-italic">&#931;</mo></mrow></math> is the covariance between the scalar random variables ![images](images/c16-i0187.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0188.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>:

(16.24)![equation](images/c16-math-0022.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#931;</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Cov</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>j</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> </mfenced> <mo>:</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#54588;</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#54588;</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>j</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#54588;</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>j</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where we notice that, in this notation for covariance of two random variables, ![images](images/c16-i0189.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Cov</mi></mrow></math> has two arguments, whereas, in the notation ![images](images/c16-i0190.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Cov</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> for the covariance matrix, ![images](images/c16-i0191.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Cov</mi></mrow></math> has a single argument.

The key properties of covariance matrices are: first, it is symmetric, and second, it is positive semidefinite. To show that ![images](images/c16-i0192.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo mathvariant="bold-italic">&#931;</mo></mrow></math> is symmetric:

When we work with data, we often say we calculate covariance matrix and talk about values of the covariance matrix coming from the given sample. In this case, we talk about the sample covariance matrix, which is given by

(16.31)![equation](images/c16-math-0025.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msup> <mi>&#8477;</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#215;</mo> <mi>p</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where![images](images/c16-i0195.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the ![images](images/c16-i0196.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th row of the data matrix ![images](images/c16-i0197.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> written as a column vector and ![images](images/c16-i0198.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math> is the sample mean, also written as a column vector. We are still modelling ![images](images/c16-i0199.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> as a random variable, but now we have a data sample; for a concrete data sample (for a concrete data matrix ![images](images/c16-i0200.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>), we could obtain a specific matrix ![images](images/c16-i0201.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi></mrow></math> and use it as an estimator of the covariance matrix ![images](images/c16-i0202.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Cov</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> of the hypothetical random variable ![images](images/c16-i0203.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math>.

Thus the sample covariance matrix is a generalisation of the sample covariance, whereas the covariance matrix is a generalisation of the variance of a random variable. However, people often use the term “covariance matrix” for both these things, so beware of the confusion!

The sample covariance matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite. We will leave it to the reader to construct proof of this assertion. Please keep in mind that we have to use sums over all realisations in the sample data ![images](images/c16-i0204.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>. Another important feature of the sample covariance matrix is to be an unbiased estimator of the true covariance matrix ![images](images/c16-i0205.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Cov</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c16-i0206.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math>. This assertion follows from:
