and![images](images/c16-i0349.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#923;</mi></mrow></math> a diagonal matrix with ![images](images/c16-i0350.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mrow></math>’s eigenvalues as its diagonal entries:

(16.74)![equation](images/c16-math-0058.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#923;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> <mtd/> <mtd/> <mtd/> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> <mtd/> <mtd/> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd/> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8945;</mi> </mtd> <mtd/> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd/> <mtd/> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

Since, for any matrices ![images](images/c16-i0351.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0352.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi></mrow></math>, such that both products ![images](images/c16-i0353.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0354.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> exist, ![images](images/c16-i0355.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="normal">tr</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext mathvariant="normal">tr</mtext><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>,

(16.75)![equation](images/c16-math-0059.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="normal">tr</mtext> <mspace width="0.15em"/> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mtext mathvariant="normal">tr</mtext> <mspace width="0.15em"/> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#923;</mi> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mtext mathvariant="normal">tr</mtext> <mspace width="0.15em"/> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#923;</mi> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mtext mathvariant="normal">tr</mtext> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#923;</mi> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

Thus the first ![images](images/c16-i0356.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c16-i0357.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>, principal components account for the proportion

(16.76)![equation](images/c16-math-0060.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msubsup> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <msubsup> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </math> 

of the total variation.

 

### 16.4.5 Dimensionality Reduction

Finding the patterns in the data which can help us to explain the dependent variable suffers the bias-variance trade-off. This can be explained as follows. The squared bias typically decreases with increasing model complexity, and variance increases with increasing model complexity, and total error is the sum of the squared bias and variance components, so there is usually an optimal model complexity at which the total error is minimised.

Restricting complexity can be achieved by considering only a subset of available features. In particular, we may truncate our vector at ![images](images/c16-i0358.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> columns by removing the columns ![images](images/c16-i0359.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>:

(16.77)![equation](images/c16-math-0061.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mtd> <mtd/> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mtd> <mtd/> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msup> <mi>&#8477;</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#215;</mo> <mi>p</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

Thus we keep only the first ![images](images/c16-i0360.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> principal components:

(16.78)![equation](images/c16-math-0062.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <mo>:</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo mathvariant="bold-italic">&#8242;</mo> </msup> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msup> <mi>&#8477;</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#215;</mo> <mi>d</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

Since

(16.79)![equation](images/c16-math-0063.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Var</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Var</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Var</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mfenced> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mo>&#8776;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#923;</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

and, similarly,

(16.80)![equation](images/c16-math-0064.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Var</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi> <mi>d</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#923;</mi> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

the truncated principal components decrease variance

![equation](images/c16-math-0065.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="normal">tr</mtext><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#923;</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#923;</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> 

at the expense of introducing bias.

 

### 16.4.6 PCA Regression (PCR)

The natural extension of the dimensionality reduction using the PCA is the PCA regression, or PCR. Recall that, in linear regression, we work with the model

(16.81)![equation](images/c16-math-0066.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mover class="overset"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mover> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c16-i0361.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>&#8477;</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> is the output vector; ![images](images/c16-i0362.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover class="overset"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></mover><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>&#8477;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mi>p</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is the data matrix ![images](images/c16-i0363.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> – our input, possibly augmented with a vector of ones on the left to allow intercept (in which case ![images](images/c16-i0364.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>p</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>) or not (in which case ![images](images/c16-i0365.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>p</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>); ![images](images/c16-i0366.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>&#8477;</mi><msup><mi>p</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></msup></mrow></math> is the vector of parameters of the model, and it is our task to estimate this vector; and ![images](images/c16-i0367.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>&#8477;</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> is the vector random variable representing some noise or disturbance.

Instead of regressing ![images](images/c16-i0368.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> on ![images](images/c16-i0369.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math>, we could regress ![images](images/c16-i0370.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> on ![images](images/c16-i0371.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow></math>:

(16.82)![equation](images/c16-math-0067.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mover class="overset"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mover> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#947;</mi> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#951;</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c16-i0372.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover class="overset"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></mover><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>&#8477;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is the matrix of principal component scores ![images](images/c16-i0373.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi></mrow></math>, possibly augmented with a vector of ones on the left to allow intercept (in which case ![images](images/c16-i0374.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>) or not (in which case ![images](images/c16-i0375.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>); ![images](images/c16-i0376.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#947;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>&#8477;</mi><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></msup></mrow></math> is the vector of parameters of the model, and it is our task to estimate this vector; and ![images](images/c16-i0377.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#951;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>&#8477;</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></math> is the vector random variable representing some noise or disturbance.

The properties of the estimator ![images](images/c16-i0378.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#947;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow></math> can be derived as follows: from linear regression theory, we know that the ordinary least squares (OLS) estimator of ![images](images/c16-i0379.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#947;</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow></math> is

(16.83)![equation](images/c16-math-0068.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#947;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msubsup> <mover class="overset"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mover> <mi>d</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msubsup> <msub> <mover class="overset"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mover> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <msubsup> <mover class="overset"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mover> <mi>d</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msubsup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

We know that this estimator is unbiased,

(16.84)![equation](images/c16-math-0069.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#54588;</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#947;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi> <mi>d</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#54588;</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#947;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#947;</mi> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

and that its variance is given by

(16.85)![equation](images/c16-math-0070.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">Var</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#947;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>d</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#951;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msubsup> <mover class="overset"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mover> <mi>d</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msubsup> <msub> <mover class="overset"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mover> <mi>d</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

This concludes the theory behind the PCA. Since this is a popular method, we have devoted more space to several related topics. In the following section, we utilise our implementation of the eigensystem and provide utility for calculation of the PCA.

 

## 16.5 IMPLEMENTATION OF PCA

Let us implement the basics of PCA. We use the calculation of eigensystem provided at the initial part of this chapter. Let us start with simulating the sample data we use:

![](images/c16-gra-0059.png)

Let us provide a function, which calculates the covariance matrix efficiently:

![](images/c16-gra-0060.png)

The PCA is in fact applying the eigensystem decomposition on the sample covariance matrix:

![](images/c16-gra-0061.png)![](images/c16-gra-0062.png)

We have stated that the eigenvectors corresponding to the individual principal components are orthogonal – in fact, they are orthonormal due to unit norm. We can verify this as:

![](images/c16-gra-0063.png)![](images/c16-gra-0064.png)

The second and third components are not zero. This is due to our small sample and our numerical precision. Let us centre the data set:

![](images/c16-gra-0065.png)

We can verify the data are centred as:

![](images/c16-gra-0066.png)![](images/c16-gra-0067.png)

We can now apply the principal components to calculate the variance captured by each of the components: the first component captures

![](images/c16-gra-0068.png)![](images/c16-gra-0069.png)

variance. Analogously for second and third components, we get:

![](images/c16-gra-0070.png)![](images/c16-gra-0071.png)

and

![](images/c16-gra-0072.png)![](images/c16-gra-0073.png)

respectively.

Let us confirm the properties of the principal components. In particular, the correlation of the first principal component with itself is obviously one:

![](images/c16-gra-0074.png)![](images/c16-gra-0075.png)

where the correlation between the first and second component is close to zero:

![](images/c16-gra-0076.png)![](images/c16-gra-0077.png)

despite the fact that data itself is correlated:

![](images/c16-gra-0078.png)![](images/c16-gra-0079.png)

We can finally construct the routine which provides the PCA decomposition and on top of that the relative variance each component captures. The following function takes as an argument the matrix with data and returns the PCA decomposition:

![](images/c16-gra-0080.png)![](images/c16-gra-0081.png)

Let us apply the function on our sample data.

![](images/c16-gra-0082.png)

First, we examine the `‘tab`, which contains the PCA decomposition and basic information about each component:

![](images/c16-gra-0083.png)![](images/c16-gra-0084.png)

We see that first component is capturing slightly more than ![images](images/c16-i0380.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of total variance while the first two components are together describing approximately ![images](images/c16-i0381.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>86</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of variance.

Further, the PCA function returns as well the `‘dataTransformed` element, which is the table with transformed data, component by component. We can see that by examining the correlation between the first two columns of the transformed data set:

![](images/c16-gra-0085.png)![](images/c16-gra-0086.png)

while original data carry correlation:

![](images/c16-gra-0087.png)![](images/c16-gra-0088.png)

This concludes the PCA in `q`. We leave it to readers as an interesting exercise to develop the routine to perform the PCR. All the necessary components are within this book; they just need to be appropriately piped together. Such a routine will nicely complement the provided algorithms.

 

## 16.6 APPENDIX: DETERMINANT

In this section, we provide an algorithm to calculate the determinant of the matrix. We need a determinant in the central part of this chapter to calculate eigensystems. The determinant of a matrix also proves a necessary piece of theory/toolset for data analytics.

 

### 16.6.1 Theory

Let us consider a square real matrix ![images](images/c16-i0382.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>:

(16.86)![equation](images/c16-math-0071.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>11</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>12</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mi>n</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>21</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>22</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mi>n</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8945;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mn>2</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mi>n</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

For every square real-valued matrix (we do omit the complex matrices in this section, though the determinant can be extended to complex matrix domain), we can define the determinant as a real-valued function, with inputs being the elements of the matrix. The determinant is a polynomial of the order 2 in entries of the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0383.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>. The determinant is usually denoted as ![images](images/c16-i0384.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>, or, ![images](images/c16-i0385.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></math>. The determinant is met across the various topics in the linear algebra. In this chapter, we have encountered the determinant when we have been constructing the algorithm to calculate the eigensystem of a real matrix. It can be further used to determine the linear independence of a system of ![images](images/c16-i0386.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> vectors, or calculating Jacobians.

The determinant also has a geometric interpretation. Let us consider a unit ![images](images/c16-i0387.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional cube and ![images](images/c16-i0388.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional square matrix ![images](images/c16-i0389.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>. The columns of the matrix can be considered as edges which define the parallelotope, with one corner being at the origin. The parallelotope is a deformed cube, which is deformed by the matrix transformation ![images](images/c16-i0390.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>. In 2-dimensions, the parallelotope is a parallelogram, which is nothing but deformed square. Then, the determinant is the volume of such a parallelotope.

Before we dive into the definition of the determinant, we first present the useful properties of the determinant:

*   ![images](images/c16-i0391.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </math> for any unit matrix ![images](images/c16-i0392.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi></mrow></math>.
*   ![images](images/c16-i0393.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </math>.
*   ![images](images/c16-i0394.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> </mfenced> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </math>.
*   ![images](images/c16-i0395.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> </mfenced> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> where matrices ![images](images/c16-i0396.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0397.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi></mrow></math> are square matrices of the same dimension.
*   ![images](images/c16-i0398.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>c</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>c</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msup> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> with ![images](images/c16-i0399.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> being a constant.
*   ![images](images/c16-i0400.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi> </mfenced> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> for matrices ![images](images/c16-i0401.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0402.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi></mrow></math> being of the same size and both positive semidefinite.
*   ![images](images/c16-i0403.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="normal">tr</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>A</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>A</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> with ![images](images/c16-i0404.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="normal">tr</mtext></mrow></math> being the trace of a square matrix.
*   ![images](images/c16-i0405.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>A</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#8719;</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math> where ![images](images/c16-i0406.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> are eigenvalues of the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0407.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>.

The listed properties are useful when we manipulate with determinants.

 

### 16.6.2 Techniques to Calculate a Determinant

In the following, we consider matrix ![images](images/c16-i0408.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> to be a square matrix of the dimension ![images](images/c16-i0409.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. Let us define a procedure to calculate the determinant recursively.

  

#### *Trivial case*

Let us start with trivial case of ![images](images/c16-i0410.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. In such a case, we can consider a scalar number to be a matrix of the dimension ![images](images/c16-i0411.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. The determinant in this case is obvious:

(16.87)![equation](images/c16-math-0072.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>11</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>11</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

i.e. the constant itself.

We have stated in the introductory part that a determinant is a polynomial of order ![images](images/c16-i0412.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> in the matrix elements. This is satisfied in this case.

 

#### *Leibniz formula*

Let us proceed with ![images](images/c16-i0413.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>. In this case, the determinant is defined as:

(16.88)![equation](images/c16-math-0073.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>11</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>12</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>21</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>22</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>11</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>22</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mn>12</mn> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>21</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

which is polynomial of order 2 in the matrix elements.

 

#### *Sarrus rule*

In the case of ![images](images/c16-i0414.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, the determinant is given as:

(16.89)![equation](images/c16-math-0074.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>11</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>12</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>13</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>21</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>22</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>23</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>31</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>32</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>33</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>11</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>22</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>33</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>12</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>23</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>31</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>13</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>21</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>32</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>13</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>22</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>31</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>12</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>21</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>33</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>11</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>23</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>32</mn> </msub> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

The formula is polynomial of order 3 in matrix elements and it becomes quite cumbersome. Luckily, there is simple tool to get this formula, called Sarrus rule. We start with a matrix ![images](images/c16-i0415.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> and append the first and the second column to the right-hand side of the matrix:

(16.90)![equation](images/c16-math-0075.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>11</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>12</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>13</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>21</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>22</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>23</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>31</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>32</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>33</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>&#8594;</mo> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>11</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>12</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>13</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>11</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>12</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>21</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>22</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>23</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>21</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>22</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>31</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>32</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>33</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>31</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>32</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mi>,</mi> </mrow> </math> 

and then we form three products of elements placed on the diagonals: ![images](images/c16-i0416.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>11</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>22</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>33</mn></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c16-i0417.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>12</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>23</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>31</mn></msub></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c16-i0418.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>13</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>21</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>32</mn></msub></mrow></math>, respectively. Then, we form three analogous products lying on the anti-diagonal ![images](images/c16-i0419.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>13</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>22</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>31</mn></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c16-i0420.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>12</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>21</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>33</mn></msub></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c16-i0421.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>11</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>23</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>32</mn></msub></mrow></math>, respectively. Finally, the determinant is calculated as a sum of the six products, where those originating from the diagonal are added with ![images](images/c16-i0422.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> sign while those from the anti-diagonal come with ![images](images/c16-i0423.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math> sign.

 

#### *Laplace formula*

For the general case of ![images](images/c16-i0424.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> (which includes any ![images](images/c16-i0425.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>), we can use recursive Laplace formula to calculate the determinant. First, we define a minor of a matrix. For a square ![images](images/c16-i0426.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> matrix ![images](images/c16-i0427.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>, the minor ![images](images/c16-i0428.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">M</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the determinant of ![images](images/c16-i0429.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced><mo>&#215;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> matrix, which is obtained from the matrix ![images](images/c16-i0430.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> by removing all ![images](images/c16-i0431.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8226;</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0432.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo>&#8226;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> elements, i.e. by removing ![images](images/c16-i0433.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th row and ![images](images/c16-i0434.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>\-th column.

Second, we define the cofactor, which is defined as ![images](images/c16-i0435.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">M</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Then, the determinant of a matrix ![images](images/c16-i0436.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> is defined as expansion along the ![images](images/c16-i0437.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th row:

[(16.91)](#c16.xhtml#R_c16-disp-0076)![equation](images/c16-math-0076.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>j</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mfenced> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msup> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">M</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

Alternatively, we may define expansion along the ![images](images/c16-i0438.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>\-th column as

(16.92)![equation](images/c16-math-0077.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="normal">det</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mfenced> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msup> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">M</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mi>.</mi> </mrow> </math> 

The determinant of the ![images](images/c16-i0439.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> matrix is thus expressed as a sum of cofactors, where each cofactor is in fact determinant of the ![images](images/c16-i0440.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced><mo>&#215;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> matrix. This is a basis of a recursive formula we can use to calculate any determinant.

 

### 16.6.3 Implementation of the Determinant

Let us implement the calculation of the determinant for a square matrix ![images](images/c16-i0441.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>. In the implementation below, we use the recursive relationship provided in [equation 16.91](#c16.xhtml#c16-disp-0076). We expand the matrix always along the first row. This is easy to implement but not the most efficient approach, as expansion along the row/column with the most significant proportion of zeros can save computational time.

Let us proceed with the function which takes as an input a square matrix, and two indices for row/column, and returns a matrix which is used to calculate the minor:

![](images/c16-gra-0089.png)

Let us test it:

![](images/c16-gra-0090.png)![](images/c16-gra-0091.png)

Then, we proceed directly with the function, which calculates the determinant. In order to illustrate the methods for calculating the determinant discussed in the previous section, we use different methods based on the dimensionality of the problem. In particular, for ![images](images/c16-i0442.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, we use the Sarrus rule explicitly, even though it is not necessary, as the Laplace expansion would be sufficient. For the Laplace expansion, we use recursion. In particular, we use `.z.s`, which refers to the function itself when called from within the function. We could use the name of the function itself instead of the “dotzetdotes” construct. The function reads:

Let us test the calculation of the determinant for ![images](images/c16-i0443.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>:

![](images/c16-gra-0093.png)![](images/c16-gra-0094.png)

and for ![images](images/c16-i0444.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>:

# CHAPTER 17  
Outlier Detection

 

Outlier detection, or anomaly detection, is a data science technique aiming to identify observations which do not fit into the data set and are way too different from the “normal” data. In general, there are two reasons why such nonconformity in the data may exist. First, the anomalous data points can be produced by some technical error, where, for example, the data recording technique failed, or the survey has not been correctly scanned, among others. A particular example can be limit order book data, where bid price is recorded as ![images](images/c17-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>999</mn></mrow></math>. Such a datum corresponds to a failed print rather than to a situation where the interest in the particular asset is negative. Such a transaction would not be technically possible in properly working venues.

Second, the more critical reason corresponds to actual anomalous behaviour in the data. This may correspond, for example, to cases of bank frauds in the context of bank activity records. When a fraudster commits the unlawful act, she often tries to make the transaction to look usual. This, however, is not possible as the knowledge of usual transactions is not publicly available. The outliers may thus appear in the data analysis as records with the unusual size of the transaction, timing of trades, or their frequency do not fit into the common patterns.

The outlier detection is by its nature a data science technique, where the objective “being outlier” is rather vaguely defined. It is thus without surprise that outlier detection technique mimics the machine learning techniques. The non-supervised outlier detection techniques work with unlabelled data. The majority of data is assumed to be valid, and the property of being an outlier is understood relative to the majority. Such a method can be illustrated by a PCA technique for dimensionality reduction. The reduced set of principal components replaces the data. Then, every observation is recovered back from the reduced set, and the error of the reduction is recorded. The outliers are then observations with significant errors.

The supervised outlier detection techniques assume that we have a labelled training set, where data are labelled as “normal” or “outlier”. One can then formulate a model, either theoretical or econometric, for “being outlier” and estimate the parameters. The typical choice can be a logistic regression model, which is well suited for modelling binary dependent variables. The usual problem for such techniques rests in the need for correct classification and presence of outliers, which are often very rare. The techniques thus have to be able to deal with unbalanced data sets, where one of the classes is present sparsely. The alternative methods model probability, or likelihood, for an observation to be outlier instead of the discrete decision rule of “normal/outlier”. One can also formulate outlier detection techniques based on Bayesian principles.

The examples of the outlier detection techniques are:

*   Cluster analysis–based outlier detection, Campello et al. (2015).
*   Support vector machines–based models, Schölkopf et al. (2001).
*   Correlation-based outlier detection techniques, Kriegel et al. (2012).
*   Feature bagging–based techniques, Lazarevic and Kumar (2005).
*   Bayesian networks, Hawkins et al. (2002).
*   Density-based techniques (k-nearest-neighbour based), Knorr et al. (2000), and local outlier factor, which is explained in detail below.

 

## 17.1 LOCAL OUTLIER FACTOR

In this section, we delve into the details of the local outlier factor – see Breunig et al. (2000) – and implement the method directly along with its explanation. The local outlier factor technique estimates the local density of the data and determines the property of “being outlier” from the anomalous values of the data point density. The local density is derived based on the k-nearest neighbours principles (see subsequent chapters for more details). The density of a point within a data set is derived from the distance between the point and its local neighbourhood relative to the density of the neighbourhood itself. The values, which are far from their neighbours relative to the distance among the neighbours, are deemed to be considered outliers. On the other hand, one can define the inverted notion of “inliers” as observations, where the distance between the point and its local neighbourhood relative to the density of the neighbourhood itself is unusually small. The method calls the distance mentioned above as the reachability distance.

Let us assume a data set of ![images](images/c17-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> features, ![images](images/c17-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math> spanning the ![images](images/c17-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional space. First, we need to define a notion of distance between two ![images](images/c17-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional points. The distance has to be data-sensible definition of the length between two observations, and it has to satisfy the usual properties imposed on distance metric. The suitable candidates are any of the ![images](images/c17-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> norms:

(17.1)![equation](images/c17-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Y</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msup> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>Y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mi>p</mi> </msup> </mfenced> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mi>p</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c17-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c17-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> are two ![images](images/c17-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional points in the feature space.

Let us stress at this point that we cannot just take features as they are but rather to normalise them across the board. The distance based on any ![images](images/c17-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> tacitly assumes that all dimensions have the same scale. The features in this method thus have to be normalised such that the distance in the different directions (features) are comparable. The normalisation to be done is rather a matter of art; there is no clear recipe and method chosen should reflect the data. The two possible candidate methods are:

*   For each feature, demean the observations and divide them by the sample standard deviation.
*   For each feature, demean the observations and divide the observations by the sample range.

The essential element of the two methods above is division by scale – either standard deviation or range. The demeaning part is applied to be able to apply the scale. If any of the methods is applied, every new data point has to be normalised in the same way. The common mistake appears especially for splitting the sample into in-sample, where the model is calibrated, and out-of-sample, where the model is tested. Still, many researchers take the entire sample, calculate the sample mean and sample scale – range or variance – and normalise the entire sample. Then, they split the normalised sample into two pieces. This approach is wrong, as the in-sample uses information coming from the out-of-sample and thus the calibration of the model in the in-sample is not independent of the out-sample.

We introduce the local outlier factor technique along with the example implementation. For the sake of clarity, we restrict ourselves to ![images](images/c17-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, where we can depict the data. First, we define the model data set in which we apply our method. The data set is composed of two features `‘x0‘x1`, defined on the square ![images](images/c17-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>. The data are formed of two dense clusters overlaying the noisy background.

The first cluster is defined within the lower left corner of the support set:

![](images/c17-gra-0001.png)

The second cluster is defined in the upper-right corner of the support set:

![](images/c17-gra-0002.png)

and the noise is evenly spread over the support space:

![](images/c17-gra-0003.png)

Finally, we merge the data into a unique table:

![](images/c17-gra-0004.png)

[Figure 17.1](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0001) depicts the `dataSet`. The objective of the outlier detection technique is to recognise points within each cluster as not outliers and those being on the boundaries as well as those outside the clusters as outliers.

![FIGURE 17.1 Scatter plot of the dataSet, which is composed of two data clusters and the background noise](images/c17f001.png)

[**FIGURE 17.1**](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0001) Scatter plot of the `dataSet`, which is composed of two data clusters and the background noise

In order to define the local outlier factor, we have to fix the definition of the distance between two points in the feature space. We employ the one based on the ![images](images/c17-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math>\-norm, and in particular we set ![images](images/c17-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, i.e.

(17.2)![equation](images/c17-math-0002.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Y</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msup> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>Y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mfenced> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mn>2</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

for any two points ![images](images/c17-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c17-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>.

For our purpose, we implement the ![images](images/c17-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>\-norm as a function of two arguments, where the first one is a reference point and the other is a vector of points. The function calculates the distance between the reference point and each point of an array:

![](images/c17-gra-0005.png)

We can verify the implementation against the test point by updating the table `dataSet` by extra column `distanceToPoint`, which contains the distance between the test point and the feature array `‘x0‘x1`:

![](images/c17-gra-0006.png)![](images/c17-gra-0007.png)

The`distanceToPoint` thus contains the distance to the reference point. We can sort the table and identify the nearest neighbours, or inspect the histogram of the distances.

The local outlier factor is based on the ![images](images/c17-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-nearest neighbours. We choose ![images](images/c17-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> conveniently as:

![](images/c17-gra-0008.png)

where the neighbourhood will be defined as 12 nearest points in the sense of ![images](images/c17-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>\-norm. The value is arbitrary, and we encourage the reader to vary the parameter in the exercise.

Being equipped with the distance, we define the ![images](images/c17-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-distance of the point ![images](images/c17-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> to be the distance of ![images](images/c17-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> from ![images](images/c17-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-th nearest neighbour. It may happen that within the ![images](images/c17-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-distance of the point ![images](images/c17-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>, there is more than ![images](images/c17-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> elements; let us denote the number of such points as ![images](images/c17-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>X</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>. This happens when data points lie on the circle of radius ![images](images/c17-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-distance with ![images](images/c17-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> being in origin.

We implement the ![images](images/c17-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-distance of the point ![images](images/c17-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and the number of points within the ![images](images/c17-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-distance within one function:

![](images/c17-gra-0009.png)

The function has three arguments: first, the size of the neighbourhood `k`, data-set `data`, and the reference point denoted as `point`. The reference point does not have to be part of the data set and is considered as a separate point. We illustrate the use of the function `getKNNProperties` as follows:

![](images/c17-gra-0010.png)![](images/c17-gra-0011.png)

Further, we define the reachability distance of the point ![images](images/c17-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> from the point ![images](images/c17-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> as:

(17.3)![equation](images/c17-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mtext>reachability</mtext> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Y</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>X</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Y</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> <mi>k</mi> <mtext>-distance</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>Y</mi> </mfenced> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where the meaning is such that the reachability between the two points is a maximum of their true distance and the ![images](images/c17-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-distance of the point ![images](images/c17-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>. The meaning of this definition is such that the ![images](images/c17-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-distance is the minimum distance around the point ![images](images/c17-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>, or the recognition scale of the neighbourhood of the point ![images](images/c17-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>. Any point within the ![images](images/c17-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-distance is considered to be the same.

We implement the `reachability` distance as a function of three arguments: the point `X`, the index of the point `Y` within the data-set `data`, and the size of the neighbourhood `k`:

![](images/c17-gra-0012.png)

In the table `data`, we assume that the features are in the common column `x`, each observation being an array of the features for a given observation.

We can illustrate the function by using a test point and the first row of the `dataSet`:

![](images/c17-gra-0013.png)![](images/c17-gra-0014.png)

We use the reachability distance to define the local reachability density of the observation ![images](images/c17-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> as:

(17.4)![equation](images/c17-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>Y</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </msub> <msub> <mtext>reachability</mtext> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Y</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfrac> </mfenced> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where the density ![images](images/c17-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math> is the inverse of the average reachability distance of the observation ![images](images/c17-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> from its neighbours. The definition can show singularity for the identical points. The density ![images](images/c17-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math> is implemented as:

![](images/c17-gra-0015.png)

Let us illustrate the calculation of the density ![images](images/c17-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math> for the reference point used above:

![](images/c17-gra-0016.png)![](images/c17-gra-0017.png)

Finally, we define the local outlier factor, or LOF, as the average local reachability distance of the neighbourhood of point ![images](images/c17-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> normalized by the local reachability distance of the point ![images](images/c17-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> itself:

(17.5)![equation](images/c17-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mi>O</mi> <msub> <mi>F</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>Y</mi> <msub> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </msub> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>Y</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>X</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The value of ![images](images/c17-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>O</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math> around 1 implies that the observation is comparable to its neighbours. This means that the point is not an outlier. On the other hand, values above 1 indicate an outlier with the observation having a lower density relative to its neighbourhood. Further, we can interpret the values smaller than one as “inliers” – points which have higher density compared to their neighbourhood.

We implement the ![images](images/c17-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>O</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math> function as follows:

![](images/c17-gra-0018.png)

Let us calculate the LOF to the reference point `(0.5;0.5)`:

![](images/c17-gra-0019.png)![](images/c17-gra-0020.png)

The point lies in the middle of the square, in the corner of two clusters. This point is thus hard to be identified as an outlier, in particular when ![images](images/c17-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math> neighbours are considered. Let us increase the size of the neighbourhood to ![images](images/c17-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow></math>:

![](images/c17-gra-0021.png)![](images/c17-gra-0022.png)

The values increase as intuition suggests as the neighbourhood “sees” the vast region around itself and references itself to a broader set.

Let us further calculate the local outlier factor for list of points:

![](images/c17-gra-0023.png)

The first two points from the list lie in one of the clusters `cluster1` and `cluster2`, respectively. The remaining two points lie outside of the clusters and are produced by the noise background only. The list of the corresponding LOFs reads:

The results clearly support our intuition, where the LOF of the first two points is lower than the LOF of those coming from the noise background. The result is more prominent with larger neighbourhood:

![](images/c17-gra-0026.png)![](images/c17-gra-0027.png)

With larger neighbourhood, the difference between the points is prominent and straightforward criteria can be defined. Further, the `cluster1` is denser than the other cluster, `cluster2`, and as such, the ![images](images/c17-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> reaches a value below 1, suggesting the dense region.

Finally, we illustrate how to calculate the LOF for every point of the data set `data`:

![](images/c17-gra-0028.png)![](images/c17-gra-0029.png)

The table `dataSet` updated by the LOF for each of its points is then obtained as:
