It appears that there exists ![images](images/c20-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></math> such that ![images](images/c20-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>. This is (one of) the reasons the ridge regression is useful.

It remains to answer the obvious question, how to identify the value of such ![images](images/c20-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></math>. The performance of the model for a given ![images](images/c20-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> has to be assessed in the out-of-sample context. An intuitive tool to use is the cross-validation technique we have discussed in the previous section. It is convenient to perform the cross-validation estimation across a grid of ![images](images/c20-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> values and optimise for ![images](images/c20-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> based on the estimated landscape in terms of chosen measure like ![images](images/c20-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math>. We will show the details in the implementation section.

In conclusion, the ridge regression is a friendly and easy to implement method to deal with bias–variance trade-off. The method imposes a penalty in terms of shrinking the regression coefficients. The ridge regression shrinks the entire vector of parameters at the same time, trying to balance the proper mixture of re-weighted parameters. The ridge regression is not functional when our objective is to select a subset of regressors.

 

## 20.4 IMPLEMENTATION OF THE RIDGE REGRESSION

We implement the ridge regression suite of functions within the namespace `.quantQ.reg`. Let us first start with the data set we will employ. We will build upon the data set created in [Chapter 13](#c13.xhtml), but we will add another feature, `‘x4`, which is identical to feature `‘x3`. The data set thus contains perfectly collinear data, where features are linearly dependent. Let us denote the new data table `tabData2` and define it as follows:

![](images/c20-gra-0001.png)

We have to add a constant term as well:

![](images/c20-gra-0002.png)![](images/c20-gra-0003.png)

The consequence of linear dependence among features is that the rank of the `xtx` matrix is less than the number of features and this matrix cannot be inverted. The OLS fails in such a case, and the algorithm for the OLS calculation cannot be used. Let us illustrate it as follows:

![](images/c20-gra-0004.png)

and we can solve the OLS by:

![](images/c20-gra-0005.png)![](images/c20-gra-0006.png)

The solution is a list of missing values. This indicates that the method has not been able to find any solution and the entire procedure fails. The reason the method fails is the rank of the matrix `xtx`. We can introduce a perturbation along the matrix diagonal such that the rank of the matrix will be full, i.e. equal to many features:

(20.32)![equation](images/c20-math-0032.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8594;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#945;</mi> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c20-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> is a perturbation parameter and the matrix ![images](images/c20-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> is a unit matrix. The regularised term is of full rank, and the OLS procedure can be used as usual. Let us explore the regularisation in the code. We will need a function which calculates the diagonal matrix. This was introduced in [Chapter 16](#c16.xhtml):

![](images/c20-gra-0007.png)![](images/c20-gra-0008.png)

We can now solve the OLS with a regularised term and perturbation parameter 0.1 as:

![](images/c20-gra-0009.png)![](images/c20-gra-0010.png)

Let us explore explicitly the value of the parameters for the 3rd and 4th component, respectively. The true value in the data generating process is 2. We have introduced `‘x3` and `‘x4` to be identical and thus we expect that the sum of the two coefficients adds up to a value close to 2. This is indeed the case:

![](images/c20-gra-0011.png)

the value is close to 2. The regularisation thus leads to a meaningful solution.

We have illustrated the ridge regression at a semi-manual level. Let us automate the process and define the function which performs the regularised ridge regression – an analogue to the OLS function. The function has an additional parameter which is a regularisation parameter (recall that we kept that parameter explicitly in the ridge estimator):

![](images/c20-gra-0012.png)

The function returns a dictionary with four keys: the estimated parameters, number of observations, number of degrees of freedom, and regularisation parameter. We can verify the functionality of the function at this point. First, we run the function using the data set employed for the OLS algorithm and with a regularisation parameter set to 0.0. In such a case, the function returns the usual OLS output:

![](images/c20-gra-0013.png)![](images/c20-gra-0014.png)

Let us check the regularised solution with the OLS one explicitly:

![](images/c20-gra-0015.png)![](images/c20-gra-0016.png)

The ridge regression function is thus equal to the OLS regression, at least in the provided example, when regularisation is set to 0.0.

In the next step, we introduce a collinear variable and run regression with regularisation set to 0.0, corresponding to no regularisation:

![](images/c20-gra-0017.png)![](images/c20-gra-0018.png)

The outcome is as expected; non-regularised regression is not able to provide a meaningful estimate, and we thus see missing values. It is worth remembering that missing parameters may imply collinearity in the data set.

Let us add some non-zero regularisation. We choose a value of 0.1 as an initial value to explore the outcome:

![](images/c20-gra-0019.png)![](images/c20-gra-0020.png)

The estimated numbers are close to the correct data generating process. The regularisation thus makes sense and should enter our toolkit of useful routines. We should not stop at this point, though, and try to understand what value to choose for our regularisation parameter . Our value of 0.1 seems to provide a meaningful result; however, in a general case we do not know the correct data generating process, and we need some statistical assessment.

Let us start with the notion of in-/out-of-sample and implement a function analogous to `.quantQ.ols.inOut`. We split the sample into two parts: the in-sample part is used to fit the model. The out-of-sample part is used to evaluate the model using the data which has not been used to calibrate the model.

It is also important to stress that regularisation is used only during training. Once the parameters (regularised) are found, they are used on the out-of-sample data while ![images](images/c20-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> is ignored. When the model is applied to predict values and compare them with the correct values, regularisation does not play any role. In fact, at this point, the estimated parameters are treated the same as if they came from the plain OLS model. The regularisation parameter does not enter any measure we use to assess the performance of the model.

We implement the in/out procedure in the following function. The additional parameter is `inOutFlag`, which works in the same way as for `olsInOut`. It decides how we split the sample into two subsamples; it adds the ![images](images/c20-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> statistics into the output bucket to be able to judge the quality of a fit:

![](images/c20-gra-0021.png)

and apply it on our test data set. We use a scalar value for `inOutFlag` to take the initial ![images](images/c20-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>80</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of the data set as a training set and the remaining part as a test data set:

![](images/c20-gra-0022.png)![](images/c20-gra-0023.png)

and focus on ![images](images/c20-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math>:

![](images/c20-gra-0024.png)![](images/c20-gra-0025.png)

The value we have obtained is very close to the one obtained with a fully specified OLS model. We can use this procedure to test several values for the regularisation parameter. We keep this as an exercise for the reader and proceed directly with cross-validation, which gives us the tool we ultimately want to achieve and use on our data.

We take the `ridgeInOut` function and wrap it within a routine which is preparing ![images](images/c20-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-fold splits of the data. The routine further collects the values of ![images](images/c20-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> from every run and returns them back to the user for further analysis:

![](images/c20-gra-0026.png)

In our example, we can run a 12-fold cross-validation as:

![](images/c20-gra-0027.png)![](images/c20-gra-0028.png)

The outcome is an array of 12 values of ![images](images/c20-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math>s. The average value is:

![](images/c20-gra-0029.png)![](images/c20-gra-0030.png)

Again, the value is close to the ones obtained previously. This can be considered as a verification test of our implementation.

 

### 20.4.1 Optimisation of the Regularisation Parameter

The cross-validation technique is used as a procedure to find out the meta-parameters in estimations. The regularisation parameter is such a parameter. In order to find the optimal value of the regularisation parameter, we want to solve the following equation:

(20.33)![equation](images/c20-math-0033.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mi> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi> <mi>&#945;</mi> </munder> <mi>R</mi> <mi>M</mi> <mi>S</mi> <mi>E</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> <mi>F</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mi>&#945;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c20-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>n</mi><mi>F</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> stands for the cross-validated ![images](images/c20-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> across the entire sample using ![images](images/c20-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> folds with regularisation parameter equal to ![images](images/c20-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>. In this exercise, we fix ![images](images/c20-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> even though this parameter can be optimised in the same way as we do for ![images](images/c20-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>. The cross-validated ![images](images/c20-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> is defined as the average ![images](images/c20-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> across folds for a given ![images](images/c20-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>.

The optimisation expressed in the previous display can be tested on our existing example. In particular, we choose the full model with features `tabData2[‘x1‘x2‘x3‘const]`. The corresponding ![images](images/c20-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> matrix is regular and thus does not need regularisation; however, since the model is finite, we may still see some improvement when regularisation is being applied. We choose this problem as opposed to the one with additional collinear variable `‘x4` because we know the correct solution. It is also the problem where we would likely use the OLS without any hesitation.

Let us explore the optimisation graphically. We run the `.quantQ.reg.ridgeCV` function across a range of regularisation parameters and plot the average of the ![images](images/c20-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> for every regularisation parameter as a function of the regularisation parameter. We create a simple table:

![](images/c20-gra-0031.png)

[Figure 20.1](#c20.xhtml#c20-fig-0001) depicts the average ![images](images/c20-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> in a cross-validation run with 12 folds as a function of the regularisation parameter. The function has a global minimum over the range of plotted values, and the minimum is different from zero. This means that even though we know the true model, we may obtain better results in terms of minimising ![images](images/c20-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> when we will use some form of regularisation.

![FIGURE 20.1 images as a function of the regularisation parameter in a cross-validation with 12 folds](images/c20f001.png)

[**FIGURE 20.1**](#c20.xhtml#R_c20-fig-0001) ![images](images/c20-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>R</mi> <mi>M</mi> <mi>S</mi> <mi>E</mi> </mrow> </math> as a function of the regularisation parameter in a cross-validation with 12 folds

The value of the regularisation parameter which minimises the cross-validated RMSE can be found by exploring the outcome stored in table `ridgeOptimum`. Using the precision in the previous queries, we see that the global minimum is rather shallow and several values of regularisation parameter solve the problem:

![](images/c20-gra-0032.png)![](images/c20-gra-0033.png)

Values from 0.124 to 0.14 are within our precision the possible solutions as suitable candidates, which improves the out-of-sample quality of the fit. We could narrow the search and iterate the procedure around the candidate values. The procedure shows that we can get a better outcome in terms of overall model performance when we use regularisation.

We encourage the reader to repeat the exercise we have run when `‘x4` is included. The regularisation, in this case, is needed, where value ![images](images/c20-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> will not produce a model which could be used outside of the sample. In particular, the question which is to be answered is whether the optimal ![images](images/c20-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> when `‘x4` is included will be the same as in the case of `‘x4` being missing and thus having the regular data set.

Note that our function does not have explicit demeaning within the estimation routines. The data enter the functions with the assumption of having a zero mean. The function thus needs to be extended to handle demeaning properly. We leave this as an exercise for the reader as the change is straightforward and rewarding.

 

## 20.5 LASSO REGRESSION

The second regularisation technique we introduce is the lasso regression. First of all, why do we introduce a new technique given the ridge regression is straightforward to implement and apply? The main reason is that ridge regression tends to penalise all the coefficients across the board, but in many instances, it may be suitable to select a subset of features, i.e. remove some of the features instead of suppressing them significantly but still keeping them within the model. More importantly, feature selection can frequently be our starting point when working with advanced machine learning methods. The lasso regression assists us in feature selection as it has a different way to impose a penalty.

The lasso regression is a formulation of the OLS solution with imposed penalty having a form of an ![images](images/c20-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> norm. The lasso estimator is a solution to the problem:

[(20.34)](#c20.xhtml#R_c20-disp-0034)![equation](images/c20-math-0034.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mi>o</mi> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mi> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </munder> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mfenced> <mo>&#8890;</mo> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#955;</mi> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>j</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where term ![images](images/c20-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>p</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></math> corresponds to the ![images](images/c20-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> distance. Analogously to ridge regression, we keep an explicit dependence on ![images](images/c20-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math>.

When ![images](images/c20-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, we recover the OLS solution, while for large values ![images](images/c20-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math>, the parameters are suppressed significantly, ultimately leading to a trivial solution. We still tacitly impose demeaning on the dependent and independent variables. This will be stressed in the implementation part again.

We are tempted to ask for the analytic solution to the lasso regression. It is, however, challenging to obtain such a solution, so we are left with solving the problem numerically. The lasso optimisation, as in [eq. (20.34)](#c20.xhtml#c20-disp-0034), is ![images](images/c20-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>\-hard and thus is on the frontier of solvable numerical problems. If we want to implement this, we need a reliable optimisation technique. Luckily for us, there is another, lesser known regularisation technique, least angle regression, or LAR, which is close to the lasso regression (there is an interesting theoretical relationship), which does not need optimisation to provide a solution and mimics the lasso solution. Further, thanks to its construction it helps us to make feature selection.

The least angle regression was introduced by Efron et al. (2004). The method emerges from forward stepwise regression. Forward stepwise regression starts with no feature selected and tests addition of a variable into the active set of features. The one with the most significant contribution to the fit is then added. The process continues until a stopping rule. The procedure also allows us at every step to test removing a feature from an active set.

The LAR, on the other hand, is defined as follows: it starts with an empty active set of features. First, it identifies the variable which is the most correlated with the dependent variable. A small portion of the variable is added to the model and residuals are generated. The procedure is repeated. When another variable reaches comparable correlation to the first variable, the second variable joins the active set. The two variables are then added in a tied manner and contribute to the model by small portions. This continues until all the variables are in the model. In the end, the model reaches the OLS fit.

The notion of a small portion in the description above is best understood as an infinitesimal step, which would imply that the variable contribution to the model is continuously increasing. This is not feasible in a statistical procedure, and thus a small step is taken. The procedure works even if ![images](images/c20-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> because zero residuals will be reached during the iteration and the entire algorithm stops.

Let us demonstrate the mechanics of the least angle regression using pseudocode:

*   Demean and normalise data with independent variables.
*   Set residuals ![images](images/c20-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>avg</mtext><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> and the parameters ![images](images/c20-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
*   Find ![images](images/c20-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> which is the most correlated to ![images](images/c20-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></mrow></math>.
*   Change ![images](images/c20-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> from 0 towards the OLS solution of ![images](images/c20-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>. The value chosen, ![images](images/c20-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msubsup></mrow></math>, is such that there is a new variable ![images](images/c20-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>, which has the same correlation with ![images](images/c20-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> as ![images](images/c20-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> itself.
*   Change![images](images/c20-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c20-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math> jointly. The OLS coefficients give the direction ![images](images/c20-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> with residuals being updated by the previous steps. The value is updated until there is another variable ![images](images/c20-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math>, which has the same correlation with updated residuals as the two variables.
*   This process continues until all variables have been included (![images](images/c20-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, then the process stops when ![images](images/c20-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> variables have been included).

The procedure outlined above can be stopped at any iteration step. At the initial stage, the situation corresponds to ![images](images/c20-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></math>. The more we progress in the iteration and keep adding ![images](images/c20-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math>’s, the outcome corresponds to lower and lower ![images](images/c20-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math>. In the end, we end up with a full OLS solution which corresponds to ![images](images/c20-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. If we keep track of estimated coefficients ![images](images/c20-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> during the iteration process, and for every such vector of ![images](images/c20-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> we perform a cross-validation test, we can reach the optimally regularised estimator. The process is similar to choosing ![images](images/c20-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> for lasso procedure itself.

The least angle regression will be giving the same results as the lasso procedure until the first coefficient goes through zero. At this point, solutions start to deviate from each other and least angle regression will be a different regularisation scheme. There is a possible correction to the presented algorithm which makes the solution mimic lasso regression precisely:

*   Once any coefficient ![images](images/c20-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math> crosses zero, it is excluded from the active set. At this point, the linear regression for the remaining set is recalculated without ![images](images/c20-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

Once this rule is added, the lasso procedure is recovered. Excluding ![images](images/c20-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math> does not mean it may not return to the active set later. Given our stopping rule is to include all the variables (if ![images](images/c20-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>), it will return into the active set. In the following section, we implement the least angle regression procedure.

We encourage the reader to extend the provided algorithm and implement the lasso correction. It will be a rewarding project, at the end of which the reader will strengthen their knowledge of regularisation and the lasso implementation, an inherently ![images](images/c20-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>\-hard problem.

 

## 20.6 IMPLEMENTATION OF THE LASSO REGRESSION

In this section, we implement the other regularisation scheme, which is the least angle regression. The least angle regression is a numerically feasible proxy for the lasso regression, as we have argued. We continue using the `.quantQ.reg` namespace.

We prepare a test data set. We use the `.quantQ.simul.multiNormal` function to generate randomly distributed features and error term. We prepare a different data set to illustrate another way of using the previously developed functions to verify the implemented functionalities.

First, we simulate the 4-dimensional random array, where each of the array has 1000 observations:

![](images/c20-gra-0034.png)

and combine the data into a linearly dependent data set. We ultimately obtain three features and one error term:

![](images/c20-gra-0035.png)

All three features have by construction zero mean. Features `x2` and `x3` are created as a linear combination of more than one underlying random array, thus introducing the explicit correlation between features. The dependent variable `y` is defined as:

![](images/c20-gra-0036.png)

Let us further analyse the correlation between the variables used in the definition of `y`:

![](images/c20-gra-0037.png)![](images/c20-gra-0038.png)![](images/c20-gra-0039.png)![](images/c20-gra-0040.png)![](images/c20-gra-0041.png)![](images/c20-gra-0042.png)![](images/c20-gra-0043.png)![](images/c20-gra-0044.png)![](images/c20-gra-0045.png)![](images/c20-gra-0046.png)![](images/c20-gra-0047.png)![](images/c20-gra-0048.png)

We arrange the dependent and independent variables into a table, which is the format we will face in real situations:

![](images/c20-gra-0049.png)

We add a constant feature into the table such that we can more easily incorporate the constant term into regressions.

![](images/c20-gra-0050.png)

We run a simple OLS on the data created:

![](images/c20-gra-0051.png)![](images/c20-gra-0052.png)

The values are in principle close to the real parameters; however, the error term of the estimated parameters is large due to the magnitude of the error term. Let us measure the ![images](images/c20-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> distance between the true solution and the estimate:

![](images/c20-gra-0053.png)![](images/c20-gra-0054.png)

We proceed now with the implementation of the least angle regression algorithm. The algorithm is implemented as a function which performs one iteration step. The argument of the function is a dictionary with all the model parameters and variables, referred to as `bucket`. One step is an update of the vector of ![images](images/c20-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> by an amount which is normalised in every step using an ![images](images/c20-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> measure. The amount by which the parameters are updated is in `bucket[‘step]`.

The algorithm distinguishes three regimes:

*   `step 1, find the first variable`: This corresponds to the initial stage of the algorithm. Only one variable is in the active set.
*   `step 2++, there is space for improvement`: This corresponds to the stage of the algorithm when the new variable can enter the active set. The algorithm tries to include new variables into the active set.
*   `step 2++, there is no space for improvement`: This is the last stage of the algorithm when there are no variables to be included, and the algorithm thus tries to finish the run by adding as much of the features loading as possible.

The dictionary `bucket` contains several variables monitoring the state of the iteration; they are needed during the iterations only. The function utilises the `ols` function in order to find the common direction in which to increase the parameters. The decision to include the variable or continue in the present direction is done using the built-in `cor` function. The algorithm is aimed to work with finite sets, and thus the notion correlation is a random variable with a certain error. We use ![images](images/c20-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> criteria to decide whether the correlation is significant or not. Once correlation is within ![images](images/c20-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mfenced></mrow></math>, the two variables are considered uncorrelated.

Demeaning of variables is not part of the one step of the iteration. This has to be done before engaging with the iteration. We will discuss it later on within a wrapper which creates the estimation suite for the entire LAR algorithm. At the end of every iteration, the vector of residuals `r` is updated accordingly. The vector of residuals thus contains a cumulative unexplained part of variance at the end of each step. The algorithm is supposed to stop once we cannot find any more correlation of the remaining residuals to the data (within our precision).

![](images/c20-gra-0055.png)

Let us run the LAR algorithm altogether. We need to first initialise the `bucket` with all the variables:

![](images/c20-gra-0056.png)

and combine all the individual variables into the dictionary:

![](images/c20-gra-0057.png)

Having among the variables the flag `continue`, we can use iteration to run the algorithm until all the possible dependence in the data is exploited:

![](images/c20-gra-0058.png)

The results of the LAR algorithm can be now reviewed. First, the mean of the dependent variable is in the `meanY` variable:

![](images/c20-gra-0059.png)![](images/c20-gra-0060.png)

Second, the estimated ![images](images/c20-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math>s read:

![](images/c20-gra-0061.png)![](images/c20-gra-0062.png)

The parameters are visually of the same magnitude as those obtained by the standard OLS. We can confirm it by calculating the ![images](images/c20-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>\-distance to the true solution:

![](images/c20-gra-0063.png)![](images/c20-gra-0064.png)

The result is improved compared to the one corresponding to the OLS case. For convenience, we create a table with the estimated path which will be indexed by the `arcLength`. This stands for the cumulative sum of `bucket[‘step]` performed during the iteration so far. First, we extract the betas from the `path` table:

![](images/c20-gra-0065.png)

then add the `arcLength`:

![](images/c20-gra-0066.png)

When we select a subset from the table, we get the full estimation path:

![](images/c20-gra-0067.png)

[Figure 20.2](#c20.xhtml#c20-fig-0002) depicts the entire path we have obtained using the LAR algorithm as captured by table `pathLAR`. The colour convention used is as follows: light gray colour corresponds to `beta1` coefficient, dark gray colour corresponds to `beta2` coefficient, and black colour corresponds to `beta3` coefficient.

![FIGURE 20.2 The plot of the entire path of the LAR algorithm for tabData. Light gray colour corresponds to beta1, dark gray colour corresponds to beta2, and black colour corresponds to beta3](images/c20f002.png)

[**FIGURE 20.2**](#c20.xhtml#R_c20-fig-0002) The plot of the entire path of the LAR algorithm for `tabData`. Light gray colour corresponds to `beta1`, dark gray colour corresponds to `beta2`, and black colour corresponds to `beta3`

At this point, we would like to encourage the reader to run the `oneStepLAR` function step by step with large `step` and see how the estimation path emerges. A possible weakness of the `oneStepLAR` function is that there is no limit on the number of steps the function can take. The function can in the extreme case run indefinitely. It is wise to amend the function such that there is a safety feature to prevent this case.

We wrap the algorithm into a function. The function will have two arguments: the table with data, where the first column is the dependent variable, and the remaining columns capture the features in the linear relationship to be estimated. The second argument is the size of the step. Due to the normalisation, it determines the `arcLength` the algorithm moves in every iteration:

![](images/c20-gra-0068.png)

The function is tested on the same data set `tabData`. We explicitly keep the constant feature among the variables even though the function performs demeaning before engaging in the iterative process:

![](images/c20-gra-0069.png)

Viewing the last 10 rows of the table `pathLAR2`:

![](images/c20-gra-0070.png)![](images/c20-gra-0071.png)

We have obtained the same result. There is a 0 coefficient on the constant term, which means that the function operating on the demeaned time series does not assign any value to the constant feature. It can thus ignore irrelevant features. This shows that even though the constant feature is not in fact demeaned, the algorithm performs well.

Following the previous sections, we further develop a function which tests the validity of regularisation on the out-of-sample data. The function performs the same regularisation path as in the `LAR` function using the in-sample data while the validity of the given regularisation is assessed using the ![images](images/c20-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> measure on the out-of-sample part of the data. The outcome of the function is a table with a regularisation path, where each point of the path got assigned the ![images](images/c20-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> value.

![](images/c20-gra-0072.png)

The function has two modes of operation depending on the format of the `inOutFlag` variable. We calculate an example using the first ![images](images/c20-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>80</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of the sample as the in-sample, and the results are verified on the ![images](images/c20-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of the sample outside the training part.

![](images/c20-gra-0073.png)

We plot the outcome of `LARInOut`:

![](images/c20-gra-0074.png)

[Figure 20.3](#c20.xhtml#c20-fig-0003) depicts the regularisation path. The ![images](images/c20-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>\-axis corresponds to the ![images](images/c20-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> on the out-of-sample part of the data while the ![images](images/c20-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>\-axis is equal to the `arcLength`. The model is estimated for every value of the `arcLength` on the in-sample data.

![FIGURE 20.3 images as function of the arcLength within the LAR algorithm tested out of sample](images/c20f003.png)

[**FIGURE 20.3**](#c20.xhtml#R_c20-fig-0003) ![images](images/c20-i0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>R</mi> <mi>M</mi> <mi>S</mi> <mi>E</mi> </mrow> </math> as function of the `arcLength` within the LAR algorithm tested out of sample

The model shows the optimal ![images](images/c20-i0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> value, i.e. the lowest value, at the end of the path. This means that the optimal regularisation is no regularisation. The optimal model is instead the one corresponding to the OLS.

Further, we provide a routine which employs cross-validation to explore the validity of the regularisation path. For every fold, the sample is split into in-sample and out-of-sample. For such a split, the `LARInOut` function is used. In the end, the ![images](images/c20-i0123.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> is averaged across the validation folds:

![](images/c20-gra-0075.png)

There are some points to be made. First, for every validation fold, the regularisation path can be of different length. In order to be able to aggregate across different paths, we extend the regularisation path beyond the last estimated point using the last value. This approximation corresponds to the fact that the larger the `arcLength` value, the less regularisation and the last point of the regularisation path is equal to the plain OLS model. The OLS plays the role of the asymptotic model. In `q`, this can be achieved by `fills`. Besides, the values of the `arcLength` are float numbers. This may cause numerical discrepancies between the values coming from different folds. Thus, we round the `arcLength` at the `step` precision explicitly before we use `select ... by arcLength ...` functionality. Finally, the average value of the ![images](images/c20-i0124.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> by `arcLength` across the folds is calculated and populated for the regularisation path.

Let us calculate the example with 12 folds in the cross-validation:

![](images/c20-gra-0076.png)

[Figure 20.4](#c20.xhtml#c20-fig-0004) depicts the full regularisation path. The path captures the average ![images](images/c20-i0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> as a function of the `arcLength`, calculated across 12 folds of the cross-validation scheme. [Figure 20.5](#c20.xhtml#c20-fig-0005) zooms in on the end of the regularisation path. There is a visible minimum. The cross-validation scheme thus shows that optimal linear regression is the one with regularisation, though quite small. The result corresponds to the conclusion we have made with the ridge regression, where optimal linear regression was the one with small regularisation.

![FIGURE 20.4 images as function of the arcLength within the LAR algorithm using the cross-validation with 12 folds](images/c20f004.png)

[**FIGURE 20.4**](#c20.xhtml#R_c20-fig-0004) ![images](images/c20-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>R</mi> <mi>M</mi> <mi>S</mi> <mi>E</mi> </mrow> </math> as function of the `arcLength` within the LAR algorithm using the cross-validation with 12 folds

![FIGURE 20.5 images as function of the arcLength within the LAR algorithm using the cross-validation with 12 folds with a focus around the minimum](images/c20f005.png)

[**FIGURE 20.5**](#c20.xhtml#R_c20-fig-0005) ![images](images/c20-i0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>R</mi> <mi>M</mi> <mi>S</mi> <mi>E</mi> </mrow> </math> as function of the `arcLength` within the LAR algorithm using the cross-validation with 12 folds with a focus around the minimum

The value of the optimal `arcLength` can be recovered as:

![](images/c20-gra-0077.png)![](images/c20-gra-0078.png)

The precision we use suggests many values be used. Thus, for a given chosen value of `arcLength`, we take the estimated parameters as the estimator of the model. We can choose different criteria to stop the iteration. Imagine we are provided with ![images](images/c20-i0128.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> variables, and we want to make a feature selection such that we want to use the subset of features of size ![images](images/c20-i0129.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math>. We run the algorithm but as a stopping rule, we adjust `bucket[‘continue]` to work with `sum not 0=bucket[‘beta]`. We can alternatively run the full algorithm as it stands and then find a first row in the output table, which has ![images](images/c20-i0130.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> non-zero ![images](images/c20-i0131.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi></mrow></math> coefficients. Those components will consist of the chosen subset.

Similar to ridge regression, we have not included the demeaning and normalisation of the features within the functions. This part is left as an extension. In particular, the regularisation has to be included in the provided function, including in-/out-of-sample and cross-validated ones. The implementation should not, at any step, mix any information from out-the-sample into the in-sample. A common mistake is to calculate the average of variables across the entire data, demean the data and *then* split them into a training sample and validation sample. Such an approach has information leakage from the validation part into the training one through the global mean.

The provided algorithm opens many possible applications which have to be tailored to the problem at hand. We encourage the reader to implement an extension of the algorithm to mimic the lasso regularisation path as is described in the introduction. We can then explore the deviation of the two algorithms and link their predictive accuracy. Even without doing the last step, the least angle regression implemented in this chapter provides a tool which regularises the model and can perform robust feature selection.

# CHAPTER 21  
Nearest Neighbours

 

Nearest neighbours algorithms are popular with data exploration and pattern recognition. In this chapter, we cover the foundation of the nearest neighbours techniques and present three particular algorithms. These methods are by definition model free. We only need to impose mild – or no – assumptions on the data. The outcome is fully derived from the data set itself. The inevitable consequence of this is the black-box nature of the model. We can barely introduce a narrative for the link between independent and dependent variables without looking into the raw data itself.

The nearest neighbour–based algorithms are quite successful in classification problems. They can be used for regression, but the power of the algorithm is not as good as it is with classification. In particular, high-dimensional problems are challenging for nearest neighbour–based regressions. A regression is thus better to be run with other methods discussed in this book, such as linear regression (with regularisation), trees/forests, or neural networks.

In this section, we present three specific algorithms based on the principles of nearest neighbours and implement them in `q`:

*   ![images](images/c21-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> </mrow> </math>\-nearest neighbours classifier
*   Prototype clustering
*   Feature selection based on the local nearest neighbourhood

 

## 21.1 *k*\-Nearest Neighbours Classifier

The first method of the machine learning approach we present is the ![images](images/c21-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-nearest neighbours, or ![images](images/c21-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>, one of the most simple and basic machine learning algorithms. The ![images](images/c21-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> is a non-parametric method for classification and/or regression of the data. For the object which we want to classify or for which we want to regress the characteristic value, we use voting based on the set of objects from the nearest neighbourhood.

The ![images](images/c21-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> is very simple in terms of no model being inferred from the data, and all computation is postponed. Whenever the inference has to be drawn, the entire training set is used, and the neighbourhood is identified. Therefore, the method itself is very intensive in terms of computational resources needed to deal with the full training data set when the method is employed during the inference stage. When the problem at hand requires dealing with extensive data, both in cross-sectional dimension and number of samples, the method becomes infeasible for languages which are not able to deal with a large volume of data quickly. This is where `q` will show it is powerful in dealing with large in-memory data sets.

Assume we are equipped with a training data set, which contains ![images](images/c21-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> independent variables, ![images](images/c21-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, all of numeric type, and one dependent variable, ![images](images/c21-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>, also of numeric type. We defer discussion of non-numeric types until the end of this section. A typical data set will take the following form:

![](images/c21-gra-0001.png)

![images](images/c21-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mi>N</mi> <mi>N</mi> </mrow> </math> prescribes the following procedure: consider an out-of-sample observation `point`, which is an array of features `x1; x2;...;xN`. From the training sample `tableFunction`, we identify the subset of ![images](images/c21-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> entries closest to the out-of-sample point. The subset then determines our expectation of the value ![images](images/c21-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> corresponding to the `point`. The expectations have to be derived from the values in the neighbourhood: this can be based on a majority vote, or we can use probability derived from the proportions within the neighbourhood.

In order to find the subset of observations close to `point`, we use a distance measure, given in general as ![images](images/c21-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>L</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></mrow></math>, i.e.

(21.1)![equation](images/c21-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>y</mi> </mfenced> <mo>&#8801;</mo> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msup> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mi>X</mi> </msup> </mfenced> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>X</mi> </mfrac> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

We consider the general form of a distance metric as we introduce the voting system and the value of ![images](images/c21-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> will play the role of a metaparameter of the model. ![images](images/c21-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> recovers the standard Euclidean distance, for ![images](images/c21-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> the distance metric is derived from absolute values, while for ![images](images/c21-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8599;</mo></mrow></math>, the maximum of the distances of individual feature differences is chosen.

We implement the ![images](images/c21-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>L</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></mrow></math>\-distance as a function which takes a `point` and training sample and returns a vector of distances of the `point` from each entry in the training sample:

![](images/c21-gra-0002.png)

We illustrate the distance measure for three values ![images](images/c21-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c21-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c21-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>. We use point `(0.2;0.3;0.0)` and a randomly generated table with three rows.

![](images/c21-gra-0003.png)![](images/c21-gra-0004.png)

Ordering of points based on their distance to the `point` depends on the value of parameter ![images](images/c21-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>. The third row is classified as the closest observation by choice of ![images](images/c21-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> while the other measures classify the same point as the most distant. The choice of the parameter ![images](images/c21-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> thus may affect results, and its role has to be investigated.

We can proceed with construction of the ![images](images/c21-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-nearest neighbour classifier. The implementation is done in two steps:

*   Identify the ![images](images/c21-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> neighbourhood of the test point.
*   Classify the point.

In the first step, we consider the given point and calculate the distance to every point in the training sample. Then, we select ![images](images/c21-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> points from the training sample which are closest to the given point. We have to store only the value of a dependent variable for every chosen point and the distance to the point. The following function captures such a procedure:

![](images/c21-gra-0005.png)

The function takes four arguments: the point for which the neighbourhood is being sought, the training sample with data in the form of a table, the parameter of the distance measure, and the size of the neighbourhood to be returned. The output is a dictionary of classes and corresponding distances.

Let us examine an example. First, define a point to be classified,

![](images/c21-gra-0006.png)

then, the training data. We use a randomly generated table without any pattern,

![](images/c21-gra-0007.png)

and then find the corresponding neighbourhood of size `10` and with Euclidean distance metrics:

![](images/c21-gra-0008.png)![](images/c21-gra-0009.png)

The neighbourhood is sorted by distance.

In the second step, we proceed with classification based on the selected neighbourhood. The conventional approach is the majority vote: the point is classified based on the most common class within the selected neighbourhood. If there is a tie between two or more classes, one is chosen randomly.

Function `kNNclassifyMajorityVote` takes as an argument the outcome of function `kNNneighbours` and returns class based on the majority vote. The function is implemented as follows:

![](images/c21-gra-0010.png)

Continuing with the setup introduced above:

![](images/c21-gra-0011.png)

which returns class:

![](images/c21-gra-0012.png)

The majority vote is not the only option we can use to classify the unknown observation. The distance-weighted rule looks not at just the number of points in the neighbourhood of the given class, but also their distance to the point itself. The distance-weighted classification works as follows: consider ![images](images/c21-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> points in the selected neighbourhood, where each point is described by two values ![images](images/c21-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c21-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c21-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> being the distance of ![images](images/c21-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th point, and ![images](images/c21-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> its class. First, we normalise the distances to sum up to 1:

(21.2)![equation](images/c21-math-0002.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>d</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <msub> <mi>d</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mrow> <msub> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>d</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

with ![images](images/c21-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> being normalised distances.

The distance-weighted scheme chooses the class based on the following formula:

(21.3)![equation](images/c21-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>c</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mi> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi> <msup> <mi>c</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </munder> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>c</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </munder> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>d</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msubsup> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The weight in the scheme is ![images](images/c21-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup></mfenced></mrow></math>. The higher the weight, the closer the given point is. We consider such quantity as “proximity”. The class is chosen based on the overall amount of proximity within the chosen neighbourhood. The alternative explanation for ![images](images/c21-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup></mfenced></mrow></math> is a probability to classify ![images](images/c21-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th neighbourhood point as ![images](images/c21-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c21-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup></mfenced></mrow></math> otherwise.

The distance-weighted decision rule is implemented in function `kNNclassifyDistanceWeighted`, which works in the same manner as `kNNclassifyMajorityVote`.

![](images/c21-gra-0013.png)

Let us continue in the example above and classify `point` based on the distance-weighted scheme:

![](images/c21-gra-0014.png)

gives the same class as the method above.

![](images/c21-gra-0015.png)

The two rules can be wrapped within one function. For example, we can create a dictionary, and the classification function is in fact a dictionary with a chosen argument. We encourage the reader to construct such a dictionary as an exercise.

 

## 21.2 PROTOTYPE CLUSTERING

The previous method is compelling as it does not assume any parametric form and can be tuned well to fit many examples. Both regression and classification have the same functional form. The distinct disadvantage is a requirement to have the large data set in memory as a “model” (training sample used on the fly), and whenever the classification/regression is performed, we have to work with the full sample. Depending on how much RAM we have availble on our processing server, this may become problematic.

In this section, we focus on the prototype method, which is a classification method where we identify regions in the parametric space which exhibit the same support of the dependent variable. The centre then characterises such a region. Every region may have several centres, which are learned in the training sample. In the prediction/out-of-sample step, the predicted value of the dependent variable is determined by the value of the nearest centre.

Let us proceed more specifically, where we are equipped with a training data set as in the previous method, which contains ![images](images/c21-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> independent variables, ![images](images/c21-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, all of the numeric type. Let us further assume that these variables are each normalised using the ![images](images/c21-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math>\-score. Further, the data set contains one dependent variable, ![images](images/c21-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>, which is of integer value. The support of ![images](images/c21-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> is finite, and we further assume that cardinality of each value of the variable ![images](images/c21-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> is rather large. This is not a mathematical constraint but rather a practical constraint, where the reader should appropriately treat all the pathological cases with having isolated values. Let us assume the dependent variable ![images](images/c21-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> takes ![images](images/c21-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> different values which we need to classify.

The following algorithm defines the prototype method based on the nearest neighbours:

*   Split the sample by the value of the dependent variable ![images](images/c21-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> into ![images](images/c21-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> subsamples. Further, proceed for each subsample independently:

1.  *    For a given subsample, choose ![images](images/c21-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> observations randomly. Those observations are centres or the prototypes for a given subsample.
    *    For each centre, find ![images](images/c21-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> nearest neighbours from the subsample.
    *    Replace the centre by the new centre, which is the average of the ![images](images/c21-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> neighbours and the centre itself.
    *    Iterate this procedure until convergence.

*   Replace the training sample by ![images](images/c21-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> centres. Each centre carries information about the value of ![images](images/c21-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>.
*   Predict the class of the out-of-sample observation by the class of the nearest neighbour.

This procedure is known in the literature as ![images](images/c21-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>\-means clustering.

Let us implement the prototype method using the following case: each observation is formed by ![images](images/c21-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c21-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>, for ![images](images/c21-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, and the dependent variable is defined as

(21.4)![equation](images/c21-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>&#60;</mo> <mo form="prefix">=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c21-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow></math> is the indicator function taking value one when the argument is true and zero otherwise. We thus have a dependent variable which classifies whether the point – in feature space – lies within a circle with centre in origin and radius equal to one. In `q`, such data can be generated as follows:

![](images/c21-gra-0016.png)

We have generated 10,000 points. We can illustrate the data using the following “trick”:

![](images/c21-gra-0017.png)

which can be depicted with the scatter plot option. [Figure 21.1](#c21.xhtml#c21-fig-0001) depicts the result, where all points within the unit circle are dark gray and the remaining ones are plotted in light gray.

![FIGURE 21.1 Scatter plot of true clusters as defined in tableKNN](images/c21f001.png)

[**FIGURE 21.1**](#c21.xhtml#R_c21-fig-0001) Scatter plot of true clusters as defined in `tableKNN`

It is convenient to work with the following data arrangement,

![](images/c21-gra-0018.png)

where we have only two variables: the first one is an array of the factors, the second one being the classifier, in our case the binary variable ![images](images/c21-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>. The implementation assumes such a form of data where array ![images](images/c21-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is of any dimension. The `q` function reads:

![](images/c21-gra-0019.png)

The function uses ![images](images/c21-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> distance as implemented previously in `distanceLX`. The function is also prepared for parallelisation in the topmost loop where `peach` is applied over all distinct values of the dependent variable.

We can run an example for ![images](images/c21-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> centres; each centre is found using ![images](images/c21-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math> nearest neighbours, and each search is iterated 1000 times:

![](images/c21-gra-0020.png)![](images/c21-gra-0021.png)

The graphical output can be obtained by scatter plot option using the table transformed by the following:

![](images/c21-gra-0022.png)

We have explicitly generated points on the boundary, so we see where the centres were identified. The graphical output from `qPad` can be seen in [Figure 21.2](#c21.xhtml#c21-fig-0002), which contains the trained centres using the function `prototypeKNN`. The black points correspond to the case of ![images](images/c21-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and gray ones to ![images](images/c21-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.

![FIGURE 21.2 Black and gray plots are the prototypes for each class as identified by .quantQ.knn.prototypeKNN function](images/c21f002.png)

[**FIGURE 21.2**](#c21.xhtml#R_c21-fig-0002) Black and gray plots are the prototypes for each class as identified by `.quantQ.knn.prototypeKNN` function

The trained points are not sufficient to serve as trustworthy and accurate prototypes to the two regions selected. This can be solved by increasing the number of prototypes. Let us illustrate how the prototypes perform for the out-of-sample test. Let us create a function which assigns a class to a point based on the proximity to the trained centres.

Moreover, we can test it as

The recovered shape indeed resembles the original shape. The accuracy of the trained prototypes can be seen from the contingency table obtained as:
