We see that accuracy in assigning the correct class is ![images](images/c21-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>93.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, which is not bad given we have replaced the structure in the entire region by 10 points–centres. A further step could be to explore the tools in more depth by finding out what the optimal size of ![images](images/c21-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> is in terms of the power of the out-of-sample test and various regions/number of classes.

 

## 21.3 FEATURE SELECTION: LOCAL NEAREST NEIGHBOURS APPROACH

The concept of nearest neighbours as introduced above is a rather brute force approach which aims to exploit similarity between past observations for the prediction of future states. This can be used out-of-sample or even in real time. In this section, we employ the nearest neighbours for feature selection as was introduced by Navot et al. (2006). The aim of the presented method is not a prediction, but dimensionality reduction in the space of the independent variables.

The method comes from the field of biostatistics; it was invented for analysing cortical neural activity, namely, to search through the high-dimensional space of neural features and explain the particular neural activity. The proposed algorithm extends the leave-one-out algorithm with mean-squared-error, where the optimal feature set is found using the forward selection algorithm, investigating the importance of features one by one. The proposed algorithm assigns weights to features and also a score. This makes the problem differentiable, so the gradient can be calculated analytically and gradient descent type of algorithms can be used to find the optimal weights. The features can therefore be sorted based on the assigned weights.

The method can be also viewed as an extension of the ![images](images/c21-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> regression, which assigns the value of a dependent variable for a point ![images](images/c21-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, being ![images](images/c21-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional vector of independent variables, based on the average value of the neighbourhood ![images](images/c21-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> as:

(21.5)![equation](images/c21-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mtext>card</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi>N</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi>N</mi> </mrow> </munder> <mi>y</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

the average of the value of the dependent variables in the neighbourhood of ![images](images/c21-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>x</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>. The neighbourhood is defined in the same way as in the previous sections. Analogously to the distance-weighted function `kNNclassifyDistanceWeighted`, we can define the weighted average for regression based on the proximity, ![images](images/c21-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> distance, as:

(21.6)![equation](images/c21-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <msub> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi>N</mi> </mrow> </msub> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>&#946;</mi> </mfrac> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <msup> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi>N</mi> </mrow> </munder> <mi>y</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mfenced> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>&#946;</mi> </mfrac> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <msup> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The factor in front of the sum normalises the estimate – average – based on the weights derived from ![images](images/c21-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8741;</mo></mrow></math>. The weights themselves do not have to be normalised.

The purpose of the algorithm is to assess the importance of individual independent variables. We thus introduce the weighted norm:

(21.7)![equation](images/c21-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mrow> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>&#8741;</mo> </mrow> <mi>w</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msubsup> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msubsup> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c21-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is an ![images](images/c21-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional vector of weights, which puts different emphasis on different independent variables. We do not need to impose any normalisation on weights.

Having in hand the weighted norm, we define the weighted regression equation:

(21.8)![equation](images/c21-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mi>w</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <msub> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi>N</mi> </mrow> </msub> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>&#946;</mi> </mfrac> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <msubsup> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <mi>w</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi>N</mi> </mrow> </munder> <mi>y</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mfenced> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>&#946;</mi> </mfrac> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <msubsup> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <mi>w</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> </mrow> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Finally, we define a score function which assesses the performance of each vector of weights, ![images](images/c21-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math>. The score is defined as the negative mean-squared error:

(21.9)![equation](images/c21-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>e</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>w</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mi>x</mi> </munder> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>y</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mi>w</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> </mfenced> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where we have used a factor of ![images](images/c21-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> for convenience. The method itself incorporates leave-one-out cross-validation approach as the estimated value of ![images](images/c21-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> for a given ![images](images/c21-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> does not use ![images](images/c21-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> itself.

Further, it is important to stress that the function is continuous in ![images](images/c21-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math>. This is an essential feature as it allows us to obtain an analytic expression for the first derivative of the score concerning weights. Gradient-descent type of methods can be employed in order to find out weights, which optimise score. This is detailed below.

The algorithm for feature selection can be specified as follows:

*   Initialize ![images](images/c21-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>, set ![images](images/c21-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
*   Perform an update of weights:

1.  *    Pick datum ![images](images/c21-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> from the training set.
    *    Calculate the gradient of the loss function (![images](images/c21-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" ### 21.3.1 Implementation

In the following part we implement the procedure in `q`. We build the implementation in several steps for the sake of illustration. We encourage the reader to simplify the code into one robust and optimised function.

Let us consider our data set to be of the following format:

![](images/c21-gra-0031.png)

where we consider ![images](images/c21-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> independent variables `coordi` and one dependent variable `val`. We further assume that dependent variables are normalized using one of the normalization techniques. The feature selection based on nearest neighbours is built as follows.

First, we define the weighted ![images](images/c21-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>\-norm, ![images](images/c21-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><msubsup><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi>w</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math>, as:

![](images/c21-gra-0032.png)

where `x`, `y`, `weight` are three vectors of the same length, ![images](images/c21-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, and the function returns ![images](images/c21-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>w</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math>.

We implement a local estimator of the value function in the neighbourhood coordinates of a given point, ![images](images/c21-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></mrow></math>, where the neighbourhood is weighted by its proximity to the point using the weighted ![images](images/c21-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>\-norm as calculated by `weightedL2norm`:

![](images/c21-gra-0033.png)

In order to implement the algorithm, we have to implement several building blocks. In particular, we define five separate functions which form the basis of the algorithm. First, we implement the error function, ![images](images/c21-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>e</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>w</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>, a negative of the mean-squared error of the weighted estimator and unweighted one. The function has the same arguments as the previous function `kNNMeanFunction`:

![](images/c21-gra-0034.png)

Let us further define an ![images](images/c21-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> function and ![images](images/c21-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> function, respectively:

![](images/c21-gra-0035.png)![](images/c21-gra-0036.png)

We can proceed with the definition of the gradient of the function, ![images](images/c21-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi>w</mi></msub><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mi>w</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>x</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>:

![](images/c21-gra-0037.png)

Finally, we construct the gradient of the error, ![images](images/c21-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi>e</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>w</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>, along which we will search for the features explaining most of the dependent variables:

![](images/c21-gra-0038.png)

We combine all the above-defined functions into the iterative algorithm to select the features following the gradient descent approach from data set `coordFull` and `valueFull`. The iterative algorithm initiates the weights to 1. The function defines an internal function `kNNUpdateWeights`, which represents one run of the algorithm, i.e. one update of weights. The updating is based on the gradient of the error, where the updates are being weighted by the decaying learning ratio, driven by `learningRatio` and `decay`. The algorithm relies on nearest neighbours and the size of the neighbourhood used for the ![images](images/c21-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> regressions is given by `kNN`, which enters as another parameter. Further, the parameter ![images](images/c21-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math>, or inverse temperature, is provided as `beta`. In every iteration, we need to calculate the properties of score measure and the derivatives. We do not use the full sample for these calculations, but a fraction of the entire data set, `fractionS`. Finally, we specify as the last input the number of iterations, `nIterations`, the algorithm will take. The parameters are wrapped within a dictionary for convenience.

![](images/c21-gra-0039.png)

Time to illustrate its usage with an example. We define a data set with three independent variables and one dependent variable:

![](images/c21-gra-0040.png)

The dependent variable `val` does not depend on variable `coord3` while the strongest link is with `coord2`. Let us then pack the variables within a table:

![](images/c21-gra-0041.png)

The `kNNFeatureSelection` function requires as an input dictionary with number of parameters. Defining the following values:

![](images/c21-gra-0042.png)

and wrapping them into the dictionary:

![](images/c21-gra-0043.png)

The values chosen, among others, do not provide any decay of the learning ratio. The number of iterations is fixed to 100 while the ![images](images/c21-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> neighbourhood size is to be small, 5. In every iteration, half of the sample is used.

The iteration is run as:

![](images/c21-gra-0044.png)

saving the result into the table `kNNtab`.

We can explore the outcome:

![](images/c21-gra-0045.png)![](images/c21-gra-0046.png)

The weights for three features are `coord1:1.122086`, `coord2:1.209277`, and `coord3:1.036502`. The second feature gets the highest weight, suggesting the largest importance, while least importance is on the third feature. This conforms with the underlying data structure.

Let us depict the evolution of weights:

![](images/c21-gra-0047.png)

[Figure 21.4](#c21.xhtml#c21-fig-0004) depicts the evolution of three weights corresponding to the three features as a function of the number of iterations taken. The three lines are `coord1` (light gray line), `coord2` (black line), and `coord3` (dark gray line). The figure shows that the difference between three weights is growing in absolute value. The values are not by any means saturated and the system is still evolving. Since the weights are not forced to be normalised, the value of interest is rather the relative difference between the weights.

![FIGURE 21.4 Evolution of weights for three features coord1 (light gray), coord2 (black), and coord3 (dark gray), as a function of number of iterations](images/c21f004.png)

[**FIGURE 21.4**](#c21.xhtml#R_c21-fig-0004) Evolution of weights for three features `coord1` (light gray), `coord2` (black), and `coord3` (dark gray), as a function of number of iterations

The exercise can be further extended for more complex problems. It is also interesting to investigate the evolution of weights. They are random as we are using only a fraction (random one) of the data set in each iteration. It is also worth considering renormalisation of the weights in every iteration step, for instance, to fix ![images](images/c21-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>&#8741;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. The absolute values of weights could be then used to assess the importance of features across different problems.

To motivate readers to extend the presented exercise, [Figure 21.5](#c21.xhtml#c21-fig-0005) depicts the evolution of three weights corresponding to the three features as a function of the number of iterations taken for ![images](images/c21-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></math> steps. The three lines are `coord1` (light gray line), `coord2` (black line), and `coord3` (dark gray line). Compared to [Figure 21.4](#c21.xhtml#c21-fig-0004), current figure has weights normalised as ![images](images/c21-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>&#8741;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, where normalisation was done ex post. The dynamics of weights get more stable after approximately 1000 runs. The weight for the third feature tends to 0 as expected while the other two features have weights different from zero, both sorted by value according to their importance. The figure suggests an extension towards an algorithm where we iterate for as long as we eliminate features with weights reaching 0.

![FIGURE 21.5 Evolution of normalised weights for three features coord1 (light gray), coord2 (black), and coord3 (dark gray), as a function of number of iterations, for images runs](images/c21f005.png)

[**FIGURE 21.5**](#c21.xhtml#R_c21-fig-0005) Evolution of normalised weights for three features `coord1` (light gray), `coord2` (black), and `coord3` (dark gray), as a function of number of iterations, for ![images](images/c21-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></math> runs

# CHAPTER 22  
Neural Networks

 

The focus of this chapter is nothing less than neural networks. The term covers a number of related methods and techniques and represents one of the most rapidly growing domains in the machine learning literature. In this chapter, we aim to convince the reader that `q` can be used to work with neural networks as well. We implement a neural network–based classifier and regressor within a few lines of code and successfully apply it in practice.

We do not claim that `q` on its own is the language of choice for neural networks and their applications to complex problems. Deep networks, convoluted neural networks, or long short-term memory (LSTM) could be programmed in `q`, but their implementation would require a significant time investment. This is beyond the scope of our book, and we keep this for future work.

The terminology of neural networks comes from their original purpose: to model the functions of the human brain. The model was microscopic, i.e. modelling each neuron explicitly and parameterising how the signal spreads across the network of neurons. The most straightforward implementation was using step functions with certain thresholds as models for neurons' responses. The terminology from its original purpose persisted into current days; further, it gives the neural network models a certain metaphysical flavour.

 

## 22.1 THEORETICAL INTRODUCTION

Let us start with an introduction to neural networks. Our objective is to acquire an understanding of neural networks with a single hidden layer. It is called hidden, because it is neither the input nor the output layer, but appears inside the neural network. This is a slightly simplified setup while there are a plethora of more elaborate setups of neural networks in the literature. We encourage interested readers to fulfil their curiosity in specialised publications; see, for instance, Aggarwal (2018).

Despite the simplicity of our choice, neural networks with a single hidden layer capture all nonlinear relationships between the dependent variable and features. Thus we shall restrict our attention to neural networks with a single hidden layer.

We are provided with an ![images](images/c22-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional array of features ![images](images/c22-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>X</mi><mi>M</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and our aim is to predict ![images](images/c22-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> dependent variables ![images](images/c22-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>Y</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></math>. The general dimension of the dependent variable allows us to formulate regression and ![images](images/c22-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>\-class classification within one framework. For regression we usually set ![images](images/c22-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> while for ![images](images/c22-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>\-class classification each ![images](images/c22-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c22-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>, corresponds to one of the classes.

The application of a neural network is a two-stage procedure:

*   *The first stage:* Map between the input features and the hidden layer.
*   *The second stage:* Map between the hidden layer and the dependent variable.

The neural network is frequently depicted using the following scheme:

(22.1)![equation](images/c22-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>X</mi> <mi>M</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mover accent="true"> <mo>&#8594;</mo> <mrow> <mtext>Stage 1:</mtext> <mi>&#951;</mi> </mrow> </mover> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>N</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mover accent="true"> <mo>&#8594;</mo> <mrow> <mtext>Stage 2:</mtext> <mi>&#964;</mi> </mrow> </mover> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub> <mi>Y</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>Y</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

We have added ![images](images/c22-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c22-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>, respectively. Those variables are frequently referred to as the bias and represent a constant shift in the model. The vector ![images](images/c22-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math> corresponds to the hidden layer. This layer is not visible outside of the model and corresponds to the latent variables of the model. This layer is essential to capture nonlinearities. For more complex neural network topologies, the hidden layers encapsulate memory and perception of general features.

   

***The first stage***

First, the map between the observed data, ![images](images/c22-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>X</mi><mi>M</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and the hidden layer, ![images](images/c22-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>Z</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math>, is provided. The map is modelled as:

(22.2)![equation](images/c22-math-0002.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mn>0</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>M</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>X</mi> <mi>M</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c22-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c22-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>m</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>n</mi></mfenced></msubsup></mrow></math> are parameters of the map. The activation function ![images](images/c22-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math> can be thought of as neuron. There are a number of popular choices:

*   Sigmoid function: ![images](images/c22-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.
*   Hyperbolic tangent function: ![images](images/c22-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.
*   RELU, or rectified linear unit function: ![images](images/c22-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>.

Thus, in general, every node of the hidden layer, ![images](images/c22-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>, is a function of all input nodes and the bias node. The hidden layer nodes serve as input for the second stage with the output layer.

 

***The second stage***

Second, the map between the hidden layer, ![images](images/c22-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>Z</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and the dependent variable(s), ![images](images/c22-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>Y</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></math>, is defined. The form of the function ![images](images/c22-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> depends on the problem at hand and the particular neurons can have the following form (the function in the output layer is usually also called an activation function):

*   Regression with ![images](images/c22-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>: Linear activation function: (22.3)![equation](images/c22-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#964;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>N</mi> </msub> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>N</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>N</mi> </msub> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>N</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 
*   Classification with ![images](images/c22-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> classes: Softmax function assigning probability to every class: [(22.4)](#c22.xhtml#R_c22-disp-0004)![equation](images/c22-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#964;</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mn>0</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>l</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>l</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>N</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>l</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>N</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <msubsup> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msup> <mi>l</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>L</mi> </msubsup> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mn>0</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi>l</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi>l</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>N</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msup> <mi>l</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>N</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The provided functions are for illustration. In general, the activation function of the output layer depends on the cost function. We require that the first derivative of the cost function with respect to the hidden layer be easy to compute. For instance, for ![images](images/c22-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, we set the cost function to be the square of the difference between the predicted output value and the true value:

(22.5)![equation](images/c22-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>Y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Z</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#964;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>Z</mi> </mfenced> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

then the first derivative reads:

(22.6)![equation](images/c22-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>Y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Z</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>Z</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#964;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>Z</mi> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

which is a straightforward expression to operate with. Analogously, the same argument can be applied to classification and the cross-entropy cost function.

Keep in mind that the activation function may affect the performance of the algorithm and thus its form is a hyper- or meta-parameter of the model. It is worth trying several forms based on the problem at hand.

There are many ways to interpret a neural network. For regression, we can think of the neural network as a standard linear regression, where independent variables entering the regression is a “neuron” expansion of the original input variables. This method is similar to methods where input variables are expanded in a particular basis, and the expansion is used in the linear model. It can thus be thought of as some form of generalisation of the linear regression, where nonlinearity is brought in through the basis – neuron – expansion. For classification problems, we may interpret the neural network as an “advisory committee” where individual “advisors” – nodes in the hidden layer – are weighted according to an activation function.

The hidden nodes thus play an important role, either as a basis for the expansions or as “advisors”. They are referred to as hidden as they are not directly observable. They can, however, play a significant role and in specific problems they may be needed to be known explicitly. In particular, if ![images](images/c22-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>, the map from the input data to the hidden layer is a compression, since we reduce the dimensionality of the data. This itself can be utilised in dimensionality reduction problems (in fact, the autoencoder neural network with one hidden layer containing ![images](images/c22-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> neurons would be similar to extracting first ![images](images/c22-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> components within principal component analysis (PCA), which is frequently used for dimensionality reduction).

 

### 22.1.1 Calibration

The neural network itself is rather intuitive, and two-stage regression/classification interpretation makes it transparent. What is less clear, however, is the procedure for the calibration of the weights, as the parameters of this model are frequently called. There are all together

(22.7)![equation](images/c22-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>m</mi> <mi>s</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>L</mi> <mo>&#183;</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>N</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#183;</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>M</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> 

parameters. The dimensionality of the problem is large.

Let us first propose an exact solution. We index the observations by index ![images](images/c22-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c22-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> observations in total.

  

***Regression***

Let us assume we want to regress the ![images](images/c22-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional dependent variable ![images](images/c22-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></math>. The loss function used is the sum of squared residuals:

The linear activation function usually works well for regression problems. The loss function ![images](images/c22-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> is minimised with respect to all the parameters ![images](images/c22-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi></mrow></math>.

 

***Classification***

When we want to classify the ![images](images/c22-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional dependent variable ![images](images/c22-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></math> into ![images](images/c22-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> classes, a convenient loss function is the cross-entropy function:

(22.9)![equation](images/c22-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>s</mi> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mrow> <mi>c</mi> <mi>l</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mi>s</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>Y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </munderover> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>L</mi> </munderover> <msubsup> <mi>y</mi> <mi>t</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>l</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <msub> <mi>&#964;</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mn>0</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>l</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>X</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mi>&#945;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>l</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>Z</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>X</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mi>&#945;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>N</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>l</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>N</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>X</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mi>&#945;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where the same description as for the regression holds. The choice of the activation function will affect the resulting model. Using the softmax function defined in [eq. (22.4)](#c22.xhtml#c22-disp-0004) and the majority vote, i.e. choosing the class according to:

(22.10)![equation](images/c22-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>L</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mi> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mi>l</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>&#964;</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

is a convenient choice. In addition, it affects the interpretability of the model. The model can be understood as a logistic regression in ![images](images/c22-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></math>. This corresponds to a class of models which are extensively studied in the literature and are frequently used in practice.

 

#### *22.1.1.1 Backpropagation*

The exact solution for the parameter set ![images](images/c22-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi></mrow></math> may not always be accessible or optimal. The solution can be overfitted as the neural network contains a large number of parameters and the expression for the parameters themselves may be cumbersome. A better approach is based on Rumelhart et al. (1986), a technique for backpropagation of errors for training neural networks. It is based on the optimisation method of gradient descent. It works as follows:

*   Set the parameters of the model randomly.
*   Propagate forward the input data and calculate the error of prediction at the output layer.
*   Propagate backwards the errors through the network.
*   Update the parameters of the model throughout the network based on the gradient of the error at each part of the network.

This mechanism, where the propagation goes forward and then backward, gives rise to an alternative name of the procedure, the *forward-backward* propagation. The procedure requires the knowledge of the gradient at each node. This is technically feasible for neural networks as chain rule can be used for calculating derivatives at each node. The procedure allows us to progress layer-by-layer and the information relevant for a given layer/node can be stored.

Let us derive the equations needed for the backpropagation algorithm, namely the gradients at each node. For that purpose, we will employ the square loss function for the regression problem with ![images](images/c22-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> dependent variables. Further, we need to express the equations describing the neural network for each observation. Thus, we denote every feature and dependent variable observed as ![images](images/c22-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub></mfenced><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c22-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub></mfenced><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math>, respectively, where the observations are indexed by ![images](images/c22-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. Analogously, the state of the hidden node of the neural network when ![images](images/c22-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-th observation is read by the network follows:

(22.11)![equation](images/c22-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>z</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mn>0</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mn>0</mn> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>M</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>M</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The gradient to be calculated is derived from [eq. (22.8)](#c22.xhtml#c22-disp-0008). We need to calculate derivatives with respect to the parameters ![images](images/c22-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c22-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math>, respectively. We will use the chain rule for derivatives and thus will derive derivatives starting at the output node and proceeding towards the input node. Every node is chained to the previous one: the first derivative with respect to the parameter ![images](images/c22-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>n</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>l</mi></mfenced></msubsup></mrow></math> driving the error of the activation function reads

<mi>z</mi> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>X</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mi>&#945;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mfenced> <msub> <mi>z</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Then, using the chain rule, we can write down the first derivative with respect to ![images](images/c22-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>m</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>n</mi></mfenced></msubsup></mrow></math>:
