</mfenced> </mfenced> <mo>&#215;</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> (22.16)![equation](images/c22-math-0016.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd> <mspace width="1.22em"/> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>l</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msup> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mn>0</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mn>0</mn> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>M</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>X</mi> <mrow> <mi>M</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

Both derivatives allow us to quantify how much each node contributes to the error obtained by evaluating ![images](images/c22-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-th observation. It drives the correction of the parameter(s) to be made in response to the observed error:

(22.17)![equation](images/c22-math-0017.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msub> <mi>R</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>l</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <msubsup> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>z</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>z</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> (22.18)![equation](images/c22-math-0018.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msub> <mi>R</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>m</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <msubsup> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

We have written two derivatives as a product of the error for the current model evaluated against the ![images](images/c22-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>\-th data point, ![images](images/c22-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>z</mi></mfenced></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c22-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>x</mi></mfenced></msup></mrow></math>, respectively, and the value of the node. We can define the iterative procedure to update the parameters according to the gradient of the error:

[(22.19)](#c22.xhtml#R_c22-disp-0019)![equation](images/c22-math-0019.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>l</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <mo>&#8594;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>l</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#955;</mi> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </munderover> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msub> <mi>R</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>l</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </math> [(22.20)](#c22.xhtml#R_c22-disp-0020)![equation](images/c22-math-0020.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>m</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <mo>&#8594;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>m</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#955;</mi> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </munderover> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msub> <mi>R</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>m</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where we keep the ordering of the equations from the output layer towards the input layer. The parameter ![images](images/c22-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> is the learning rate. It reflects how much we want to update the parameter as a function of the error. We consider the parameter constant at this stage, but we cease this assumption below. The set of equations for classification is derived analogously. We will see the functional form when we discuss the implementation below.

The updating procedure then works as advertised. In the forward stage, we use the current model and propagate observations forwards through the network until we produce output values. Thus, we obtain ![images](images/c22-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#964;</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></math>'s from which we can calculate errors. Then, we calculate ![images](images/c22-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>z</mi></mfenced></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c22-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>x</mi></mfenced></msup></mrow></math>, respectively, and the corresponding values at nodes (input layer is given and does not have to be calculated while the hidden nodes have to be). Finally, we update the parameters according to [eqs. (22.20)](#c22.xhtml#c22-disp-0020) and [(22.19)](#c22.xhtml#c22-disp-0019). The entire procedure is simple to implement, as we will demonstrate in the following section.

Further, [eqs. (22.20)](#c22.xhtml#c22-disp-0020) and [(22.19)](#c22.xhtml#c22-disp-0019) contain a sum over the sample used in the training phase. We have used the full sample in those equations, but we can implement different setups. For instance, we can use one observation at a time, and the procedure can be performed in an *online* manner, where the current observation updates the network and is forgotten. This allows us to use large data sets which do not fit into memory. Another technique for dealing with large data sets is to use batches. A batch is a subset of the training sample. The learning by batches works so that we perform a single update of the parameters using a batch of data. The iteration then progresses to the next step, when another batch is chosen and the parameters are further updated. It is convenient to refer as an epoch to the set of iterations which went through the entire training data set.

 

### 22.1.2 The Learning Rate Parameter

The critical parameter in the backpropagation algorithm is the learning rate ![images](images/c22-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math>. If the parameter is too big, the update is massive and may respond too harshly to the errors. This would be unpleasant especially when we are close to the solution: we would be forced to step over the optimum. On the other hand, a small value will cause the convergence to be too slow and thus numerically inefficient.

These problems could be overcome by letting ![images](images/c22-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> depend on the progress through iterations. Let us denote the index of the iteration by ![images](images/c22-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></math>. Then, we denote ![images](images/c22-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></mrow></math> the learning rate parameter as a function of the iteration stage. It was shown in Robbins and Monro (1985) that for ![images](images/c22-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> as ![images](images/c22-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></math>, such that ![images](images/c22-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mi>&#957;</mi></msub><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c22-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mi>&#957;</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>&#957;</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></math>, the gradient search will converge.

We can also consider more advanced procedures. The learning rate parameter can depend on the error and be progressively chosen as needed. Besides, it can contain elements of stochastic annealing, where even when converging to a specific value, the learning rate parameter can be suddenly increased, thus trying to probe the neighbourhood and prevent being stuck in the local solution. Even more advanced techniques, suitable for deep networks, would involve periodically decreasing ![images](images/c22-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></mrow></math> and then resetting it into the initial value while at every instance when ![images](images/c22-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>&#957;</mi></msub></mrow></math> reaches its minimum the solution is taken and stored. The set of all such solutions then constitutes the set of weak learners, which can be combined as trees in the forest.

 

### 22.1.3 Initialisation

The iteration starts with a specific choice of parameters (weights). The natural choice is to set all of them to 0.0. We encourage the reader to explore what form the updating equations take. The derivatives will be zero, and the iteration will get stuck at zero values. It is therefore necessary to choose nonzero values. Initialising the starting parameters at random values, rather small, allows the algorithm to pick up and navigate through the parametric space.

Let us mention one more item related to initialisation. The input parameters should be normalised such that they are demeaned and the variance is normalised to 1.0. This assures that parameters in the network are operating at the same scale and the same initial random initialisation can be used for every parameter.

 

### 22.1.4 Overfitting

Neural networks are prone to overfit the model. They potentially contain a large number of parameters and fully connected networks tend to adapt to the data too much. A popular choice is weight decay, where the loss function ![images](images/c22-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> contains additional penalty proportional to the magnitude of the parameters of the model:

(22.21)![equation](images/c22-math-0021.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>Y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>&#8594;</mo> <mi>L</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>Y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mi>n</mi> </mrow> </munder> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msubsup> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>l</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mi>m</mi> </mrow> </munder> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>m</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </msubsup> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

with ![images](images/c22-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math> driving the regularisation.

Another popular method is dropout, see Srivastava et al. (2014). The dropout is de facto equivalent to ridge regression and works as follows. At every iteration step, we select which nodes will be updated according to a predetermined probability ![images](images/c22-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> (this is a parameter of the regularisation analogous to ![images](images/c22-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math> in the preceding paragraph). The nodes which have not been selected are physically removed from the network with all the connections and are not updated during the given iteration step. After the iteration, the updated nodes are merged with the nodes which have been excluded.

Further, excluding the node from training means that we lose some information and tend to emphasise the effect of the nodes which have been preserved. This means that we have to weigh the output of all nodes at the end by probability ![images](images/c22-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>. This will create a fully connected network with all the nodes included in the training situation.

Additional to regularisation, with ![images](images/c22-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow></math>, we cut the number of parameters to half, which may significantly speed up the calibration. Dropout technique is both a regularisation method as well as a speed-up improvement and is gaining popularity in the machine learning community, especially for complex networks.

 

### 22.1.5 Dimension of the Hidden Layer(s)

We consider the neural network with one hidden layer. In general, nothing prevents us from creating a topology of the neural network with more hidden layers. It is in fact topology with a large number of hidden layers which brought fame to neural networks. Deep networks – how the neural networks with a large number of hidden layers are known – can learn very complex patterns and, mainly, generalise the concepts. It is still not fully understood what makes the deep networks so successful in generalisation.

Let us put aside deep networks and discuss the dimension of the hidden layer(s). Going beyond one hidden layer allows us to create a network able to model highly complex and nonlinear features. This brings the need for optimisation of a large number of weights. For this, not only a huge data set is needed, but also proper training techniques and regularisations have to be well thought out.

For the case of one hidden layer, the question is what should be the dimension of the hidden layer, ![images](images/c22-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>. Since the dimension of the input (features) is ![images](images/c22-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>, we compare the dimension of the hidden layer relative to the size of the input. In the case of ![images](images/c22-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>, there is information suppression in the hidden layer as we aim to represent ![images](images/c22-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional input through the ![images](images/c22-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional variables. Thus, it is recommended to have ![images](images/c22-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> such that we can model nonlinear dependencies in the features.

There is, in fact, a reason to use ![images](images/c22-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>. Imagine the case when ![images](images/c22-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and thus ![images](images/c22-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>. Such a setup aims to model the input variables and use the features to explain themselves. If we set ![images](images/c22-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>, the role of the hidden layer is to compress the input such that we can recover the input as much as possible. This is nothing but dimensionality reduction, given we can use the hidden layer to represent the input data. It can be shown that this is equivalent to the PCA. We can thus obtain PCA without the need to perform advanced matrix manipulations. The extreme case of ![images](images/c22-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> means that we want to compress the input into a single scalar factor.

 

## 22.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF NEURAL NETWORKS

In this section, we turn the theory of the previous paragraphs into functional code. We implement a function which can perform either classification or regression. It is further convenient to split the classification of the binary variable and general classification for ![images](images/c22-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.

First, we define some useful routines and functions, which will then be wrapped into the function comprehending the neural network training. We aim to add a few extra features into learner functions in order to achieve various functionalities. All will be wrapped in a user-friendly interface with several options to choose from using a simple set of switches.

 

### 22.2.1 Multivariate Encoder

It is convenient to map the ![images](images/c22-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>\-class classification problem, where the dependent variable can take ![images](images/c22-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> discrete values into an ![images](images/c22-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional variable where every individual component is a binary variable. Such a transformation is not the most economical one; we waste at least one dimension. Models are conveniently simple ones, and the extra dimension of the dependent variable does not cause in most of the situations problems during learning.

To implement the multivariate classifier, we will need to encode the ![images](images/c22-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>\-class discrete variable into ![images](images/c22-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> binary variables. The function `encoderMulti` takes as an argument list (![images](images/c22-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> discrete cases of the dependent variable) and returns a dictionary, which can be itself used as a function to create a list of binary variables:

![](images/c22-gra-0001.png)

The construction `arg=/:arg` works as follows: the list `arg` is compared with each element of the list `arg` and creates boolean lists marking the match of the compared elements. Namely,

![](images/c22-gra-0002.png)![](images/c22-gra-0003.png)

We can test the function using the simple case where the argument of the function is a list of elements which are to be classified:

![](images/c22-gra-0004.png)

and creates a dictionary which has for each element of the list entering the function an entry:

![](images/c22-gra-0005.png)

We use the encoder function to convert the column containing the categorical variable into an array of indicator time series:

![](images/c22-gra-0006.png)![](images/c22-gra-0007.png)

The map is for a variable `val`, which has three distinct values. As the outcome of the encoding procedure, we have created a new variable `class`, which has for every atom a three-dimensional array of binary variables. The array has always one of the elements equal to `1b` while the rest are zero, denoting which class is present.

 

### 22.2.2 Neurons

The critical component of any neural network is neurons. These are functions which transform a signal coming from different nodes into a response. We consider both hidden layer neurons and the activation function (the neurons mapping the hidden layer into the output variable) as neurons. In addition to the response of the neuron itself, we also need first derivatives to calculate the gradient of the errors for backward propagation.

  

***Binary classification***

First, we specify the functional form of function ![images](images/c22-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math> for classification problem. We consider the so-called sigmoid function

(22.22)![equation](images/c22-math-0022.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mrow> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>y</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mi>x</mi> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

In addition to the multi-encoder, we define the objective functions which will be used for either of the three modes. Further, for each objective function, we have to define the error function which allows us to train the neural network based on the error feedback.

For bivariate classifier, the objective function used is based on the typical sigmoid function. The function reads:

![](images/c22-gra-0008.png)

and the corresponding error function used for training of the network is the cross-entropy function ![images](images/c22-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> provided in [eq. (22.9)](#c22.xhtml#c22-disp-0009):

![](images/c22-gra-0009.png) 

***![images](images/c22-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>M</mi> </mrow> </math>\-class classification***

In the case of multivariate classification, we use the softmax function defined in [eq. (22.4)](#c22.xhtml#c22-disp-0004) for response of neurons:

![](images/c22-gra-0010.png)

Corresponding error function, the cross-entropy, is functionally similar to the bivariate classification case:

![](images/c22-gra-0011.png) 

***Regression***

Finally, we utilise the neural network for regression. The output of the neuron is thus a simple pass by the input argument:

![](images/c22-gra-0012.png)

with the corresponding squared error function:

![](images/c22-gra-0013.png)

Finally, we wrap the functions and the error function terms into two dictionaries. We will call corresponding functions based on the purpose the neural network is used for, i.e. as a `‘classifier`, `‘multiClassifier`, or `‘nonlinearReg`:

![](images/c22-gra-0014.png)

The purpose of dictionaries is to put the functional forms under the surface and make the functions more convenient for users.

 

### 22.2.3 Training the Neural Network

We can proceed with implementing the training procedure for the neural network itself. At the beginning of the iteration procedure, we need to initialise the parameters of the neural network. Function `weightNNInit` takes two arguments: the size of the input nodes, `argIn`, and the size of the layer itself, `argOut`. The output is the array for a given layer, where every parameter is initialised as a random number drawn from ![images](images/c22-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>U</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>:

![](images/c22-gra-0015.png)

We proceed with defining one iteration of the gradient descent update. The function `forwardBackwardNNwError` performs one iteration. It takes the following arguments: the input and output arrays, `inputValue` and `outputValue`, respectively, `learningRatio` being the constant learning rate parameter, `func` standing for the type of the problem to solve in order to choose a correct function for the neuron and the gradient of the error for learning (choose from three options `‘classifier`, `‘multiClassifier`, and `‘nonlinearReg`, respectively), and dictionary of parameters, `params`, which are updated during iteration. The dictionary contains the output of the model, `‘out`, parameters of the hidden layer and of the activation function, `‘parsHid2out` and `‘parsIn2Hid`, respectively, error from ![images](images/c22-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> function, `‘Error`, and a counter of iteration `‘Counter`.

![](images/c22-gra-0016.png)

The hidden layer uses by the default sigmoid activation function. This can be easily changed if needed by modifying the definition of `hiddenLayer` and `deltaLayerI2H` accordingly. The function performs three steps. First, the forward step is done by propagating the input value through the network by stacking the layers atop each other. Then, the error is recorded and propagated back, keeping track of the gradient in each node. Finally, the parameters in dictionary `params` are updated and iteration is concluded.

We further wrap the one iteration step into the complete function `modelNN`. Similarly to one iteration step, the function has a number of input arguments to be specified: the input and output arrays, `input` and `output`, respectively; the number of neurons of the hidden layer, `nNeurons`; the control for the terminal condition and corresponding parameter of the terminal condition, `typeTerminal` and `argTerminal`, respectively; a binary variable to track the progress during convergence, `monitorConvergence`; and, finally, specification of the problem, `func` (choose from three options `‘classifier`, `‘multiClassifier`, and `‘nonlinearReg`, respectively).

There are two terminal conditions supported: `‘count`, standing for a case where provided number of iterations is performed, and `‘relativeError`, being the required minimum error to be achieved during the convergence process. The function is implemented as follows:

![](images/c22-gra-0017.png)

The function proceeds as follows: First, the initial parameters are instantiated using `weightNNInit`. Then, the terminal condition is decided and the appropriate rule for the iteration procedure is defined. This step can be potentially outsourced into another function. Then, depending on the choice whether we want to see every iteration step or not, based on the value of variable `monitorConvergence`, the iteration is performed. When we aim for monitoring convergence, we do record the dictionary `params` in every step. From this record, we can understand the evolution of errors as well as variance in the parameters. This is a useful option when we want to gain intuition about the problem itself.

 

## 22.3 EXAMPLES

Finally, we illustrate the neural network on three cases, each exploiting one possible option defined for neural networks: `‘classifier`, `‘multiClassifier`, and `‘nonlinearReg`, i.e., options for the neuron functions and the error terms.

 

### 22.3.1 Binary Classification

We test the binary classification model on the following setup. We consider four features. Each feature can take two values only; we can treat them as *true* and *false*. The dependent variable is defined as ![images](images/c22-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> operator with four input arguments:
