where ![images](images/c22-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> are variables taking values ![images](images/c22-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>. In the case of having two arguments only, the operation would be the logical operator ![images](images/c22-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>.

We first define four input features ![images](images/c22-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Instead of using the range of variables for every feature as ![images](images/c22-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>, we define the variables to be taking values ![images](images/c22-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>. Value of ![images](images/c22-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> corresponds to logical *false* while 1 is *true*. The advantage of the redefined range is the zero mean of the input features, which is suitable for neural networks. We define them as:

![](images/c22-gra-0018.png)

and define the dependent variable as being *true* when sum of the four features is ![images](images/c22-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, which corresponds to ![images](images/c22-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> function:

![](images/c22-gra-0019.png)

The probability of observing *true* value of `yA` is ![images](images/c22-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.25</mn></mrow></math>, as can be verified by simple algebra. We can verify this assertion by:

![](images/c22-gra-0020.png)![](images/c22-gra-0021.png)

Having the data set comprising four input features `xA1`, `xA2`, `xA3`, and `xA4`, and dependent variable `yA`, we can train the neural network. We use 6 neurons in the hidden layer (excluding bias), which exceeds the dimension of the features. As a terminal rule, we use `‘count` and 1000 iterations. The learning rate is 0.01, and we do monitor the output of every iteration step. Further, the problem is binary classification, which has to be specified as a last argument for the function. The following call invokes the learning of the neural network:

![](images/c22-gra-0022.png)

The outcome is stored into object `modelA`, which is nothing but a table:

![](images/c22-gra-0023.png)![](images/c22-gra-0024.png)

The table has a single row for every iteration step. The first row is the initialisation of the routine. The columns correspond to the `pars` dictionary defined above. Let us focus on the `Error` and analyse how it evolves during the iteration of the algorithm. This can be done as:

![](images/c22-gra-0025.png)

where we have excluded the first row of the table.

[Figure 22.1](#c22.xhtml#c22-fig-0001) depicts the error during the learning process of the neural network. The error is depicted against the iteration index. The reason to exclude the first row is because `Error` is set to 0.0, which does not have any meaning. The error drops during the initial stages of the learning, approximately the first 20 steps. Then, the steepness of the error descent slows down while the model keeps improving. From approximately 200 steps, the improvement of the model slows down significantly; the model reaches a plateau with no further progress. The optimal learning should avoid overtraining. Training should stop before reaching the plateau.

![FIGURE 22.1 Learning path (errors) for classification problem of four binary variables with images operation](images/c22f001.png)

[**FIGURE 22.1**](#c22.xhtml#R_c22-fig-0001) Learning path (errors) for classification problem of four binary variables with ![images](images/c22-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> operation

Once we have trained the model, we need to verify the validity of the model on the test data set. Our data set is rather trivial in the sense that the space of possible values is limited. The features can take 16 different configurations and thus the size of our sample is largely overshot. We encourage the reader to repeat the exercise once small noise is introduced to the features.

Our focus is rather the implementation itself, though. We extract the model parameters and weights at the end of the training (what we would observe under the option of not monitoring performance). The weights are recovered as:

![](images/c22-gra-0026.png)

Defining a table with all 16 configurations of our feature space:

![](images/c22-gra-0027.png)

we can list the full table:

![](images/c22-gra-0028.png)![](images/c22-gra-0029.png)

We add to the table `tabA` an extra column which is the prediction of the dependent variable; we call it `yPredict`. The prediction is simply stacking the neural network layer by layer and evaluating it on the input data:

![](images/c22-gra-0030.png)

The updated table and validity of the prediction can be in this case eye-checked:

![](images/c22-gra-0031.png)![](images/c22-gra-0032.png)

The predicted value is a real-valued number from ![images](images/c22-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>. We could further round the number to integers 0 and 1, respectively, to get the corresponding number format. Table `tabA` shows perfect agreement between `y` and `yPredict` as we can consider the small values to correspond to true 0 while values very close to 1 can be treated as true 1.

 

### 22.3.2 ![images](images/c22-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>M</mi> </mrow> </math>\-class Classification

The second example involves testing the ![images](images/c22-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>\-classification, where the dependent variable can take ![images](images/c22-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> distinct values. We test our implementation on Fisher's Iris data set iri. Let us recall the meaning of the variables in the data set:

*   *Feature 1:* sepal length in cm,
*   *Feature 2:* sepal width in cm,
*   *Feature 3:* petal length in cm,
*   *Feature 4:* petal width in cm,
*   *Dependent variable:* class: Iris Setosa, Iris Versicolour, and Iris Virginica, respectively.

The data set has 150 rows. We assume we have the data on the local drive (in root directory). First, we load the data:

![](images/c22-gra-0033.png)

and verify the structure of the table with all the names of variables:

![](images/c22-gra-0034.png)![](images/c22-gra-0035.png)

Further, we split the data set into a training sample with 100 observations, and test sample with 50 observations. Since the data set itself can be sorted based on the class, we do the random split of the data:

![](images/c22-gra-0036.png)

We verify that all three classes are represented in the training sample:

![](images/c22-gra-0037.png)![](images/c22-gra-0038.png)

We train the model using 8 neurons in the hidden layer with learning rate parameter 0.01 and run the algorithm for 1000 steps. We monitor the convergence of the algorithm:

![](images/c22-gra-0039.png)

[Figure 22.2](#c22.xhtml#c22-fig-0002) depicts the error during the learning process of the neural network for the iris data set. The learning pattern shows complex episodes during the iterations. The improvement is somewhat volatile and shows a brief burst when the error gets worse though the overall improvement is apparent. During the final stages of the learning process, the error oscillates around two values, both representing improvement. This suggests that the algorithm cannot rest in the optimum but slightly oscillates around it. This could be prevented by having the learning rate decreasing during the last stages of the iteration process.

![FIGURE 22.2 Learning path (errors) for images-class classification of the Iris data set](images/c22f002.png)

[**FIGURE 22.2**](#c22.xhtml#R_c22-fig-0002) Learning path (errors) for ![images](images/c22-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>\-class classification of the Iris data set

The data have been extracted as:

![](images/c22-gra-0040.png)

Further, we extract the model parameters at the end of the training process:

![](images/c22-gra-0041.png)

We arrange the out-of-sample data into a new table `tabB`, and add an encoded dependent variable:

![](images/c22-gra-0042.png)

Then, we predict the class of the iris using the trained model. The prediction is done by stacking the network together:

![](images/c22-gra-0043.png)

The predicted variable `classEncPredict` is an encoded array of three values, where each value represents probability that given observation is of a given class. The class with highest probability wins. We can check the accuracy of our prediction model as:

![](images/c22-gra-0044.png)![](images/c22-gra-0045.png)

The model predicts correctly 47 out of 50 cases, i.e. ![images](images/c22-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>94</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> accuracy. Let us further inspect the table itself; we view 10 random rows for illustration:

![](images/c22-gra-0046.png)![](images/c22-gra-0047.png)

It is worth noting that 5th and 8th row represent a case where the model does not work. In the cases where the model works, the probability for a correct class is usually close to 1, while in the confused case, the probabilities are instead distributed across classes. This fact can be further utilised in interpreting and adding some measure of uncertainty for every prediction.

 

### 22.3.3 Regression

The third case to explore is the regression, where the dependent variable is a real-valued array. We have mentioned in the introductory part that by suitable choice of the neural network parameters, we can turn the neural network into a dimensionality reduction tool. We explore this situation in our example as it provides a handy and practical tool.

In particular, we stick to the case of four real-valued features. Each feature is constructed as a linear combination of a common factor and an idiosyncratic noise:

[(22.24)](#c22.xhtml#R_c22-disp-0024)![equation](images/c22-math-0024.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#183;</mo> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msqrt> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> </mrow> </msqrt> <mo>&#183;</mo> <msub> <mi>e</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mtext>with</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c22-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is a parameter within ![images](images/c22-i0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c22-i0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is an idiosyncratic noise, and ![images](images/c22-i0123.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow></math> is a factor shared across different features. The factor and the idiosyncratic noise have the same variance and thus all the features have the same variance as well.

We employ the uniform distribution to define factors and idiosyncratic noise variables:

![](images/c22-gra-0048.png)

The features themselves are defined as linear combinations defined in [eq. (22.24)](#c22.xhtml#c22-disp-0024) with corresponding coefficients:

![](images/c22-gra-0049.png)

The last feature is not correlated to the common factor. Let us confirm that the correlation between factor and the features reflects the corresponding factors:

![](images/c22-gra-0050.png)![](images/c22-gra-0051.png)![](images/c22-gra-0052.png)![](images/c22-gra-0053.png)![](images/c22-gra-0054.png)![](images/c22-gra-0055.png)![](images/c22-gra-0056.png)![](images/c22-gra-0057.png)

We can proceed to train the neural network. We start with a similar parametric set-up as in the binary classification case. In particular, we choose 1 neuron in the hidden layer:

![](images/c22-gra-0058.png)

The focus is on the evaluation of the error during the iteration. The provided model does not converge, as the reader could realise when the number of iteration steps would be set too large. This brings a useful insight: we should start with a smaller case using a few iteration steps and investigate the evolution of the training. Then, set the full-scale learning.

[Figure 22.3](#c22.xhtml#c22-fig-0003) depicts the learning path as a function of the iteration index. Contrary to previous cases, we plot ![images](images/c22-i0124.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi></mrow></math> of the error in order to visualise the divergence of errors. The model does not converge, and thus we have to change the parameters of learning. The suspected parameter to be changed is the learning rate which may be too coarse, thus dragging us from the optimal values.

![FIGURE 22.3 Learning path (images errors) for dimensionality reduction and large learning rate](images/c22f003.png)

[**FIGURE 22.3**](#c22.xhtml#R_c22-fig-0003) Learning path (![images](images/c22-i0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> errors) for dimensionality reduction and large learning rate

The data for the figure has been extracted as:

![](images/c22-gra-0059.png)

Let us repeat the training of the model with smaller learning rate parameter, in this case 0.01. We show the run of the model for 3000 steps:

![](images/c22-gra-0060.png)

[Figure 22.4](#c22.xhtml#c22-fig-0004) depicts the learning path (error without the ![images](images/c22-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi></mrow></math> transformation) as it progresses during the iterations. The procedure converges in this case; the model is learning. The improvement of the error is approximately ![images](images/c22-i0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>, relatively mediocre improvement compared to all the previous cases when the improvements have been in the orders of magnitude. This confirms the failure to converge for large learning rate parameter as the improvement is rather subtle. The data for the figure has been extracted as:

![](images/c22-gra-0061.png)![FIGURE 22.4 Learning path (errors) for dimensionality reduction and moderate learning rate](images/c22f004.png)

[**FIGURE 22.4**](#c22.xhtml#R_c22-fig-0004) Learning path (errors) for dimensionality reduction and moderate learning rate

Having the converging model, which compress the information in the hidden layer, we extract the model:

![](images/c22-gra-0062.png)

and recover the value in the hidden layer, which compresses the information of four features (and constant bias node). The following table contains four features, the common factor, and the value in the hidden layer corresponding to given features, denoted as `factorModel`:

![](images/c22-gra-0063.png)

We hypothesise that the value in the hidden layer will correlate well with the `factor`. [Figure 22.5](#c22.xhtml#c22-fig-0005) depicts the scatter plot of `factor` vs. `factorModel`. There is a clear positive correlation between the two variables, though dependency is rather noisy.

![FIGURE 22.5 Scatter diagram of factor vs factorModel](images/c22f005.png)

[**FIGURE 22.5**](#c22.xhtml#R_c22-fig-0005) Scatter diagram of `factor` vs `factorModel`

We can check the correlations between the factor, the hidden value and the features:

![](images/c22-gra-0064.png)![](images/c22-gra-0065.png)

the correlation between the `factor` variables and the `factorModel` values is rather large, exceeding ![images](images/c22-i0128.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>. This is a reasonable value given we have not a priori used any correlation or covariance criteria to train the hidden layer.

On the other hand, the correlation between individual features and the `factorModel` values is more complex:

![](images/c22-gra-0066.png)![](images/c22-gra-0067.png)![](images/c22-gra-0068.png)![](images/c22-gra-0069.png)![](images/c22-gra-0070.png)![](images/c22-gra-0071.png)![](images/c22-gra-0072.png)![](images/c22-gra-0073.png)

In particular, the feature `xC2` is more correlated to `factorModel` than the feature `xC3` is. The underlying data, however, would suggest otherwise. This means that the value in the hidden layer does not manifest in our numerical exercise as a correlation preserving proxy for `factor`. This was not an objective during the training.

In summary, the extracted `featureModel` value correlates to the common factor, `factor`, well. It allows us to reduce the dimension of the data set, in our case from 4 to 1. For the sake of completeness, let us explore the case where we want to model the four features on itself. We can do it by setting number of neurons in the hidden layer to be greater than 4, namely, we choose 8:

![](images/c22-gra-0074.png)

[Figure 22.6](#c22.xhtml#c22-fig-0006) depicts the learning path as a function of the iteration index. The procedure converges well; the improvement is back to orders of magnitude as we would normally expect. The number of iterations is set to be large again. The underlying data have been obtained from table `modelC3` as:

![](images/c22-gra-0075.png)![FIGURE 22.6 Learning path (errors) for modelling the input on itself with images hidden neurons](images/c22f006.png)

[**FIGURE 22.6**](#c22.xhtml#R_c22-fig-0006) Learning path (errors) for modelling the input on itself with ![images](images/c22-i0129.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> hidden neurons

We extract the model:

![](images/c22-gra-0076.png)

and recover the four features using the trained model:

![](images/c22-gra-0077.png)

Finally, we confirm that the trained neural network models the input well. We calculate the correlation between the component of the input and the corresponding modelled value:

![](images/c22-gra-0078.png)![](images/c22-gra-0079.png)![](images/c22-gra-0080.png)![](images/c22-gra-0081.png)![](images/c22-gra-0082.png)![](images/c22-gra-0083.png)![](images/c22-gra-0084.png)![](images/c22-gra-0085.png)

In all four cases, the correlation is very close to 1.0. We can thus confidently say the model recovers the input values. We keep in mind that the exercise is performed in the sample. The purpose of the exercise was to validate the implementation rather than show the power of the neural networks.

 

## 22.4 POSSIBLE SUGGESTIONS

Our implementation of the neural networks narrows to the vanilla case of single hidden layer topology. There is a plethora of possible extensions:

*   Accessing the trained model and applying it on the out-of-sample data is done manually. It would be more convenient to have a suitable function, where stacking the neural network together would be hidden from the user.
*   The learning rate is implemented as constant. The function for training network contains an iterations counter. It would be worth extending the function such that the learning rate is a function of the iteration step. A suitable candidate is a function where the learning rate will be inversely proportional to the iteration steps.
*   It is worth exploring the dimensionality reduction when more than 1 neuron is used in the hidden layer. The measure of overall correlation captured by more than one value would be higher. The proper exercise can be through measuring ![images](images/c22-i0130.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> in linear regression using value(s) from hidden layers. We further encourage readers to verify the dimensionality reduction results with the PCA analysis introduced in [Chapter 16](#c16.xhtml).

# CHAPTER 23  
AdaBoost with Stumps

 

In this section, we introduce a particular machine learning technique called AdaBoost and apply it on stumps. We aim to provide a working example of the AdaBoost technique with a simple weak learner – a binary decision stump. There are numerous extensions of this technique as well as interesting theory to be covered, which are not within our scope. This chapter serves as a gentle introduction for the next section, which focuses on decision trees and related techniques.

 

## 23.1 BOOSTING

Boosting, in general, is one of the most powerful techniques for machine learning. In practice, we have the frequently available number of “weak” classifiers, each of them being able to explain a small fraction of the dependent variable. Forming a suitable committee of such weak classifiers which can appropriately combine their power will provide a considerable advantage.

In principle, the Boosting algorithm works as follows. Let us assume we have a set of weak classifiers denoted as ![images](images/c23-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c23-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> and the data set. Boosting uses the following logic:

*   Start with the original data set.
*   Apply the first weak classifier ![images](images/c23-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> using the original data set, adjust the data set by the outcome of the weak classifier.
*   Apply the second weak classifier ![images](images/c23-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> using the adjusted data set from the previous step, adjust the data set by the outcome of the second weak classifier.
*   Continue with third, fourth, fifth, etc.
*   Apply the ![images](images/c23-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>\-th weak classifier ![images](images/c23-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>G</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></math> using the adjusted data set from the previous step, adjust the data set by the outcome of the last weak classifier.
*   Combine the weak classifiers with appropriate scheme reflecting how each classifier performed.

The AdaBoost, or Adaptive Boosting was introduced by Freund and Schapire (1997). The boosting was originally introduced for classification problems, but it was successfully extended to regression problems as well. In our example, we stick to the classification problem where we aim to explain and predict a binary dependent variable. The weak classifier we implement in this section is a decision stump.

 

## 23.2 DECISION STUMPS

A decision stump is a one-level decision tree. The rule is formed by a root node and two child nodes. Each node corresponds to a class predicted by the rule based on the one-dimensional feature split according to a chosen threshold. For the sake of simplicity, let us consider a case where we have a binary variable ![images](images/c23-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> taking values ![images](images/c23-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and 1 and single real-valued feature ![images](images/c23-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>. The decision stump ![images](images/c23-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math>:

(23.1)![equation](images/c23-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>g</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mi>&#958;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mtext>if</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>&#958;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mtext>if</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#62;</mo> <mi>&#958;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c23-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#958;</mi></mrow></math> is a threshold of the decision stump.

Let us implement the stump function as follows:

![](images/c23-gra-0001.png)

where we have defined the stump as a function of two variables, the array of features and the threshold. The inequality in the stump is fixed. For that reason, we define later on every feature its negative counterpart. This gives us flexibility in terms of inverted proportionality between feature values and the class.

Let us create a small sample, contained in the following table:

![](images/c23-gra-0002.png)

and add the stump using the threshold of 0.5

![](images/c23-gra-0003.png)![](images/c23-gra-0004.png)

The stump is thus classifying the observations according to the value of the selected feature. The stump then constitutes our weak classifier. Further, the function allows us to operate on the features stored in the table.

 

## 23.3 ADABOOST

We now introduce the discrete version of the AdaBoost algorithm. Let us consider a case where we have a binary variable ![images](images/c23-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> taking values ![images](images/c23-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and 1 and a set of features ![images](images/c23-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math>. The range of variable ![images](images/c23-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> is chosen for convenience, and any binary variable can be easily recast into this form. Concerning variables representing features, we require them to be of any ordinal type, i.e. such that we can order them and apply the inequality operation. Thus, aside from obvious candidates of floats, integers, and various date and time types – which are either floats or integers under the surface – we also allow for strings and characters.

The ultimate aim of the model we want to develop is to find the relationship between ![images](images/c23-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c23-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> such that we can write:

(23.2)![equation](images/c23-math-0002.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>G</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>x</mi> <mi>N</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where function ![images](images/c23-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> models the relationship between features and the dependent variable.

Let us assume that we are equipped with weak classifiers ![images](images/c23-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c23-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> indexes the weak classifier, ![images](images/c23-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the corresponding parameter set (in the case of stumps the threshold), and ![images](images/c23-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the feature chosen for the given classifier.

Let us define the loss function for a general single-valued classifier ![images](images/c23-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> at sample point ![images](images/c23-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math>:

(23.3)![equation](images/c23-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>E</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>g</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mi>g</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where the loss function distinguishes the sign and not the numerical value itself, and ![images](images/c23-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> indexes observation points with ![images](images/c23-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>. We do not need to restrict ourselves to any numerical values for the model. In the case of regression, the corresponding loss function would be the square of the differences, the one used with a least squares method or neural networks. Using the exponential function implies that the error of the additive model is the product of error at each stage. Thus, AdaBoost aims to minimise the exponential loss function by iterative updates of the model. It brings a computational advantage for additive modelling as the model is consecutively re-weighted as estimation progresses. It is also noted that AdaBoost with an exponential loss function is equivalent to forward stagewise additive modelling.

AdaBoost is defined as follows:

*   Initialise every observation weight ![images](images/c23-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c23-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>.
*   Initialise the model ![images](images/c23-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
*   For ![images](images/c23-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>:

1.  *    Fit classifier ![images](images/c23-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> to the data that minimises sum of errors for misclassified observations: (23.4)![equation](images/c23-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>e</mi> <mi>r</mi> <msub> <mi>r</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mi>j</mi> <mi>M</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>g</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8800;</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 
    *    Compute parameter ![images](images/c23-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mfenced></mrow></math>.
    *    Update the ensemble of models as: ![images](images/c23-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>.
    *    Update the observation weights ![images](images/c23-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>&#8592;</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mfenced></mrow></math> for every observation ![images](images/c23-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>.
    *    Normalise weights as ![images](images/c23-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>&#8592;</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mi>j</mi><mi>M</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> for every observation ![images](images/c23-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>.

*   The model ![images](images/c23-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the AdaBoost model for the data set.

Finally, the model determines the class based on the sign of ![images](images/c23-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></math>, i.e.

(23.5)![equation](images/c23-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>g</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mi>m</mi> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msub> <mi>G</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where the case of zero means indecisive outcome. We decide the value in such a case randomly; however, the probability to obtain such a case is theoretically zero (numerically, it is still possible).

Let us note that ![images](images/c23-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is a meta-parameter of the algorithm. A suitable way to determine it is through the cross-validation technique.

 

## 23.4 IMPLEMENTATION OF ADABOOST

We start by specifying the format of the data set. The hypothetical `meta` of the data table reads:

![](images/c23-gra-0005.png)

The first column corresponds to the dependent variable `y` taking values ![images](images/c23-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>. The second column is a vector of weights ![images](images/c23-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math>. The third and further columns correspond to the independent variables or features. Due to the nature of the stump, we need to add for every column its negative counterpart. Such a construction allows us to capture both direct proportionality as well as inverse proportionality. Adding the negative features is done through the function `addNegFeatureTable`:

![](images/c23-gra-0006.png)

Let us create a sample data set with two independent variables. The data set contains 110 observations, where 100 observations are pure random noise while 10 observations reveal a strong link between features and the dependent variable. In addition, the data set contains the column of weights, each having the same value ![images](images/c23-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>110</mn></mrow></math>. The data set is stored in the table `tab`:

![](images/c23-gra-0007.png)

Let us add the negative counterparts for two features:

![](images/c23-gra-0008.png)

and print out a subset of the data. This time, we choose 10 random entries from the table:

![](images/c23-gra-0009.png)![](images/c23-gra-0010.png)

The `weights` column in the table will be updated during the AdaBoost algorithm. Besides the table `tab`, we need to store the individual weak classifiers – the feature used and the corresponding threshold – as well as corresponding ![images](images/c23-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>'s. We keep this information in the following table:

![](images/c23-gra-0011.png)

During the run of the algorithm, new selected weak classifiers will be added one by one into the table. The complete model will be then recovered from the table.

Further, we follow the procedure used throughout this book and create a dictionary which will contain both tables. The AdaBoost algorithm will then process the dictionary and update it.

![](images/c23-gra-0012.png)

Before we implement the algorithm itself, we define the loss function, which is optimised when the weak classifier is being fit. The loss function is in plain terms equal to the sum of weights for observations, which are not correctly predicted. The function is implemented as follows:

![](images/c23-gra-0013.png)

We have all the components we need to implement one iteration of the AdaBoost algorithm outlined above. The function `runOneAdaBoost` takes as an input the dictionary `bucket` and identifies the new weak classifier using stumps and appends it into the existing model. Along the way, we update the weights.

![](images/c23-gra-0014.png)

It is worth making several comments. First, `feature: first 1?colsx` implements how the feature for a given stump is chosen, namely, we choose a feature randomly. This simplifies the code we are using. It keeps randomness in the model. The apparent disadvantage is that our implementation of the AdaBoost does not allow us to use it as a feature selection technique, though the validity of the technique is still preserved. Second, given the feature chosen, the optimal stump is chosen by iterating through all the possible splitting points – which are nothing but the unique values of the feature itself – and chooses the one with least loss. Finally, all the variables are updated.

Let us use the data set we have created so far and run AdaBoost with ![images](images/c23-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>, i.e., to add 10 weak stump classifiers and create their boosted committee. The procedure can be run as:

![](images/c23-gra-0015.png)

Let us first explore the information about the weak classifiers stored in the `‘ada` variable:

![](images/c23-gra-0016.png)![](images/c23-gra-0017.png)

We can reconstruct the stumps from the provided table. The first split is based on feature `‘x1`, split at the threshold ![images](images/c23-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.938132</mn></mrow></math>. The given split gives loss function, or error, of the size 0.3818182. This number itself can be interpreted as an overall error as the weights have been initialised being equal and normalised to 1. In the subsequent iterations, it cannot be interpreted in the same way as weights are not equal. Due to the overall normalisation, the value of error should be decreasing over time for improving the algorithm. If we accept this premise, the outcome of the algorithm suggests that the algorithm is not improving much beyond the first stump. This is highly likely given how we have constructed the data set, where one of two features split around threshold close to 0.98 is sufficient choice. We encourage the reader to run the function with a large ![images](images/c23-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and graphically explore the evolution of errors.

The step which we miss is a function which would give us the prediction based on the entire AdaBoost committee we have collected by the algorithm. This is done in the following function, which takes as the input `bucket` and returns a table with four columns: `‘res` containing the numerical value provided by the model, `‘y` containing true value of the dependent variable, `‘prediction` containing the predicted dependent variable based on sign of the numerical value, and `‘isPredicted` column, which shows whether the observation has been correctly predicted, value 1, or not, value ![images](images/c23-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.

![](images/c23-gra-0018.png)

Let us predict the dependent variable using the example:

![](images/c23-gra-0019.png)![](images/c23-gra-0020.png)

The first ten observations are perfectly predicted. Those observations are ones with a straight link between dependent and independent variables. The rest does not show any apparent pattern. Let us create the following table:

![](images/c23-gra-0021.png)

which contains index `i`, and the cumulative sum of the `‘isPredicted` column.

[Figure 23.1](#c23.xhtml#c23-fig-0001) depicts the cumulative sum of `‘isPredicted` variable as a function of the index. Besides the straight improvement at the beginning of the sample, there are a few episodes where the algorithm picked up the dependent variable successfully. Due to the randomness in the data set, this can be a symptom of overfitting. The results thus have to be interpreted carefully. At the end of the sample, the cumulative sum reaches a value of 38. The maximum possible value is 110 and value equal to 0 corresponds to no predictive power. In this case, the model is visually interpreted as predictive.

![FIGURE 23.1 The cumulative sum of ‘isPredicted variable for AdaBoost across the sample](images/c23f001.png)

[**FIGURE 23.1**](#c23.xhtml#R_c23-fig-0001) The cumulative sum of `‘isPredicted` variable for AdaBoost across the sample

In order to understand the results, we finally implement the function which returns the series of useful statistics based on the contingency table. In particular, the function provides a dictionary with the following items:

*   `‘truePositive` – number of correctly identified cases of ![images](images/c23-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
*   `‘trueNegative` – number of correctly identified cases of ![images](images/c23-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
*   `‘falsePositive` – number of incorrectly identified cases of ![images](images/c23-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
*   `‘falseNegative` – number of incorrectly identified cases of ![images](images/c23-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
*   `‘accuracy` – the proportion of true cases among the total number of cases tested.
*   `‘recall` – proportion of true positives to number of true cases with ![images](images/c23-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
*   `‘precision` – proportion of true positives to number of cases predicted as ![images](images/c23-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#375;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
*   `‘specificity` – proportion of true negatives to number of true cases with ![images](images/c23-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
*   `‘F1score` – harmonic average of precision and recall.

The function is implemented as follows:

![](images/c23-gra-0022.png)

and gives for the case under examination:

![](images/c23-gra-0023.png)![](images/c23-gra-0024.png)

The predicted outcome is fairly symmetric. The algorithm does not favour either of the two classes. It aims to provide a balanced estimate which has been achieved in our synthetic table. Further, the analysis of the model has been done fully in-sample. We encourage the reader to repeat the exercise independently and assess whether the symmetry encountered in the output is just coincidence or native to the data set (Hint: former is the case).

Let us further remark that clear information needed to view the contingency table can be obtained as:

![](images/c23-gra-0025.png)![](images/c23-gra-0026.png)

If we investigate the part of the table which is purely random, we obtain:

## 23.5 RECOMMENDATION FOR READERS

We suggest several extensions for readers:

*   *Random feature* – The implementation of the AdaBoost algorithm selects features randomly. It would be more optimal to select the best feature, using the same criteria as is used for threshold selection.
*   *Meta-parameter selection* – The number of weak classifiers, ![images](images/c23-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, is chosen by the user. This may not necessarily provide the optimal number, as overfitting may be encountered. The cross-validation is a possible technique which can be used to find an optimal value for ![images](images/c23-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. AdaBoost can be wrapped into the cross-validation utility function, which will split the sample into parts and verify the accuracy out-of-sample.
*   *Subsampling* – The data set can be split into batches, and each weak classifier can be trained on the different batch. This will strengthen the power of the technique.
*   *Regression* – The provided method is for binary classification only. The AdaBoost technique can be well-defined for regressions as well. Current functions can be thus extended for regressions.

The recommended extensions would strengthen the power of the provided algorithm and encourage readers to master their skills writing the machine learning techniques in `q`.

# CHAPTER 24  
Trees

 

In [Chapter 23](#c23.xhtml), we have introduced the notion of decision stumps and their use within the AdaBoost algorithm. A decision stump is the simplest example of a decision tree. In this chapter, we will cover decision trees in more detail; see Morgan and Sonquist (1963) for illustration of first works in this direction, or Brieman et al. (1984) and Loh (2011). We present methods for both classification and regression. We start with a theoretical introduction and proceed with an implementation in `q`. The functions we will use to represent trees are based on the concept of treetables, first introduced by Stevan Apter; see Apter (2010).

 

## 24.1 INTRODUCTION TO TREES

Let us consider a feature space spanned over the features ![images](images/c24-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Tree-based methods partition the space into rectangle-shaped domains and then assign a simple model to each domain. The simple model is usually constant and fits over observations belonging to the given domain. This corresponds to CART, or the Classification And Regression Tree approach.

[Figure 24.1](#c24.xhtml#c24-fig-0001) illustrates partitioning for a case of ![images](images/c24-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c24-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> for ![images](images/c24-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>. We have produced this partitioning by using the following script:

(24.1)![equation](images/c24-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

We can use the tree structure built in the previous paragraph to model ![images](images/c24-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> as a function of ![images](images/c24-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>. The regression model is such that we approximate the true function in every domain by a constant ![images](images/c24-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>:

(24.2)![equation](images/c24-math-0002.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi>f</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mn>7</mn> </munderover> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msub> <mtext>domain</mtext> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c24-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""></mfenced></mrow></math> is the indicator function used to model the tree domains.

The regression is expressed in such a way that we start with the full data set. We then apply the decision rules expressed in the itemised list above. Every decision rule is binary and assigns a value to every observation of a corresponding branch. The progress is made step-by-step towards more indented rules. The decision process ends with the leaf nodes.

Creating domains using decision trees is a synthetic restriction, which affects the shape of the domains. The ease of interpreting results compensates the perceived disadvantage. If features are descriptive characteristics of a subject, the decision tree reflects the way a human analyst would classify the subject based on features. This is true in medicine, for instance, where diagnosis for a disease is based on the presence of various symptoms and measurements.

In the following subsections, we outline in detail how to build a tree which can be used to fit regression and classification problems.

 

## 24.2 REGRESSION TREES

Let us consider the following problem. We have ![images](images/c24-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> features ![images](images/c24-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and a dependent variable ![images](images/c24-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>, each observation indexed by ![images](images/c24-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c24-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow></math>. The dependent variable can take any value; here we will assume it is real-valued. In order to fit the regression model, we have to determine the loss function, i.e. how well or bad the model denoted by ![images](images/c24-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> approximated the true data generating process. We consider the loss function in the form of sum of squares:

(24.3)![equation](images/c24-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mi>s</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>j</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi mathvariant="script">T</mi> </munderover> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The decision tree model thus has to achieve the minimum loss. Let us assume we are already provided with a given decision tree, e.g. the scheme to split the domain into leaf nodes:

(24.4)![equation](images/c24-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>d</mi> </msub> </munderover> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msub> <mtext>domain</mtext> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where constants ![images](images/c24-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> remain to be determined.

In fact, if we fix the tree itself, the constants are easy to find; they are simply given as:

(24.5)![equation](images/c24-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mtext>mean</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msub> <mtext>domain</mtext> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

i.e. the mean over all observations within the corresponding domain.

This does not allow us yet to form a decision. In particular, it remains to answer how branches are formed, how many of them, and how deep the tree should be. Before we discuss these, let us point out that we tacitly consider binary recursive trees, which are created as follows:

*   First, we split the space into two halves; the way to split the space – variable and threshold – is decided based on the chosen loss function.
*   Second, we model the response by the mean in each domain.
*   Each region is further split (or not) using the procedure above.
*   This process is recursively applied until a stopping rule is reached.

The optimisation of the outcome – the entire decision tree and the corresponding means – is not computationally feasible to be achieved in one go. The problem is highly non-linear and data-dependent, which will be exploited in the next chapter when we bag trees. It is thus more convenient to proceed with a greedy algorithm, which does not aim to provide a global minimum. It instead reaches a satisfactory level for the loss function in a numerically possible manner.

The greedy algorithm for a decision tree is constructed as follows:

*   Start with root node – the entire data set.
*   Set the feature ![images](images/c24-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c24-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>, and the threshold ![images](images/c24-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> to define the binary choice: (24.6)![equation](images/c24-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"> <msub> <mtext>domain</mtext> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="left"> <mo form="prefix">=</mo> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> (24.7)![equation](images/c24-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"> <msub> <mtext>domain</mtext> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="left"> <mo form="prefix">=</mo> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#62;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

1.  *    The feature index ![images](images/c24-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> and corresponding ![images](images/c24-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is found as a solution to: (24.8)![equation](images/c24-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </munder> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </munder> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msub> <mtext>domain</mtext> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </munder> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </munder> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msub> <mtext>domain</mtext> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </munder> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 
    *    The inner minimisation is indeed trivial: (24.9)![equation](images/c24-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mtext>mean</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mtext>with</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msub> <mtext>domain</mtext> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mtext>for</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 
    *    For a given ![images](images/c24-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, the split ![images](images/c24-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is found by minimising the sum of squares across possible splits.

*   The procedure is iteratively repeated on both domains.
*   The algorithm proceeds until the stopping rule is reached.

Let us point out that the procedure itself can produce trees which will have one observation per leaf node. This will provide a seemingly optimal regression tree as every average value will be formed by one value only. This is not feasible since the number of parameters needed to achieve such a tree will exploit all degrees of freedom of the data set. This constitutes an overfit, which will be seen when tested out-of-sample.

The stopping rule is thus needed, and it represents a hyperparameter of the model. The first choice is some threshold on the improvement of the loss function itself. This is in line with the greedy approach; when a given step does not provide short-term profit, the algorithm stops. The disadvantage of the approach is that a split which does not improve the overall loss function much may well open up significant improvements in subsequent splits.

The preferred algorithm is following a slightly different philosophy. First, the decision tree is grown maximally, with the stopping rule being a minimum size of leaf nodes. The fully grown decision tree is then subsequently pruned. The motivation is to build a maximum tree and then merge any branches which do not bring significant improvements. The way to perform this operation is called “cost-complexity” pruning.

 

### 24.2.1 Cost-Complexity Pruning

In order to introduce the cost-complexity measure, which governs the pruning mechanism, we have to first introduce the relevant terminology for describing trees. The provided terminology is necessary to understand this measure and will give the reader a deeper understanding of the decision tree universe in general. Let us stress that trees have proven to be useful in the construction of a wide range of different algorithms.

  

***Full tree***

Let us denote the fully grown tree as ![images](images/c24-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>.

 

***Subtree***

The subtree of a tree ![images](images/c24-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> is formed by nodes and edges, which are a subset of those in the tree ![images](images/c24-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>.

 

***Cardinality of tree***

The cardinality of a tree![images](images/c24-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""><mi>T</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> stands for the number of leaf nodes in the tree ![images](images/c24-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>.

 

***Descendant***

A node ![images](images/c24-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> is a descendant of a node ![images](images/c24-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> in the tree ![images](images/c24-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>, if there exists a connected path down the tree from ![images](images/c24-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> to ![images](images/c24-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math>.

 

***Ancestor***

A node ![images](images/c24-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> is an ancestor of a node ![images](images/c24-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> in the tree ![images](images/c24-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>, if ![images](images/c24-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> is a descendant of ![images](images/c24-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>.

 

***Branch***

A branch ![images](images/c24-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> of the tree ![images](images/c24-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> is a subtree with a node ![images](images/c24-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> being a root node and all descendants of ![images](images/c24-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> from ![images](images/c24-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>.

 

***Pruning***

Process of pruning a branch ![images](images/c24-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> of the tree ![images](images/c24-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> consists of deleting all descendants of ![images](images/c24-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> from ![images](images/c24-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>.

 

***Pruned tree***

A tree ![images](images/c24-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> is a pruned subtree from the tree ![images](images/c24-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>, if some branches of the tree ![images](images/c24-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> have been pruned off. We denote it as ![images](images/c24-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8834;</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>.

We are now fully equipped to define the cost-complexity measure. The measure governs the second part of the algorithm outlined above:

 

***Cost-complexity measure***

The cost-complexity measure is defined as:

(24.10)![equation](images/c24-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"> <msub> <mi>R</mi> <mi>&#945;</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>T</mi> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="left"> <mo form="prefix">=</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mi>T</mi> </mfenced> </munderover> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </munder> <mi>L</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>s</mi> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>T</mi> </mfenced> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mi>T</mi> </mfenced> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> (24.11)![equation](images/c24-math-0011.png)<math <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mi>T</mi> </mfenced> </munderover> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]"
