<mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </munder> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <msub> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msub> <mtext>domain</mtext> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </msub> </mfrac> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msub> <mtext>domain</mtext> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mi>T</mi> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

The cost-complexity pruning algorithm thus starts with a fully grown tree and aims to find for every ![images](images/c24-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> the pruned tree ![images](images/c24-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub></mrow></math>, i.e., ![images](images/c24-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub><mo>&#8834;</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> such that ![images](images/c24-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>T</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> is minimised. The role of the parameter ![images](images/c24-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> is apparent: the parameter governs the trade-off between the tree size and how well it performs in fitting the data. When ![images](images/c24-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, the fully grown tree is preferred. On the other hand, as ![images](images/c24-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> grows the size is penalised more, up to the point when the tree with root node only is chosen.

The cost-complexity pruning algorithm works as follows:

*   Grow a fully grown tree ![images](images/c24-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>.
*   Choose a range of values for ![images](images/c24-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>.

1.  *    For every ![images](images/c24-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>, find a unique smallest subtree ![images](images/c24-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub><mo>&#8834;</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>, which minimises ![images](images/c24-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>.
    *    The subtree is found by pruning: the nodes are successively collapsed in a sequence, where we collapse a node, which produces the smallest per-node increase of the loss function – sum of squares. The sequence of collapsing the tree continues until the tree with root node only is obtained. This procedure contains a sequence of subtrees and the optimal tree is contained in this sequence.

*   Given the sequence of trees ![images](images/c24-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub></mrow></math>, each of them optimising the cost-complexity measure, the optimal ![images](images/c24-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> is found by cross-validation.

In the following section, we discuss the formulation of the decision trees for the classification problems.

 

## 24.3 CLASSIFICATION TREE

Let us focus on the classification problem. This means that the dependent variable ![images](images/c24-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> is assumed to take integer values ![images](images/c24-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>. This can correspond to the dependent variable being an array of ![images](images/c24-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> words or symbols, for instance. Without loss of generality, we will operate with an integer-valued dependent variable. In order to employ the decision tree on classification problems, we have to decide which loss function to use.

First, we define the proportion of class ![images](images/c24-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> observations in node ![images](images/c24-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>:

(24.12)![equation](images/c24-math-0012.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>k</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <msub> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msub> <mtext>domain</mtext> <mi>m</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> </mrow> </msub> </mfrac> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msub> <mtext>domain</mtext> <mi>m</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> </mrow> </munder> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>k</mi> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The decision rule based on majority vote classifies the node to be such a class, which maximises:

(24.13)![equation](images/c24-math-0013.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>m</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mi> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mi>k</mi> </munder> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>k</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

We can now define the loss function, ![images](images/c24-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>T</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>, which can be used within the cost-complexity pruning algorithm to find an optimal tree structure. Unlike regression, where the sum of squares of residuals keeps its monopolistic position, the classification problem offers several comparable measures, each with different advantages and disadvantages.

Misclassification error:

(24.14)![equation](images/c24-math-0014.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>s</mi> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>T</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>k</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Gini index:

(24.15)![equation](images/c24-math-0015.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>s</mi> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>T</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>&#8800;</mo> <msup> <mi>k</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>k</mi> </mrow> </msub> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <msup> <mi>k</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>K</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>k</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>k</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Cross-entropy:

(24.16)![equation](images/c24-math-0016.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>s</mi> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>T</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>K</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>k</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>k</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

In the case of two classes, ![images](images/c24-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c24-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> denoting the proportion in the second class, the three functions collapse into the intuitive functions:

<mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>p</mi> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> (24.18)![equation](images/c24-math-0018.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" <mi>s</mi> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>T</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>p</mi> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>p</mi> </mfenced> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>p</mi> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

We believe the reader may be curious about the shape of the functions. We encourage the reader to plot the above functions in `q` – implementation should be trivial.

Let us illustrate the difference using the following example. Consider a case with ![images](images/c24-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, where there are 400 observations in each class (denoted as ![images](images/c24-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>400</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>400</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>). Further, suppose that Split 1 creates nodes ![images](images/c24-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>300</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>100</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c24-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>300</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> while Split 2 creates nodes ![images](images/c24-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>200</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>400</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c24-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>200</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. The following statements hold:

*   Cross-entropy and the Gini index are more sensitive to changes in the node probabilities than the misclassification error.
*   Both splits produce a misclassification rate of 0.25; however, Split 2 produces a pure node. This can be in many cases the preferable choice.
*   The Gini index and cross-entropy are lower for Split 2.

As a rule of thumb, it is recommended that for growing the tree, the Gini index or cross-entropy are used. For the cost-complexity pruning algorithm, any measure can be used. Many researchers prefer the misclassification rate, though.

It is worth it to denote that the Gini index can be obtained as a consequence of changing the majority vote into probabilistic interpretation. Namely, if we interpret the outcome of a node in terms of probability to classify node ![images](images/c24-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> as class ![images](images/c24-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, i.e., ![images](images/c24-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, then the training error rate of this rule in the node is ![images](images/c24-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msub><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>m</mi><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. If observation is coded as 1 for class ![images](images/c24-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> and 0 otherwise, the variance within the node is ![images](images/c24-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>. We can sum the variance of all nodes and obtain the Gini index.

 

## 24.4 MISCELLANEOUS

Let us summarise several observations which are useful when considering using the decision trees on real examples. In this section we have covered CART, or Classification And Regression Tree, algorithm. There are other alternative successful methods to construct trees, for example, C4.5; see Quinlan (2014).

   

***Beyond binary trees***

It is not practical to use trees which split into more than two branches at each node. The tree will cause considerable fragmentation and not enough structure can be built due to the insufficient amount of data.

 

***Categorical predictors***

The dependent variable can be composed of categorical variables. If the dependent variable is formed of ![images](images/c24-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> possible unordered values, then there are ![images](images/c24-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> possible partitions. If ![images](images/c24-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> is large, this becomes numerically infeasible.

 

***The loss matrix***

In practical problems, the different outcomes can have a different impact. For example, in medicine, we want to minimise Type 2 error, i.e. failing to detect disease is more costly as opposed to producing false alarms. On the other hand, in the judicial system, Type 1 error is not acceptable as releasing a guilty person may be preferable to sentencing an innocent one.

In order to take this into account, we may define a ![images](images/c24-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> loss matrix ![images](images/c24-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c24-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></math> being the loss for classifying a true class ![images](images/c24-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> as class ![images](images/c24-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math>. The diagonal of ![images](images/c24-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> contains zeros. Consequently, the Gini index is modified as:

(24.20)![equation](images/c24-math-0020.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>s</mi> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>T</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>&#8800;</mo> <msup> <mi>k</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mi>L</mi> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <msup> <mi>k</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </msub> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>k</mi> </mrow> </msub> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <msup> <mi>k</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The loss matrix![images](images/c24-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> can be interpreted in Bayesian language as prior probabilities imposed on the classes.

 

***Additive structure***

Decision trees can successfully describe non-linear patterns in the data. However, the trees have a blind spot, which is nothing but models with additive structure. Let us illustrate it on a simple example where the dependent variable is a function of two factors ![images](images/c24-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c24-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> where the underlying data generating process reads:

(24.21)![equation](images/c24-math-0021.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>&#60;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>&#60;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c24-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is a zero-mean noise. It is not difficult to see that the decision tree needed such a model. In the case of more complex additive models, the decision trees needed may need a large amount of data to work. A more suitable method is using Multivariate Adaptive Splines; see Friedman (1991). This method provides smoother models as opposed to decision trees, which are by nature rough.

 

***Data dependence***

Decision trees are data dependent, where small variation in a data set can easily result in a completely different decision tree structure. This instability is a disadvantage when we want to interpret the tree as a set of rules. On the other hand, the data dependence which allows us to construct forests of trees will lead to a significant improvement in fitting various models. The next chapter will be devoted to forests and how they adress this issue.

However, before we do that, let us illustrate a way to build trees using `q`.

 

## 24.5 IMPLEMENTATION OF TREES

We now look at a sample use case, using the famous Iris data set, and build our `q` code around that. First, we load our data:

![](images/c24-gra-0002.png)![](images/c24-gra-0003.png)![](images/c24-gra-0004.png)

We start our `q` sample implementation by creating a function which can classify a vector of real values into distinct integer values. We have thus built an initial toolset to allow us to grow a tree and use the resultant tree to predict values. We have previously also performed classification with the use of neural networks. We are now equipped with two machine learning techniques for classification with the same sample data set. We encourage readers to perform a numerical comparison between the two methods to assess their strengths and weaknesses.

# CHAPTER 25  
Forests

 

In [Chapter 24](#c24.xhtml), we introduced the concept of decision trees. They represent a useful method for capturing and modelling non-linear data generating processes. They also provide results which can be easily read and interpreted by human analysts. The notion of decision trees can be extended further into a more powerful concept – the ensemble of trees – random forests; see Breiman (2001). They give rise to a method of estimation which is very powerful, due to its numerical ease in obtaining the fit and its explanatory power. Random forests attempt to address one of the main challenges of decision trees, which is overfitting, using the statistical concept of bootstrapping. In this section, building upon the previous chapter on trees, we introduce the theoretical foundations behind random forests and demonstrate an implementation.

 

## 25.1 BOOTSTRAP

Let us start with the concept of bootstrapping as it is introduced in statistics; see Efron (1992). This will equip us with the intuition on how it can be used to improve the performance of decision trees. The concept of bootstrapping stands for testing which involves random sampling with replacement. It is particularly useful when we need to estimate the sampling distribution for a particular measure or statistic. Consequently, we can obtain the significance level for sample statistics and test the various hypotheses on the given sample. The bootstrap is a general procedure and an alternative to asymptotic methods which use a parametric model for the underlying statistics. In some cases, it produces better results than a traditional normal approximation of the statistic's properties while in others we may obtain dubious results.

In order to understand the bootstrap, let us assume a random variable ![images](images/c25-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> generated by some distribution function ![images](images/c25-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> and statistic ![images](images/c25-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math>. We consider ![images](images/c25-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> realisations of the random variable ![images](images/c25-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> – the observations – which we denote as ![images](images/c25-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math> and calculate the sample statistic ![images](images/c25-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>. In order to make plausible inference about the statistic, we need to understand the statistical properties of ![images](images/c25-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> calculated from a sample of size ![images](images/c25-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>. The particular variable of interest here is the variability of the sample statistic.

The sample statistic is a function of the sample, i.e., ![images](images/c25-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>, and thus the sample statistic is a random variable with a certain sampling distribution function, denoted as ![images](images/c25-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math>. Such a function depends on the size of the sample and the underlying distribution function ![images](images/c25-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math>, i.e., ![images](images/c25-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#964;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>G</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>. There are two possible cases which can make the inference of the sampling distribution function complex:

*   ![images](images/c25-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>G</mi> </mrow> </math> is known, but ![images](images/c25-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> is too complicated to derive the sampling distribution ![images](images/c25-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>G</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>.
*   ![images](images/c25-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>G</mi> </mrow> </math> is unknown.

In both cases, ![images](images/c25-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> cannot be analytically derived. Let us stress that the asymptotic theory aims to derive the function analytically and assess its properties. The function converges to the normal distribution with variance proportional to ![images](images/c25-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> in many cases. This is not the case in the subsequent paragraphs.

   

***![images](images/c25-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>G</mi> </mrow> </math> is known, ![images](images/c25-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> complex***

Since the analytic derivations are not possible, we can derive properties of ![images](images/c25-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> numerically. In particular, we generate ![images](images/c25-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> samples ![images](images/c25-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c25-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> by sampling *with replacement*. For every sample, we calculate corresponding ![images](images/c25-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

Having in hand ![images](images/c25-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></math>, we can approximate ![images](images/c25-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> using the empirical distribution function of the observed sample. Obtaining the variability of ![images](images/c25-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> is then straightforward; we can read it from the sample. We may therefore test a hypothesis about the value of ![images](images/c25-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>. It is worth pointing out that it is our numerical limitations which affect the accuracy of the approximation: the higher ![images](images/c25-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is, the more accurate the approximation is.

 

***![images](images/c25-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>G</mi> </mrow> </math> is unknown***

We now restrict our knowledge even more and assume that we do not know ![images](images/c25-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math>. There are two possible causes of our ignorance of ![images](images/c25-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math>. First, we may know the functional form of ![images](images/c25-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> up to the parameter(s) ![images](images/c25-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></math>. If we know that parameter, we can proceed in the way outlined in the previous paragraph. In many cases, however, we can obtain an estimate of the parameter, ![images](images/c25-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>. In such a case, we can employ the *parametric bootstrap* and assume that data are coming from ![images](images/c25-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mfenced></mrow></math>. We then proceed as above.

Let us consider a more interesting case, where we do not possess any knowledge of ![images](images/c25-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math>. The only knowledge about ![images](images/c25-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> is encoded in the sample ![images](images/c25-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math>. The way to assess the statistical properties of ![images](images/c25-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> is to employ a *nonparametric bootstrap*. First, we form the empirical distribution function ![images](images/c25-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>G</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math> from the observed sample. Such a function assigns equal probability ![images](images/c25-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> to every value ![images](images/c25-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c25-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>. We consider ![images](images/c25-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>G</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math> as approximation of ![images](images/c25-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math>. Then, we proceed as above: we sample ![images](images/c25-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> samples of size ![images](images/c25-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> from ![images](images/c25-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>G</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math>. For every sample, we calculate ![images](images/c25-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msubsup></mrow></math>. Then, we can assess ![images](images/c25-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> from the empirical distribution function derived from sequence ![images](images/c25-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msubsup></mrow></math>. For instance, the standard deviation of ![images](images/c25-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> is given as:

(25.1)![equation](images/c25-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#952;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msqrt> <mrow> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>B</mi> </mfrac> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>b</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>B</mi> </munderover> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msubsup> <mi>&#952;</mi> <mi>b</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>B</mi> </mfrac> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>b</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>B</mi> </munderover> <msubsup> <mi>&#952;</mi> <mi>b</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </msqrt> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Generating a bootstrap sample from ![images](images/c25-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>G</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math> means sampling from ![images](images/c25-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math> with replacement.

 

***Tossing coins***

Let us illustrate the bootstrap with a simple example. We toss a coin and denote 1 for heads and 0 for tails. We are interested in the properties of the estimator of the average value when we toss a coin ![images](images/c25-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>\-times. Tossing the coin ![images](images/c25-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>\-times is equivalent to recording the series ![images](images/c25-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c25-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. The statistic of interest is:

(25.2)![equation](images/c25-math-0002.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mi>N</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>N</mi> </mfrac> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

In order to assess the statistical properties of ![images](images/c25-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math>, we draw ![images](images/c25-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> samples with replacement from ![images](images/c25-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Such a bootstrapped sample may read: ![images](images/c25-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi></mrow></math>. We repeat the procedure ![images](images/c25-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> times and collect ![images](images/c25-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. The empirical distribution function of ![images](images/c25-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c25-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> can be used to approximate ![images](images/c25-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mi>&#956;</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

We can illustrate this example numerically for ![images](images/c25-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c25-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.6</mn></mrow></math>. We are interested in the standard deviation of the estimator for the mean. The following code gives the answer:

![](images/c25-gra-0001.png)![](images/c25-gra-0002.png)

where we can change `N` or `B` accordingly.

An important assumption which underlyies the bootstrap is that the samples with replacement obtained from the observed sample have to be independent. It is appealing to use the bootstrap in regression problems. However, there are cases where the plain bootstrap outlined above does not work, due to this lack of independence or the presence of heteroscedasticity. For that purpose, alternative bootstrapping schemes have been derived; among others, we may list:

*   Wild bootstrap
*   Bayesian bootstrap
*   White-noise bootstrap

The bootstrap is challenging when the underlying regression problem is performed on time series data, which are not stationary. A popular method is Block bootstrap where entire consecutive blocks are drawn from the sample rather than individual observations. Another method derived in Bergamelli et al. (2015) proposes a method called Maximum Non-Extensive Entropy Block Bootstrap. The basis of the bootstrap is to use entropy of the empirical distribution function, which allows us to preserve the rank correlation between the sample and the bootstrapped sample locally. Further, the method can be extended for fat-tailed non-stationary distributions by using non-extensive entropy.

The bootstrap technique can essentially be used to improve the accuracy of the estimator, which will be addressed in the next section.

 

## 25.2 BAGGING

Bagging, or bootstrap aggregation, is a procedure to improve the accuracy of a regression or classification algorithm introduced in Breiman (1996). We will illustrate the notion of bagging on decision trees, but the method is general and can be used for any estimation technique. The estimators for which bagging, in particular, shows the most significant improvement are estimators with large variance and low bias. Decision trees fall into this category due to the provision of a very good fit on the training data when grown fully. This fit, however, may result in high variance across samples, which is why training sets and out-of-sample validation are critical for decision trees, as well as pruning, as mentioned in [Chapter 24](#c24.xhtml). Bagging helps us address these challenges.

Bagging differs in nature from boosting, introduced in [Chapter 23](#c23.xhtml), as it does not require any sequential estimation and the primary motivation is not to improve the properties of weak estimators, but rather improve the variance of unstable estimators. The bagging method averages the noisy unbiased estimators. Boosting is in many cases more powerful; however, the appealing feature of bagging rests in its simplicity.

The bagging of estimators works as follows:

*   Create ![images](images/c25-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> samples with replacement from the original sample of data.
*   For every sample, estimate the model of interest, i.e. either regression or classification.
*   Average the result across the bootstrap samples.

The procedure thus assumes that by creating bootstrapped samples and then estimating the model, we obtain a sample of individual models, where each comes from the same underlying distribution, i.e. having the same bias and (potentially large) variance. This stresses the difference to boosting, where the estimators are estimated in sequence and every estimator aims to efficiently remove bias left after the previous estimators have been taken into account.

The improvement in the variance of the bagged estimators is due to the same underlying reason that makes hedging so popular among asset managers and why we rely upon portfolio theory. Let us consider ![images](images/c25-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> draws of a random variable, each with variance ![images](images/c25-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>. There is also a correlation between observations ![images](images/c25-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math>, and let us consider the case of non-negative correlation only. The variance of the average is given:

[(25.3)](#c25.xhtml#R_c25-disp-0003)![equation](images/c25-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mi>B</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#961;</mi> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#961;</mi> </mrow> <mi>B</mi> </mfrac> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

For given ![images](images/c25-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, the variance is decreased when ![images](images/c25-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. On the other hand, for ![images](images/c25-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> the variance remains unchanged. If we want to achieve given variance reduction, then random variables with higher pairwise correlation require large sample ![images](images/c25-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.

In the case of bagging, this means that effective variance reduction occurs for uncorrelated estimators. If the underlying estimator is, for example, linear regression, the bootstrapped estimates are highly correlated, and thus variance improvement is minor. On the other hand, in the case of decision trees, the trees are noisy and non-linear in data. When we change the sample slightly, we end up growing a tree with a very different structure. Often, even a tiny fraction of data changed can lead to a very different tree topology.

The technique of random forests employs trees which optimise [equation 25.3](#c25.xhtml#c25-disp-0003). In particular, the trees grown on every bootstrapped sample are grown such that correlation between any other sample is reduced, given the variance is not affected much. A radical version of the random forest is to grow the individual trees randomly without any optimisation and then bag such trees. This, however, increases the variance of individual trees too much and thus the entire technique does not result in significant improvement. The recommended procedure is:

*   Given the sample data consisting of ![images](images/c25-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> observations of ![images](images/c25-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional vector of features ![images](images/c25-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub subscriptshift="veryverythickmathspace"><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and dependent variable ![images](images/c25-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c25-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>, we draw the bootstrapped sample – random sample with replacement – of size ![images](images/c25-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> from the sample, denoted for simplicity as ![images](images/c25-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mfenced><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></math>.
*   Using the bootstrapped sample ![images](images/c25-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mfenced><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></math>, grow a tree using the following procedure:

1.  *    For every leaf node of a tree, select ![images](images/c25-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> out of ![images](images/c25-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> features and select the best split of the node by optimising a chosen ![images](images/c25-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> function.
    *    Split the node into two nodes, which will constitute new leaf nodes.
    *    Repeat procedure until the tree with a minimum leaf node size ![images](images/c25-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is grown.
    *    Denote the tree as ![images](images/c25-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>T</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msubsup></mrow></math>.

*   Get all the bootstrapped trees ![images](images/c25-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>T</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msubsup></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c25-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and predict the outcome based on average value – for regression problems; or majority vote – for classification problems.

Trees are grown such that the correlation between two different trees is minimised. Considering in every split only a subset of variables amplifies the data dependence of the tree topology while it does not introduce a significant increase of individual variances. The suitable choice of ![images](images/c25-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> is ![images](images/c25-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msqrt><mi>M</mi></msqrt></mrow></math> for classifications and ![images](images/c25-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> for regressions.

 

### 25.2.1 Out-of-Bag

Throughout the book we have already seen the use of ![images](images/c25-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>\-fold cross-validation as a means to determine out-of-sample performance of a given method. Alternatively, we have used it as a way to determine the best possible value for meta-parameters. The cost we had to pay for running the cross-validation is the general need to re-estimate the model ![images](images/c25-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>\-times, each time for different folds.

The out-of-bag method provides a suitable alternative in the case of random forests. In order to calculate the error of an in-sample observation, we construct the random forest and predict the value only from those trees where the observation has not appeared among bootstrapped samples. Thus, if we keep for every tree an indicator of the observations used in the corresponding bootstrap, we can estimate the random forest only once, and we are already equipped with cross-validation error estimates – up to vector manipulations of aggregating the proper trees.

An alternative approach to constructing the out-of-bag estimate is to calculate the errors on the fly. Namely, after we grow the tree from the bootstrapped sample, the part of the sample not used in the bootstrap is then used to test the out-of-sample error. The error is noted. In the end, the errors are aggregated. This approach does not require storing additional data to indicate which tree has used a given observation.

We can use the out-of-bag approach to assess the importance of every variable within the data set. In particular, when we grow a given tree, we store which observations have been “in-the-bag”. We calculate the error of the prediction. We then choose a feature ![images](images/c25-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> and reshuffle the observations in the out-of-bag part of the sample. We denote the error for the case with reshuffled ![images](images/c25-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>\-th feature. Comparing two errors shows how important the ![images](images/c25-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>\-th feature is in predicting the dependent variable.

We start our implementation by first creating the bootstrapping function which will sample our data for each tree's growth:

To create a given “bootstrap“ tree, we now draw a bootstrap sample of size N from the training data using the function above and calculate the out-of-bag error. For all features which were not sampled for that tree (out-of-bag), we predict their values and measure the prediction error:

It also returns a key `‘oob` containing the out-of-bag predictions and their prediction error, and a third entry denoted by `‘ibi`, which contains the in-the-bag indices for each sample. It “tags” the tree with the value of the correponding ![images](images/c25-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> under column `B`.

The ensemble of trees – a table of treetables – and the out-of-bag predictions are both themselves, tables:

The `‘ibi` key is a dictionary (`type=99`) of indices used for each tree `B`.

Let us store the ensemble of trees:

We can then access the nodes of all trees:
