At the end of the exploration phase, the outcome is evaluated and the choice with the best outcome is chosen. The moves in the exploratory phase are chosen based on the best average outcome. The option chosen in the exploratory phase may not be constant as the performance of the best option at the end of the exploratory phase may deteriorate during the exploration phase.

 

***Random exploration greedy algorithm***

The second algorithm extends the first one by placing the proportion of the exploratory choices randomly during the iteration. In particular, at every step, we make an exploratory step with probability ![images](images/c28-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>, and an exploitation step otherwise. The exploratory step is as described above. Distributing the exploratory phase across the entire strategy improves the ability of the strategy to escape local maxima and it provides a check against heteroscedastic behaviour of the system, where choices are made.

 

***Decreasing exploration greedy algorithm***

The exploration in the greedy algorithms described in the preceding paragraphs represents learning. The rate ![images](images/c28-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> can be understood as a learning rate of the algorithm to explore the possible options. It is thus intuitive to formulate an algorithm where the learning rate decreases over time. Such an algorithm will explore more during the initial stages, and the learning rate will decrease as the iterations progress. The exploration will be still preserved during the entire lifetime of the strategy to preserve the ability to escape the local maxima. The functional dependence of ![images](images/c28-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> on the number of iterations passed is a matter of choice and object of study.

 

***Adaptive exploration greedy strategy***

The change of the learning rate during the progress of the strategy as introduced in the previous algorithm depends solely on the number of draws already taken. It may be optimal, though, to make it dependent on the outcome of the strategies as well. If the algorithm learns a stable solution, it may be a good idea to slow down the learning, i.e. less exploration, and exploit instead. The stable solution can be defined using the variability of the outcome so far realised. This is the basis of the VBDE algorithm in Tokic and Palm (2011).

 

### 28.1.3 Confidence-Based Algorithms

The popular group of algorithms to solve the multi-armed bandit problems are confidence-based algorithms with optimism. The idea can be outlined as follows. At a given point in time, we believe that the true mean ![images](images/c28-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> of each arm ![images](images/c28-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is within:

(28.6)![equation](images/c28-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c28-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is an estimator of the true mean and ![images](images/c28-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> denotes the confidence interval bounds. The width of the confidence interval decreases with time, i.e. ![images](images/c28-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8600;</mo></mrow></math> as ![images](images/c28-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8599;</mo></mrow></math>. Then, the value of arm ![images](images/c28-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is optimistically ![images](images/c28-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. At time ![images](images/c28-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, when we need to decide between arms, we choose the one with the highest optimistic value:

(28.7)![equation](images/c28-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mi> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mrow> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Auer et al. (2002a) elaborated the outlined approach and introduced the Upper Confidence Bound algorithm. In order to formulate Upper Confidence Bound algorithm and its convergence properties, we need to impose an assumption on the distribution of the individual arms: every distribution is ![images](images/c28-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>\-sub-Gaussian. Namely, we define the running average of the ![images](images/c28-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>\-th arm at time ![images](images/c28-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> as:

(28.8)![equation](images/c28-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mi>#</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfrac> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>s</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>s</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c28-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>#</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> stands for the number of instances when the strategy chosen has been ![images](images/c28-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c28-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> being the realisations of the random variable ![images](images/c28-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> in such cases.

The Upper Confidence Bound algorithms are based on the theorem which says that:

(28.9)![equation](images/c28-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msqrt> <mfrac> <mrow> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>&#948;</mi> </mfrac> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>#</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfrac> </msqrt> </mfenced> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>&#948;</mi> <mtext>or</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msqrt> <mfrac> <mrow> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>&#948;</mi> </mfrac> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>#</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfrac> </msqrt> </mfenced> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>&#948;</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

for positive real ![images](images/c28-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi></mrow></math>. Then, if the bandit is played sufficiently many times, the probability to choose the wrong one is going to zero. See Auer et al. (2002a) for proofs.

The algorithm then follows along these lines:

*   Provide ![images](images/c28-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> and a sequence of probabilities ![images](images/c28-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;.</mi></mrow></math>
*   Initialise the algorithm by choosing every arm ![images](images/c28-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> once.
*   Choose a strategy such that at every time ![images](images/c28-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, the index ![images](images/c28-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> results from:

(28.10)![equation](images/c28-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mi> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msqrt> <mfrac> <mrow> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <msub> <mi>&#948;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mfrac> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>#</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfrac> </msqrt> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Practically, if the reward of each arm is within ![images](images/c28-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math>, the parameter ![images](images/c28-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> would be a suitable choice following Hoeffding's lemma. The convenient choice for the sequence of probabilities is:

(28.11)![equation](images/c28-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#948;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <msup> <mi>t</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Such a choice of parameters provides an algorithm which optimises the Upper Confidence Bound and is adaptive enough to avoid some possible pathological cases which may occur – for instance, if one arm dominates other arms, then under certain circumstances the regret of the algorithm may be infinite. This will cause pathological behaviour as a difference between an optimal arm and any other arm will be infinite.

 

### 28.1.4 Bayesian Algorithms

Another class of algorithms to solve the multi-armed bandit problems are Bayesian algorithms. As the name suggests, the Bayesian strategies assume some prior knowledge about the bandits' distributions. This can be used to improve exploration strategies and work more accurately with information and regret.

In order to implement the strategy, we further assume that probability functions corresponding to bandits' arms are given as ![images](images/c28-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> with ![images](images/c28-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi></mrow></math> being parametric set. In the simple settings, it can correspond to a ![images](images/c28-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>\-dimensional real vector. The prior distribution imposed on the parametric space is such that ![images](images/c28-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>. In order to solve the problem, we define the Bayesian regret as:

(28.12)![equation](images/c28-math-0012.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mover accent="true"> <mrow> <mi>R</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>g</mi> </mrow> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>A</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#960;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>E</mi> <mi>&#960;</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>j</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#952;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mi>A</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#952;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c28-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></math> is the minimiser of the loss function ![images](images/c28-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math>. We have denoted the expectations with index ![images](images/c28-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></math> in order to stress the dependence on the prior distribution.

The textbook example worth mentioning is the Bernoulli bandit problem, which nicely illustrates the meaning of the parametric set and choice of ![images](images/c28-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math>. The Bernoulli bandit problem is a setup where the probability functions modelling the reward of every arm ![images](images/c28-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> are given by Bernoulli distributions with parameter ![images](images/c28-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. The pay-off of the arm ![images](images/c28-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is either 1, with probability ![images](images/c28-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, or 0 otherwise. To solve the Bernoulli multi-armed bandit problem means to find the arm with the highest ![images](images/c28-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. The loss function for the Bernoulli bandit can be suitably chosen as ![images](images/c28-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#952;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

The schema for the Bayesian algorithm then follows along the following lines:

*   Provide a prior distribution![images](images/c28-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></math> for ![images](images/c28-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi></mrow></math>, connected to probabilities ![images](images/c28-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>&#952;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
*   At each step ![images](images/c28-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, choose prior distribution![images](images/c28-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> based on past realisations and corresponding losses. The step consists of:

1.  *    Draw ![images](images/c28-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> from the prior distribution ![images](images/c28-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>.
    *    Choose an action which minimises the loss ![images](images/c28-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> over a set of admissible strategies.
    *    Obtain the outcome.

  

***Thompson sampling***

The simple implementation of the Bayesian algorithm is to follow Thompson (1933) and take prior distribution ![images](images/c28-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> equal to the posterior distribution of ![images](images/c28-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math>, conditional on the history of all observed pay-offs:

(28.13)![equation](images/c28-math-0013.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#960;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>&#952;</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#960;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>&#952;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The Thompson sampling procedure for the Bayesian algorithm at every time step ![images](images/c28-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> reads:

*   Denote ![images](images/c28-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>#</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> the number of cases when arm ![images](images/c28-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> was chosen and it resulted in a pay-off 1, and analogously, ![images](images/c28-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>#</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> the number of cases when arm ![images](images/c28-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> was chosen and resulted in a pay-off 0.
*   For each arm ![images](images/c28-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, the parameter ![images](images/c28-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is drawn as: ![images](images/c28-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mtext>Beta</mtext><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>#</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>#</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mfenced></mfenced></mrow></math>.
*   Choose an action ![images](images/c28-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> which solves ![images](images/c28-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>i</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>.
*   Observe the pay-off ![images](images/c28-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> at time ![images](images/c28-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> and update the information set for the next step.

The provided algorithm thus constitutes what is known as a Thompson algorithm. We have specified it for the Bernoulli bandit only. It can be elaborated for more general distributions, but it goes beyond the scope of this book.

 

### 28.1.5 Online Gradient Descent Algorithms

Finally, let us specify the algorithms using the online gradient descent approach to minimise the running regret or the loss function defined in the previous section. We assume that we can define a non-negative loss function for every action ![images](images/c28-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>. In order to use the online gradient descent method, we have to formulate the problem as an online convex optimisation problem, where we further know the gradient of the loss. Auer et al. (2002b) formulated the multi-armed bandit problem in a way the online gradient descent can be used. The resulting algorithm, known as ![images](images/c28-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>X</mi><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, can be specified as follows:

*   Define the step parameter ![images](images/c28-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math>.
*   Initialise the vector of probabilities ![images](images/c28-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>K</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>K</mi></mfrac></mfenced></mrow></math>.
*   At time ![images](images/c28-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, choose an action ![images](images/c28-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> proportional to probability ![images](images/c28-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Further, perform the following steps:

1.  *    Observe reward for a chosen arm and interpret it as a non-negative loss ![images](images/c28-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>.
    *    Define ![images](images/c28-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#947;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mfenced></mrow><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mfrac></mrow></math> with ![images](images/c28-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> being Kronecker delta.
    *    For every arm ![images](images/c28-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, update: ![images](images/c28-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><msub><mi>&#947;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mi>j</mi></msub><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><msub><mi>&#947;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mfenced></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.

The ![images](images/c28-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>X</mi><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> algorithm is widespread in practice. The exploration mechanism comes from the probabilities ![images](images/c28-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></math>, which ensures that all the arms can be explored. As some of the arms start to perform better, the probability assigned to them is more pronounced and they will be more likely chosen – exploitation comes into play.

This concludes the overview of the multi-armed bandit problem and various ways to construct algorithms to solve it. Our aim was not to provide an exhaustive account of all the options but rather introduce some insight into them which allows us to run numerical experiments. In practice, if a reader faces a problem which resembles multi-armed bandit setup, we strongly recommend studying various numerical techniques as every method has its merits, and one can achieve remarkable results with a suitable but still simple method. In the next subsection, we implement some of the algorithms outlined above and encourage readers to implement more of them on their own.

 

### 28.1.6 Implementation of Some Learning Algorithms

Let us implement an example of the multi-armed bandit problem and several algorithms to find the strategy which converges to the optimal one. We focus on a simple case of three-armed bandit and implement the three greedy algorithms presented above. They provide intuitive grounds for readers to develop their algorithms which could be built upon the presented principles.

First, let us define the three-armed bandit as a collection of three uniform distributions ![images](images/c28-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math>, each being given as ![images](images/c28-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi>U</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>. The set of three parameters – the upper bounds – fully defines the bandit and also the means of the bandit's arms. Without loss of generality, let us further consider ![images](images/c28-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math>. The multi-armed bandit with uniform distributions is implemented as:

![](images/c28-gra-0001.png)

The `MAB` function has two arguments: the first one is the bandit chosen, and the second one is the specification of the bandit itself through `mabSpec`. The three-armed bandit is then defined by setting the `mabSpec` input variable to a three-dimensional array. The function returns a random draw for a given choice of the bandit's arm:

![](images/c28-gra-0002.png)![](images/c28-gra-0003.png)

where each number is approximately half of the corresponding number in `mabSpec`.

  

***Exploration of first greedy algorithm***

Let us implement the greedy algorithm where all the exploration is done fully at the beginning of the iterative process followed by greedy exploitation afterwards. Let us summarise all the variables specifying our setup:

![](images/c28-gra-0006.png)

where we consider 1000 steps to be performed by the algorithm.

Let us also introduce several further variables we need during the lifetime of the algorithm to be preserved across individual iterations: all the realised pay-offs, minimum bound for any pay-off in the situation when the bandit's arm has not been explored yet but is supposed to be exploited, the counter of iterations, time series of strategies taken, and finally the multi-armed bandit function itself:

![](images/c28-gra-0007.png)

The function `mabExplorationFirstGA` takes as an input all the variables described above wrapped up into a single dictionary, performs one iteration, and updates the same dictionary:

![](images/c28-gra-0008.png)

The algorithm has two phases: the exploration phase and the exploitation phase. It is important to repeat that we allow the algorithm to choose the most optimal option during the exploitation phase. An alternative would be to fix the decision at the end of the exploration stage and not allow any switch. This may lead to a sub-optimal solution for a small number of draws when suboptimal arm can be chosen during the exploration stage. We thus stick into this algorithm – and all the following algorithms – the option to choose the arm based on the most favourable expected outcome using all up-to-date information. The algorithm thus learns even during the exploitation stage.

Let us create the dictionary of variables needed to execute the iterations:

![](images/c28-gra-0009.png)

The greedy algorithm itself is the repetitive application of the function `bucket[‘N]` steps times. Since we are interested in the outcome presented in every step of the iteration, we use `\` instead of `/`. The greedy algorithm is then applied as:

![](images/c28-gra-0010.png)

Let us extract from the table `outcomeMAB1` several important variables: the counter of steps, the chosen arm in a given step, the total average pay-off after given number of steps, and the average pay-offs for every arm after given number of steps:

Let us finally remark on two points. First, the exploration first algorithm may perform the best as all the exploitation steps are taken on the best arm, which is fully revealed after the exploration. This is not true in the other two cases, where the algorithm may exploit even when not every option has been explored at least once. This can be mitigated by forcing the algorithm to explore each option at least once before engaging into further strategies. Second, the values of parameters, namely ![images](images/c28-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>, are comparable for exploration first and random exploration algorithms, respectively, though the value for the decreasing exploration algorithm is not comparable, and thus the direct comparison is rather illustrative.

 

## 28.2 MONTE CARLO TREE SEARCH

We focus on the Monte Carlo Tree Search algorithm, which is a popular heuristic search algorithm for decision processes frequently used in AI engines. These engines are utilised in a variety of cases ranging from playing chess to driving cars to trading strategies. In a nutshell, the Monte Carlo Tree Search algorithm aims to find out at every point in time the most promising decision to be made by randomly expanding the tree of possible actions. In a game of chess, for example, this means that given the current state of the board the algorithm plays out various random continuations of the game and chooses the move which tends to result in a win with the highest likelihood. The first paper which proposed the ![images](images/c28-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> as an engine for a game AI is Chaslot et al. (2008).

In this section, we explain the Monte Carlo Tree Search, or ![images](images/c28-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>, algorithm using the examples from the gaming world. This is easy to understand and also easy to model on the desktop PC as opposed to testing the self-driving car or AI-driven execution algorithms. Ultimately, we implement the ![images](images/c28-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> for the game of tic-tac-toe, which is interesting enough to specify it in a coherent code. Still, it is easy to extend towards the more complex games and situations.

Let us focus on perfect information games. These games are turn-based, and there is no hidden information among players. There is no random element in the game like drawing cards from the shuffled deck. Tic-tac-toe or chess are examples of such games. The state of the game is determined by the position of stones on the board, which is visible to both players. We can, in theory, construct a game tree with all possible moves. Leaves of the tree are then the different ends of the game. Every node of the tree can be assigned a value which reflects the likelihood to end up in a winning leaf node. The straightforward strategy to solve such a game is the minimax algorithm.

The minimax algorithm is a strategy for decision-making which is based on selecting an option which minimises the possible loss in a maximum loss scenario. The maximin is an analogous formulation for gains. Since its development in the game theory for zero-sum games, it was extended to the situation with uncertainty and complex game rules. Mathematically, the minimax problem can be formulated as:

(28.15)![equation](images/c28-math-0015.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>v</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> </munder> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </munder> <msubsup> <mi>v</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c28-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is a value function for a player ![images](images/c28-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c28-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c28-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> denotes the action of the player ![images](images/c28-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> and the other player, respectively. In plain language, the player ![images](images/c28-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> wants to play the best action given the other player is doing the same. To be precise, the player ![images](images/c28-i0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, i.e. not ![images](images/c28-i0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, wants to minimise the value of the game for player ![images](images/c28-i0123.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>.

The minimax algorithm is frequently used backwards from the end of the game. In each iterative step, player ![images](images/c28-i0124.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> wants to maximise the chance to win while player ![images](images/c28-i0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is doing the opposite. The backward iteration can be, and thus it is frequently accompanied by some heuristic rules. The heuristic rules assign a value to every state of the game. The minimax algorithm thus does not have to run iteratively but rather serves as a decision on how to evolve from one state of the game to another.

The vanilla minimax algorithm as briefly outlined above fails when:

*   The number of different states in the game is huge. In the case of go, it is ![images](images/c28-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8764;</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>19</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mn>19</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
*   The game has high branching ratio, where at every given state of the game, there is a large number of possible actions.

The ![images](images/c28-i0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> addresses the shortcomings of the minimax algorithm. Namely:

*   ![images](images/c28-i0128.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>M</mi> <mi>C</mi> <mi>T</mi> <mi>S</mi> </mrow> </math> does not need complex heuristics, i.e. to estimate the value of any given state of the game. This can be difficult to achieve in complex games like go.
*   ![images](images/c28-i0129.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>M</mi> <mi>C</mi> <mi>T</mi> <mi>S</mi> </mrow> </math> is very good for games with a large branching factor. The nature of the algorithm is such that it explores the more promising branches. The search mechanism is asymmetric; it does not need to devote time to branches which are likely to result in a loss.
*   ![images](images/c28-i0130.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>M</mi> <mi>C</mi> <mi>T</mi> <mi>S</mi> </mrow> </math> has a flexible running time. The heuristic-based algorithms need to go through the full tree with all the game options. This may take a large amount of time. On the other hand, ![images](images/c28-i0131.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> can be run in a flexible way and stopped at any time. The bigger the time budget to run the more accurate the results of ![images](images/c28-i0132.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>.

In order to introduce the ![images](images/c28-i0133.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> algorithm, we need to elaborate more on the decision tree for a game. We consider a two-player game. The decision tree, or game tree, starts at the root node, which is a plain board. The next level of the tree is composed of child nodes of the root node, which contain all the possible moves by player 1. At the second level, the tree consists of all the moves of player 2 conditioned on the previous move of player 1. The third level, consecutively, captures the move of player 1 conditioned on the two previous moves. Switching the moves continues further down the tree by exploiting all the combinations. The leaf node of a game is such a game state where the game terminates and one of the players wins, or the game ends in a draw. In the game of go, the game ends when both players pass the move. Then, the player with the higher score wins, where the score is calculated based on the size of territory belonging to each player.

For a game of go, the root has ![images](images/c28-i0134.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>19</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mn>19</mn></mrow></math> child nodes. At the second level, every node has ![images](images/c28-i0135.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>19</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mn>19</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> child nodes. This gives altogether at the second level ![images](images/c28-i0136.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>19</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mn>19</mn></mfenced><mo>&#183;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mn>19</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mn>19</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></math> options. The branching ratio of the game is huge and suggests the infinite – in a numerical sense – dimension of all the possible states of the game. The tree is asymmetric as the difference in a number of moves between the longest and the shortest game can be huge.

When the game tree is not so huge, we can explore the full tree as we have explained in the minimax algorithm in the preceding paragraphs. Given the knowledge of the full tree, the move at every stage of the game can be optimised such that the chance to win is highest. This is not possible for complex games like go.

If we want to avoid the apparent curse of dimensionality, we have to abandon methods which rely on exploring the entire tree. The Monte Carlo comes at this point as an alternative method to full exploration. The basis for the ![images](images/c28-i0137.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> method is to start at the current state of the game and play many games out of the current point. The idea is to build a game tree from the current state and explore many possible moves. Then, we can choose the best option from those explored. In order to build the tree, we face the problem which is in nature similar to the multi-armed bandit problem. The arms of the bandit are possible moves – stones to be played at a given state – and the pay-off is a likelihood to win when a given choice has been taken.

A naive approach would be to play a number of randomly simulated playouts. In every playout, the game would start at the current state. The progress of the game would be simulated by placing stones randomly player by player, starting with the player whose best turn we aim to find out. Among the set of allowed moves at a given turn, one move will be selected randomly. Every playout is then played until one of the players wins or there is a draw if allowed by rules. After the set of random playouts is finished, the next move is determined. The way to do it is to group the randomly simulated playouts by its first move. Then, for each group, the ratio of won games to all games played is calculated and the move with the highest ratio is chosen.

Playing random games is a highly inefficient approach as we have seen with the multi-armed bandit problem. Thus, the ![images](images/c28-i0138.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> algorithm uses a more elaborate approach to find the optimal move. The ![images](images/c28-i0139.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> is based on the iteration of the following four steps:

*   Selection
*   Expansion
*   Simulation
*   Back propagation

In the selection step, the existing tree is used to find the following child nodes down the leaf node. Then, in the expansion step, the existing tree is expanded by one child node. The tree is explicitly gaining a new node. In the simulation step, the game starts at the newly added node and is simulated until the end of the game, usually using random simulation. Finally, in the back propagation step, the information in the newly expanded tree is updated. The nodes which are on the selected path include the information of the outcome of the new game.

In the following section, we elaborate on all the steps in more detail. We assume that the game is at any state, i.e. it can be the empty board or the game can be close to the end. Without loss of generality, we assume that player 1 is to make a move. The four-step procedure already took place ![images](images/c28-i0140.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math>\-times, where ![images](images/c28-i0141.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> can also be 0.

Further, every node ![images](images/c28-i0142.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> of the tree is described by a pair of numbers ![images](images/c28-i0143.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> where:

*   ![images](images/c28-i0144.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math> – is the number of simulated games which contains the node ![images](images/c28-i0145.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> and resulted in a win of the player, who made a move.
*   ![images](images/c28-i0146.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </math> – is the number of simulated games which contains the node ![images](images/c28-i0147.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>.

Every node is recorded from the perspective of the player who made a move. The nodes at the odd level of the tree correspond to the moves of player 1 while nodes at the even level of the tree correspond to the moves of player 2. The variable ![images](images/c28-i0148.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is taken from such a perspective.

 

### 28.2.1 Selection Step

There is already a built-up tree. The selection process starts at the root of the tree, which is the current state of the game. Player 1 wants to find a suitable move to maximise her chances to win. Starting at the root node, the path through the tree is selected. The path ends at the node, where there is at least one move out of the possible moves which do not have an explored node. This corresponds to the case when some – or even all – of the possible options stemming from the node have not been explored yet.

What path to take? The objective is to combine exploration with exploitation. The mechanism to select the path should favour the promising nodes but still keep an option to exploit the paths which have been so far perceived as less favourable. The multi-armed bandit problem provides a way to resolve the dilemma. In particular, Kocsis and Szepesvári (2006) proposed the procedure to employ the Upper Confidence Bound algorithm frequently used to solve the multi-armed bandit problems to form the decision to select the path in the tree. When there is a decision to make, i.e. to choose among the child nodes which have been explored and thus each of them got assigned ![images](images/c28-i0149.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>, the following quantity is calculated for every considered child node ![images](images/c28-i0150.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>:

(28.16)![equation](images/c28-math-0016.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>U</mi> <mi>C</mi> <msub> <mi>T</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfrac> <mo>+</mo> <mi>C</mi> <mo>&#183;</mo> <msqrt> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfrac> </msqrt> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c28-i0151.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the number corresponding to the parent node at which the decision is being done, and constant ![images](images/c28-i0152.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> governs the balance between exploitation – the first term, and exploration – the second term. The value of ![images](images/c28-i0153.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is a meta-parameter in the algorithm; the popular choice is ![images](images/c28-i0154.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt></mrow></math>.

The child node with the highest ![images](images/c28-i0155.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>U</mi><mi>C</mi><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is chosen in the selection step. If more than one node reaches the highest number, the node is chosen randomly with equal probability. The decision based on the formula in fact reflects the minimax algorithm. The meaning of ![images](images/c28-i0156.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> at a given point is recorded from the perspective of the player making a move. Thus, the formula makes the optimal decision for every player and thus player 1 is optimising her decision given player 2 is doing the same.

At the end of the selection step, the simulated game is at a node with at least one child node which has not been explored yet.

 

### 28.2.2 Expansion Step

The purpose of the expansion step is to extend the existing tree and include new nodes. The iteration process reaches at the end of the selection step a node which has at least one child which has not been selected before. Such a child node does not have an assigned pair ![images](images/c28-i0157.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>. The iteration progresses from the node as follows:

*   Among the child nodes which have not been visited yet, randomly choose one and extend the selection tree.

The new node is chosen uniformly as there is no preference among the unvisited nodes – or we assume a uniform prior. The new node is included in the selection tree. Using programming language, the ![images](images/c28-i0158.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> pair is initialised with 0s. This node will get assigned in last step its values ![images](images/c28-i0159.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math>.

The mechanism of the step is such that it explores new options and extends the knowledge structure – the decision tree – the algorithm is building up. Besides, the mechanism aims to expand every node fully. Namely, at a given node, there cannot be a situation where from any node there is a growing sub-tree and at the same time as there are unvisited nodes. If a specific node is promising – it is repeatedly chosen by the selection step – then all the options from the node are to be explored.

The full expansion of every node can have a disadvantage. In particular, if there is a large branching ratio, the tree will aim to progress too slowly. The selection tree being grown will be explored by moves which are deeply inferior and thus such a tree can be costly to grow. This is apparent for a game of go, for instance, where some moves are wasting of computational time. The reasonable component would be here some form of “value” function which would use heuristic rules and rule out some moves. Such an approach is taken in AlphaGo implementation of the ![images](images/c28-i0160.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> using deep neural networks. Let us omit this at this stage and follow the expansion step as outlined.

We can expand by more than one node and provide faster building up of the game tree. Even though this is possible, we have to keep in mind that our objective is not to build the full/deep selection tree. The aim is to build a knowledge about the nearest neighbourhood of the game node we want to move from. The process of building a large tree would also carry a considerable storage cost; let us recall the dimensionality of the game tree for a go. It is thus feasible to stay at expansion by one node only.

Once the new node is added into the tree and the pair ![images](images/c28-i0161.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> is initialised, the game is played out.

 

### 28.2.3 Simulation Step

The purpose of the simulation step is to finish the game from the newly expanded node. The game is simulated randomly:

*   Players are taking turns. In every turn, among all possible moves, one of the moves is chosen randomly with equal probability.

The simulation is played until the game ends. Let us assume that game is a zero-sum game, and one unit is awarded at the end:

(28.17)![equation](images/c28-math-0017.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#978;</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#978;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c28-i0162.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#978;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the award assigned to player ![images](images/c28-i0163.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>. In the game with the binary end, the number can be 0 or 1. When there is a draw as an option at the end of the game, the value of 0.5 can be assigned to both players.

The critical feature of the simulation step is that the simulation itself is not stored. Once the simulation from the newly created node is finished, only ![images](images/c28-i0164.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#978;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> are being remembered. This prevents the exhaustion of memory. During the simulation, we need to keep in memory the index of the player who makes a move and the state of the game, i.e. the arrangement of the board. As a result, the simulation step is memory efficient, and the simulation can be easily outsourced to some external resources without the need to transfer an additional amount of data. A possible option at this step is to simulate many independent games in parallel and then average ![images](images/c28-i0165.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#978;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>’s across simulations.

Once the simulation is finished, and the output of the simulated game is obtained, the iteration proceeds with the back propagation step.

 

### 28.2.4 Back Propagation Step

In the final step, the game tree is updated by the information obtained from the simulated playout. In particular, every node of the decision tree which has been chosen during the particular game is updated as follows:

(28.18)![equation](images/c28-math-0018.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8594;</mo> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

and ![images](images/c28-i0166.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is updated based on which player was making a move:

(28.19)![equation](images/c28-math-0019.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8594;</mo> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#978;</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c28-i0167.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> corresponds to the index of the player who made a move. In particular, every odd-numbered level of the tree corresponds to ![images](images/c28-i0168.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, and every even-numbered level of the tree corresponds to ![images](images/c28-i0169.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, respectively.

This step concludes one iteration of the ![images](images/c28-i0170.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>.

 

### 28.2.5 Finishing the Algorithm

The ![images](images/c28-i0171.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> algorithm is composed of many iterations. Player 1 chooses such an action which corresponds to the node with highest ![images](images/c28-i0172.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c28-i0173.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> corresponds to the index of nodes in the first level, i.e. child nodes of the root node. The decision rule at the end considers the best node as the one being chosen. The exploratory part is not employed when making a move; the move is pure exploitation.

The number of iterations is chosen based on available resources. The ![images](images/c28-i0174.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> algorithm can be interrupted anytime, and the algorithm can have dynamically set the number of iterations. For instance, the game can contain a cap on the amount of time taken to decide the move. In such a case, the ![images](images/c28-i0175.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> algorithm will try to run as many iterations as possible. Since simulated games can take a variable amount of time, such a numerical policy can be allocated resources efficiently as opposed to the fixed number of iterations. Similar policies can be adapted for variable numerical resources (CPUs or memory).

 

### 28.2.6 Remarks and Extensions

Let us make a couple of remarks about how to extend the ![images](images/c28-i0176.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> presented above. First, for some games value of every move/stone can be independent of the stones already placed. In such a setup, we can cut the number of simulations needed tremendously. Gelly and Silver (2007) proposed an extension to the algorithm called Rapid Action Value Estimation, or RAVE. This assumes that the value of a stone is independent of the state of the game. Then, the backpropagation step is changed as follows. When we are supposed to update ![images](images/c28-i0177.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> for nodes contributing to the game, we update those moves across the entire game. Namely, if player 1 placed a stone at, say, a corner and the game where she did it resulted in a win, we identify all possible games in the game tree where player 1 places such a move and update the pair ![images](images/c28-i0178.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></math> in all of them. However, it is more convenient to keep updating in the same way as we have introduced above and preferably adjust the formula for ![images](images/c28-i0179.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>U</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> as we will see below.

This extension boosts the statistics gathered by the ![images](images/c28-i0180.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>. The disadvantage of this approach is rather a strong assumption being made on the game. For the game of go, this assumption is highly unfeasible, given the game to be driven by various patterns. Further, players are introduced to the game through recognising patterns of varying complexity. The same holds for the game of chess. Since the usage of the ![images](images/c28-i0181.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> goes well beyond the world of games, this is a possible extension. In order to mimic the absolute validity of the key assumption, the formula for ![images](images/c28-i0182.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>U</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> in the Selection step can be amended to provide some flexibility:

[(28.20)](#c28.xhtml#R_c28-disp-0020)![equation](images/c28-math-0020.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>U</mi> <mi>C</mi> <msub> <mi>T</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#946;</mi> </mfenced> <mfrac> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfrac> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mfrac> <msubsup> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msubsup> <msubsup> <mi>n</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msubsup> </mfrac> <mo>+</mo> <mi>C</mi> <mo>&#183;</mo> <msqrt> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mfrac> </msqrt> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c28-i0183.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c28-i0184.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> are defined and populated as in the original ![images](images/c28-i0185.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> algorithm introduced above, ![images](images/c28-i0186.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c28-i0187.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup></mrow></math> are the total numbers of wins and the total number of games containing the given move, i.e.

(28.21) ![equation](images/c28-math-0021.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"> <msubsup> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msubsup> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="left"> <mo form="prefix">=</mo> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>s</mi> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> (28.22) ![equation](images/c28-math-0022.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"> <msubsup> <mi>n</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msubsup> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="left"> <mo form="prefix">=</mo> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>s</mi> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

with sum running over ![images](images/c28-i0188.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> of the tree which are the same.

Parameter![images](images/c28-i0189.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> introduced above is meta-parameter of the method and has to be determined separately. The parameter is problem specific and can also be a function of ![images](images/c28-i0190.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c28-i0191.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup></mrow></math>, respectively. The reasonable logic to follow is to keep ![images](images/c28-i0192.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math> large at the beginning of the simulation while slowly suppressing it towards zero as simulation progresses. This will allow us to improve statistical decisions in the initial stages of simulation while it will get marginal as more and more simulations have been run.

A further possible improvement to the ![images](images/c28-i0193.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> algorithm relates to the use of heuristics, which affects the moves either in Selection or Expansion steps mentioned above. The motivation for such an improvement is to make the simulation more efficient and potentially to cut the simulation time. In Bayesian formulation, this means that some Bayesian priors can be introduced into the formula for ![images](images/c28-i0194.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>U</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>. Alternatively, we may modify the Expansion probability. It is essential to keep in mind that such an extension should be done in a way that still allows the ![images](images/c28-i0195.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> algorithm as whole making moves, which are locally suboptimal. This is the way the algorithm can overcome the human player and find innovative game strategies.

We can roughly compare the ![images](images/c28-i0196.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> to the way humans are thinking. The human player explores the viability of a move in the game similarly as the ![images](images/c28-i0197.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>: playing forward several moves placing herself into a position of the other player and thus efficiently responding to her own moves. The best players can form strategies several stones ahead. The human brain, however, does not allow to keep in memory the full search tree and thus often only the best move in a given layer of the tree is kept in mind. The human thus builds a tree which is very narrow, not exploring all the options.

On the other hand, the human heavily relies on a heuristic. The ability of the ![images](images/c28-i0198.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> to explore the suboptimal moves presents a significant improvement against human players. The heuristic is thus what stands between the human and the computer. Moreover, this is the element AlphaGo engine and its further extensions considered and closed the gap. The computer finally got better relative to human player – at least for the game of go.

 

## 28.3 MONTE CARLO TREE SEARCH IMPLEMENTATION – TIC-TAC-TOE

In this section, we illustrate the ![images](images/c28-i0199.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> algorithm on the game tic-tac-toe. The game dates back to Roman Empire times. The rules of the tic-tac-toe are straightforward. The game is played by two players on the square board of ![images](images/c28-i0200.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>. Players are taking turns, where each player places her stone on the board in every turn. We assume that Player 1 is placing `o` and Player 2 is placing `x`. The player who places three stones in a horizontal, vertical or diagonal row wins the game. The game allows for a draw, where none of the players achieves the criteria to win while all the places on the board are covered.

The game is rather trivial as the optimal strategy from both players results in a draw. The game is, however, suitable for explanation and is easy to programme. The detailed statistical account of the game as well various extensions can be found in Beck and Beck (2008). Let us review a few numbers characterising mathematical properties of the game. The game has ![images](images/c28-i0201.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>!</mo></mrow></math> possible playouts, giving in total ![images](images/c28-i0202.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>362</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>880</mn></mrow></math>. This can be obtained because the first player has 9 possible places to place her stone, the second player only 8 possible moves. Let us point out that we do not consider symmetries. If the symmetries would be considered, the number is much lower. Namely, when symmetries are taken into account for calculations, then there are three possible initial moves: the centre, the middle of a side and a corner.

In the ![images](images/c28-i0203.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>!</mo></mrow></math> calculation, we assume that every game finishes when all 9 stones are placed. This is not true as the game may end earlier. The fastest game can end on the fifth move, assuming Player 2 is very weak. [Table 28.1](#c28.xhtml#c28-tbl-0001) captures the number of possible wins as a function of the total number of moves along with the number of draws. The table shows that there is altogether ![images](images/c28-i0204.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>255</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>168</mn></mrow></math> number of moves.

![ TABLE 28.1 The number of possible games depending on their length](images/c28-i0205.png)

 [**TABLE 28.1**](#c28.xhtml#R_c28-tbl-0001) The number of possible games depending on their length
